intro: "Hello" in Korean is 안녕하세요 (annyeonghaseyo), the polite greeting you can use with almost anyone, at any time of day. With close friends you can shorten it to 안녕 (annyeong), and on the phone Koreans answer with 여보세요 (yeoboseyo).

ways.note: The everyday safe choice for strangers, shop staff, coworkers, teachers and older people. Works morning, afternoon and night.
Hi to close friends, younger people and kids. It also means bye, so you can use it at both ends of a conversation.
Very formal. You hear it from news anchors, store staff greeting customers, in speeches and in the military.
Only for answering or starting a phone call, like "Hello?" on the phone. It is not used face to face as a greeting.

examples.context: Greeting a room full of people
Running into a friend
Answering an unknown number

tips: 안녕하세요 literally asks if you are at peace or well, but nobody treats it as a real question. It is simply "hello". Koreans often add a small bow or nod of the head when they say it, especially to older people.
Be careful with 안녕. It sounds friendly, but saying it to a stranger, a boss or someone older can come across as rude. When in doubt, use 안녕하세요.
Pronunciation tip: 안녕하세요 is said smoothly, roughly "ahn-nyoung-ha-say-yo", and the ending often rises a little and sounds cheerful.

faq.q: How do you say hi casually in Korean?
faq.a: Say 안녕 (annyeong). It is the casual hi you use with friends and people younger than you.

faq.q: Is annyeonghaseyo polite enough for older people?
faq.a: Yes. 안녕하세요 is polite and fine for almost everyone, including elders. 안녕하십니까 is even more formal and is mostly used in very formal settings.

faq.q: How do Koreans say hello on the phone?
faq.a: They say 여보세요 (yeoboseyo). It is only used on the phone, not in person.

intro: "Goodbye" in Korean is 안녕히 가세요 (annyeonghi gaseyo) when the other person is leaving, or 안녕히 계세요 (annyeonghi gyeseyo) when you are the one leaving. With friends, a simple 안녕 (annyeong) or 잘 가 (jal ga) is enough.

ways.note: Literally "go in peace". Say it to someone who is leaving while you stay, like a guest leaving your home.
Literally "stay in peace". Say it when you are leaving and the other person stays, like when you walk out of a shop.
Bye to friends and younger people. The same word as casual hi.
"Go well". Casual bye to a friend who is leaving.
A very formal goodbye, used by staff to customers or in formal announcements.

examples.context: Walking out of a shop
Seeing a guest off at the door
A friend heading home

tips: The main thing to remember is who is leaving. If they go, say 가세요 (go). If you go, say 계세요 (stay). If you both walk off in different directions, both people say 안녕히 가세요.
Mixing them up is the most common beginner mistake, but people will still understand you. If you forget, a polite bow and 안녕히 가세요 is never strange to the person leaving.
In text messages friends often write ㅂㅂ, short for 바이바이 (bye-bye).

faq.q: What is the difference between annyeonghi gaseyo and annyeonghi gyeseyo?
faq.a: 안녕히 가세요 is said to the person leaving, and 안녕히 계세요 is said to the person staying. Think of it as "go well" versus "stay well".

faq.q: How do you say bye casually in Korean?
faq.a: Say 안녕 (annyeong) or 잘 가 (jal ga) to friends. Many people also just say 바이바이 (bai bai).

faq.q: What if both people are leaving?
faq.a: Both people say 안녕히 가세요 (annyeonghi gaseyo), since you are each going somewhere.

intro: "Good morning" in Korean is 좋은 아침이에요 (joeun achimieyo), or 좋은 아침 (joeun achim) with friends. In real life, though, most Koreans simply say 안녕하세요 (annyeonghaseyo) in the morning, and families often ask if you slept well instead.

ways.note: A friendly, polite "good morning". Fine with coworkers or acquaintances, though it sounds a bit like a translation of the English.
Casual and cheerful. Common between friends, couples, in texts and on social media.
What most people actually say in the morning at work, school or a shop. Korean has no time-specific greeting that everyone uses.
"Did you sleep well?" Said as a question to family, a partner or close friends. The polite form is 잘 잤어요 (jal jasseoyo).
"Did you sleep well?" with extra respect, for parents, grandparents and older people. Said as a question.

examples.context: Arriving at the office
A morning text to a partner
Greeting grandma at breakfast

tips: Korean doesn't really split greetings by time of day the way English does. 안녕하세요 works from morning to night, so you will never be wrong using it.
좋은 아침 has become popular among younger people, in texts and on radio or social media. It is warm and casual, but you would rarely say it to a boss or an elderly person.
At home, the usual morning greeting is about sleep: 잘 잤어? to a younger family member or partner, and 안녕히 주무셨어요? to parents or grandparents. 주무시다 is the respectful word for "sleep".

faq.q: Do Koreans actually say good morning?
faq.a: Sometimes. 좋은 아침 is used casually, but most people just say 안녕하세요 in the morning, or ask if you slept well.

faq.q: How do you say good morning to your parents in Korean?
faq.a: The respectful way is 안녕히 주무셨어요? (annyeonghi jumusyeosseoyo), which means "Did you sleep well?"

faq.q: Is joeun achim polite?
faq.a: 좋은 아침 is casual. Add 이에요 to make 좋은 아침이에요 for a polite version.

intro: "Good night" in Korean is 잘 자요 (jal jayo), which literally means "sleep well". With friends or a partner say 잘 자 (jal ja), and to parents, grandparents or anyone older use 안녕히 주무세요 (annyeonghi jumuseyo).

ways.note: To a partner, close friend, younger sibling or child. The most common good night in texts.
Polite good night to someone around your age who isn't a close friend.
Respectful good night for parents, grandparents, teachers and older people. 주무시다 is the honorific word for sleep.
"Have good dreams." A sweet add-on after 잘 자. Polite form: 좋은 꿈 꿔요 (joeun kkum kkwoyo).
The English "good night" written in Korean. Common in texts between friends and couples.

examples.context: Saying good night to a partner
Before bed at your parents' home
Ending a late phone call

tips: Never say 잘 자 to an older relative or your boss. Use 안녕히 주무세요. Using the honorific 주무시다 instead of plain 자다 is what makes it respectful.
잘 자 is short, so friends often stretch it in texts as 잘 자~ or add 좋은 꿈 꿔 (sweet dreams).
Pronunciation: 잘 자 sounds like "jal ja" with a soft j, and the ㄹ in 잘 is a light l sound.

faq.q: How do you say good night to your parents in Korean?
faq.a: Say 안녕히 주무세요 (annyeonghi jumuseyo). It is the respectful way to wish someone older a good night.

faq.q: What does jal ja mean?
faq.a: 잘 자 means "sleep well". It is the casual way to say good night to friends, a partner or someone younger.

faq.q: How do you say sweet dreams in Korean?
faq.a: Say 좋은 꿈 꿔 (joeun kkum kkwo) casually, or 좋은 꿈 꿔요 (joeun kkum kkwoyo) politely.

intro: "How are you" in Korean is usually 잘 지냈어요? (jal jinaesseoyo), which means "Have you been well?" Koreans don't ask "how are you" every time they say hello, so this is mostly used when you haven't seen someone for a while.

ways.note: "Have you been well?" Said as a question to someone you haven't seen in a while. The most natural polite choice.
The same question for friends and younger people, said with a rising tone.
"Are you doing well?" when said as a question. Also the usual answer: "I'm doing well."
"How are you getting along?" Correct and polite, but it sounds a little textbook. Said as a question.
"Have you eaten?" A caring, everyday way to check on a friend or family member. Said as a question.

examples.context: Meeting a friend after months
Greeting a former teacher
Calling a friend around lunchtime

tips: In English "How are you?" is part of hello. In Korean, 안녕하세요 already does that job, so adding 잘 지냈어요? to a coworker you saw yesterday would sound odd. Save it for people you haven't seen in a while.
To answer, say 네, 잘 지냈어요 (ne, jal jinaesseoyo), "Yes, I've been well", or 잘 지내요 (jal jinaeyo), "I'm doing well". You can ask back with 잘 지냈어요?
밥 먹었어? is not really about food. It is a warm way of saying "I care about you", and a simple 응, 먹었어 (eung, meogeosseo), "Yeah, I ate", is a fine reply.

faq.q: How do you answer how are you in Korean?
faq.a: Say 잘 지내요 (jal jinaeyo), "I'm doing well", or 네, 잘 지냈어요 (ne, jal jinaesseoyo), "Yes, I've been well".

faq.q: Is eotteoke jinaeseyo natural?
faq.a: It is correct and polite, but Koreans more often say 잘 지냈어요? or 잘 지내세요?

faq.q: Why do Koreans ask if you've eaten?
faq.a: 밥 먹었어? is a friendly check-in that shows care, a bit like "How's it going?" in English.

intro: "Nice to meet you" in Korean is 만나서 반가워요 (mannaseo bangawoyo), or 만나서 반갑습니다 (mannaseo bangapseumnida) in formal settings. With people your age or younger you can just say 반가워 (bangawo).

ways.note: Friendly and polite. Good for most first meetings with people you don't know well.
Formal. Use it at work, in interviews, or when meeting someone much older.
A shorter formal version, very common when introducing yourself to a group.
Casual, for meeting a friend's friend or someone younger. Also means "good to see you".
Very formal: "I am meeting you for the first time." Often said with a bow when meeting someone important.

examples.context: First day at a new job
Meeting a friend's friend
Meeting a language exchange partner

tips: Koreans often follow it with their name and 잘 부탁드립니다 (jal butakdeurimnida), which roughly means "I look forward to getting along with you". It is very common at work and school.
반가워요 literally means "I'm glad to see you", so you can also use it when you see someone again after a while, not just the first time.
To say "Nice to meet you too", add 저도 (jeodo, "me too") politely: 저도 반가워요. Casually it is 나도 반가워.

faq.q: How do you say nice to meet you too in Korean?
faq.a: Say 저도 반가워요 (jeodo bangawoyo) politely, or 나도 반가워 (nado bangawo) casually.

faq.q: What is the difference between bangawoyo and bangapseumnida?
faq.a: Both mean "glad to meet you". 반가워요 is polite and friendly, while 반갑습니다 is more formal.

faq.q: What does cheoeum boepgetseumnida mean?
faq.a: 처음 뵙겠습니다 is a very formal way to say "It's my first time meeting you", used like "Pleased to meet you".

intro: "See you later" in Korean is 나중에 봐요 (najunge bwayo), or 나중에 봐 (najunge bwa) with friends. If you will see the person again later the same day, say 이따 봐 (itta bwa) instead.

ways.note: "See you later" to friends, with no set time.
The polite version for people you aren't close with.
"See you in a bit." Only when you will meet again later today.
Polite version of "see you in a bit", later the same day.
"See you next time" to someone older or senior. 봬요 is the humble form of 봐요.
"Let's meet again." Warm and friendly, often at the end of a first meeting.

examples.context: Heading to class before lunch
Leaving a meeting with a senior coworker
Saying bye after a first meetup

tips: 이따 means later today, and 나중에 means some time later with no fixed time. Saying 이따 봐 when you won't see them today can confuse people.
봬요 (from 뵈다) is a humble form you use toward someone you respect. Many Koreans misspell it as 뵈요, but the correct spelling is 봬요.
Friends also say 담에 봐 (dame bwa), a spoken shortening of 다음에 봐.

faq.q: What is the difference between itta and najunge?
faq.a: 이따 means later today, while 나중에 means later at some unspecified time.

faq.q: Is bwayo or bwaeyo more polite?
faq.a: 봬요 is more respectful because it uses the humble verb 뵈다. Use it with older people, teachers and bosses.

intro: "See you tomorrow" in Korean is 내일 봐요 (naeil bwayo), or 내일 봐 (naeil bwa) with friends. To a boss, teacher or someone older, say 내일 봬요 (naeil bwaeyo) or the formal 내일 뵙겠습니다 (naeil boepgetseumnida).

ways.note: To friends, classmates and younger people.
Polite and friendly, for coworkers around your age or people you aren't close to.
More respectful, for a teacher, boss or someone older. 봬요 is the humble form.
Formal and respectful. Common at work when speaking to a manager or client.
"Meet you tomorrow", when you have actual plans to meet.

examples.context: Leaving school
Leaving the office
Confirming a date

tips: The word 내일 (naeil, tomorrow) can be swapped for other times: 다음 주에 봐요 (see you next week), 월요일에 봐요 (see you Monday).
Write 봬요, not 뵈요. It is one of the most common spelling mistakes even among Koreans.

faq.q: How do you say see you tomorrow politely in Korean?
faq.a: Say 내일 봬요 (naeil bwaeyo), or 내일 뵙겠습니다 (naeil boepgetseumnida) in formal situations.

faq.q: How do you say see you next week in Korean?
faq.a: Say 다음 주에 봐요 (daeum jue bwayo), or 다음 주에 봐 (daeum jue bwa) to friends.

intro: "Welcome" in Korean is 어서 오세요 (eoseo oseyo), which you will hear every time you walk into a shop or restaurant. For signs, events and speeches Koreans use 환영합니다 (hwanyeonghamnida), and at home with friends simply 어서 와 (eoseo wa).

ways.note: "Come on in." Said by shop and restaurant staff, and by hosts welcoming guests.
"We welcome you." For signs, events, ceremonies and formal speeches.
A softer, polite "you're welcome here", for a new member of a class or club.
To a friend, partner or younger family member arriving at your place.
Very formal, used in hotels, department stores and high-end restaurants.

examples.context: A restaurant greeting a customer
A banner at the airport
A friend arriving at your door

tips: When staff say 어서 오세요, you don't need to answer. A smile, a nod or 안녕하세요 is plenty.
This page is about welcoming someone. "You're welcome" after a thank you is different: Koreans say 아니에요 (anieyo) or 천만에요 (cheonmaneyo).
어서 literally means "quickly", but here it just adds warmth, like "come right in".

faq.q: How do you say welcome to Korea in Korean?
faq.a: Say 한국에 오신 것을 환영합니다 (hanguge osin geoseul hwanyeonghamnida).

faq.q: What should I say back when a shop says eoseo oseyo?
faq.a: Nothing is required. You can nod, smile or say 안녕하세요.

faq.q: Is welcome the same as you're welcome in Korean?
faq.a: No. For "you're welcome" after thanks, say 아니에요 (anieyo) or 천만에요 (cheonmaneyo).

intro: "Long time no see" in Korean is 오랜만이에요 (oraenmanieyo), or 오랜만이야 (oraenmaniya) with friends. It literally means "It's been a long time", and is usually followed by 잘 지냈어요? (Have you been well?).

ways.note: To friends and younger people. Often with 진짜 (really) or 와 (wow) in front.
The polite everyday version for coworkers, acquaintances and older people.
Formal, for business contacts or someone much older.
The full, slightly old-fashioned form of 오랜만이에요. Same meaning.
"Have you been well?" Said as a question, and the natural follow-up.

examples.context: Bumping into an old friend
Visiting a former teacher
examples.en: Teacher, it's been such a long time.

examples.context: Texting a friend you haven't seen in months
examples.en: Let's grab a meal, it's been a while.

tips: The spelling is 오랜만, not 오랫만. Even Koreans mix this up.
오랜만에 (with 에) means "for the first time in a long time", as in 오랜만에 영화 봤어 (I watched a movie for the first time in ages).

faq.q: How do you reply to long time no see in Korean?
faq.a: Repeat it back, 네, 오랜만이에요 (ne, oraenmanieyo), and ask 잘 지냈어요? (Have you been well?).

faq.q: Is it oraenman or oraetman?
faq.a: The correct spelling is 오랜만 (oraenman).

intro: "Take care" in Korean is 잘 지내세요 (jal jinaeseyo) when you won't see someone for a while. When someone is heading home, Koreans say 조심히 가세요 (josimhi gaseyo), "get home safely", and for health they say 몸 조심하세요 (mom josimhaseyo).

ways.note: "Be well." For a goodbye before a long time apart, like the end of a trip or a job.
The casual version for friends and younger people.
"Go carefully." Said to someone leaving, especially at night or in bad weather.
"Get home safe." Very common between friends at the end of a night out.
"Take care of your health." For someone who is sick, tired or traveling.
"Stay healthy." A warm send-off, especially to older people.

examples.context: A friend leaving late at night
A coworker moving to another city
A friend who has been feeling sick

tips: There is no single word for "take care". Pick the phrase that fits: leaving for the night (조심히 가세요), parting for a long time (잘 지내세요), or worried about health (몸 조심하세요).
조심히 들어가 uses 들어가다, "go in", because you are going back into your home. Koreans say it to friends and partners all the time.

faq.q: How do you say get home safe in Korean?
faq.a: Say 조심히 들어가 (josimhi deureoga) to friends, or 조심히 들어가세요 (josimhi deureogaseyo) politely.

faq.q: How do you say take care of yourself in Korean?
faq.a: Say 몸 조심하세요 (mom josimhaseyo), or 몸 조심해 (mom josimhae) casually.

intro: "Have a nice day" in Korean is 좋은 하루 보내세요 (joeun haru bonaeseyo), literally "spend a good day". With friends say 좋은 하루 보내 (joeun haru bonae).

ways.note: The standard polite way. Fine for shop staff, coworkers, emails and messages.
For friends, a partner or younger people.
Very common in shops and customer service. Some people say it is not strictly correct grammar, but you will hear it everywhere.
"Have a fun day." A little more cheerful, good for days off.
Formal, for business emails, announcements or service staff.

examples.context: A cashier to a customer
A morning text to a friend
examples.en: Have a good day today too!

examples.context: Ending a group chat message

tips: Swap 하루 (day) for other times: 좋은 주말 보내세요 (have a nice weekend), 좋은 저녁 보내세요 (have a nice evening).
When leaving a shop or taxi, many Koreans say 수고하세요 (sugohaseyo), "keep up the good work". It is friendly to staff, but avoid saying it to your boss or someone much older.

faq.q: How do you say have a nice weekend in Korean?
faq.a: Say 좋은 주말 보내세요 (joeun jumal bonaeseyo), or 주말 잘 보내세요 (jumal jal bonaeseyo).

faq.q: Is joeun haru doeseyo correct?
faq.a: It is widely used, especially in shops, but some see it as awkward grammar. 좋은 하루 보내세요 is always safe.

intro: "Thank you" in Korean is 감사합니다 (gamsahamnida), a polite, formal thank you that works with almost anyone. With close friends you can say 고마워 (gomawo), and in between there are softer everyday forms like 고마워요 (gomawoyo).

ways.note: The safest choice. Use it with shop staff, strangers, teachers, coworkers and anyone older.
Just as polite as 감사합니다 and used in the same situations. It is built on a native Korean word, so some people feel it sounds a little warmer.
Polite but softer and friendlier than 감사합니다. Good for everyday chats with acquaintances.
A warm, polite thank you for people you know but are not very close to, or for someone a little younger.
For close friends, younger siblings and partners. Do not use it with strangers or anyone older than you.
"Thank you very much." Add 정말 (really) to any of the forms above to make it stronger.

examples.context: Thanking a friend who helped you move
Receiving a gift from a coworker
examples.en: Thank you so much for the gift.

examples.context: Thanking guests for coming to your party

tips: 감사합니다 and 고맙습니다 mean the same thing and are equally polite. 감사 comes from Chinese characters, while 고맙다 is a native Korean word. Use whichever feels easier to say.
감사합니다 is pronounced "gam-sa-ham-ni-da". The ㅂ in 합 is spoken like an m because the next sound is ㄴ, so it is not "hap-ni-da".
When in doubt, go more polite. Saying 고마워 to a shop clerk or someone older can sound rude, but 감사합니다 never will.

faq.q: What is the difference between kamsahamnida and gomapseumnida?
faq.a: Nothing important. Both are polite, formal ways to say thank you and can be used in the same situations. Kamsahamnida (감사합니다) is a little more common in shops and on TV.

faq.q: How do you say "thank you very much" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 정말 감사합니다 (jeongmal gamsahamnida) or 대단히 감사합니다 (daedanhi gamsahamnida), which is very formal and often used in speeches.

faq.q: How do you reply to thank you in Korean?
faq.a: Koreans usually say 아니에요 (anieyo), which means something like "not at all". With friends, 아니야 (aniya) or a simple smile works too.

intro: "Sorry" in Korean is 죄송합니다 (joesonghamnida), a formal, respectful apology you can use with strangers, customers and anyone older. With friends you would say 미안해 (mianhae), which is casual.

ways.note: The most respectful apology. Use it with elders, bosses, teachers, customers and strangers.
Still respectful but a little softer. Common in everyday situations like bumping into someone.
Formal, but less humble than 죄송합니다. You hear it from older people to younger people, or in announcements.
Polite and gentle. Good for people you know who are about your age or younger.
For close friends, partners and younger siblings.
A quick "sorry" or "my bad" between close friends.

examples.context: Arriving late to a meeting with your boss
Apologizing to a friend after an argument
Stepping on someone's foot on the bus

tips: 죄송 is humbler than 미안. If the person is older than you or you are not sure, choose 죄송합니다 or 죄송해요.
죄송한데요 (joesonghandeyo), "sorry, but...", is a polite way to start a request or interrupt someone, a bit like "excuse me" in English.
Korean "sorry" is an apology. To show sympathy for someone's bad news, Koreans use different words, so do not use 미안해 to mean "I'm sorry to hear that".

faq.q: What is the difference between mianhae and joesonghamnida?
faq.a: Mianhae (미안해) is casual and used with close friends or younger people. Joesonghamnida (죄송합니다) is formal and humble, used with elders, bosses and strangers.

faq.q: How do you answer when someone says sorry in Korean?
faq.a: Say 괜찮아요 (gwaenchanayo), "it's okay". With friends, 괜찮아 (gwaenchana) is enough.

intro: "Excuse me" in Korean is 저기요 (jeogiyo) when you want to get someone's attention, such as a server or a stranger. Korean uses different words for other meanings: 잠시만요 (jamsimanyo) to get past people, and 실례합니다 (sillyehamnida) when you interrupt or enter a room.

ways.note: To get attention: calling a server, or stopping a stranger to ask something. Literally "over there".
To squeeze past people in a crowd or get off a busy subway. Literally "just a moment".
When interrupting, entering an office or someone's home, or passing in front of someone. Literally "I am being rude".
"Excuse me, but..." A polite way to start a question to a stranger.
After bumping into someone or making a small mistake, Koreans usually apologize instead of saying "excuse me".

examples.context: Calling a server in a restaurant
examples.en: Excuse me, could we get some water?

examples.context: Getting off a crowded subway
Asking a stranger for directions
examples.en: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

tips: In Korean restaurants it is normal to call out 저기요 or 여기요 (yeogiyo, "over here") to get a server's attention. Many tables also have a call button.
Pick the word by the situation, not by the English. Getting attention is 저기요, getting past is 잠시만요, and interrupting is 실례합니다.
In a crowd, many people say nothing at all and just move through. A quick 잠시만요 is still polite and appreciated.

faq.q: How do you call a waiter in Korean?
faq.a: Raise your hand a little and say 저기요 (jeogiyo) or 여기요 (yeogiyo). This is normal and not rude in Korea.

faq.q: Is sillyehamnida the same as jeogiyo?
faq.a: No. 저기요 calls someone's attention. 실례합니다 (sillyehamnida) apologizes for interrupting or intruding, for example when you knock and enter a room.

intro: "Please" in Korean is usually 주세요 (juseyo), added to the end of a request, as in 물 주세요 (mul juseyo, "water, please"). Korean has no single word that works exactly like English "please", so politeness comes from how you end the sentence.

ways.note: "Please give me" or "please do it for me". Put it after a noun (커피 주세요) or after a verb (기다려 주세요).
A small softener, like "please" or "a bit". 물 좀 주세요 sounds gentler than 물 주세요.
"I ask you a favor." A formal way to say please when you ask someone to do something for you.
A softer, everyday way to ask a favor.
"Please, I'm counting on you" to a close friend.
"Please!" when begging or pleading. Too strong for ordinary requests.

examples.context: Ordering at a cafe
Asking a passerby to take your photo
examples.en: Could you take a photo for us, please?

examples.context: Begging a friend to come with you

tips: To ask someone to do something, use the verb plus 주세요: 기다려 주세요 (please wait), 도와주세요 (please help). This is the most useful pattern for beginners.
제발 is for pleading, like "please, I'm begging you". Using it when ordering food would sound strange.
좀 is tiny but powerful. Koreans add it to requests all the time to sound softer.

faq.q: Does Korean have a word for please?
faq.a: Not one single word. Most of the time you end a request with 주세요 (juseyo), and you can add 좀 (jom) to soften it.

faq.q: What does jebal mean?
faq.a: 제발 (jebal) means "please" in the sense of begging or pleading, for example 제발 가지 마 ("please don't go").

faq.q: How do you say "yes, please" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 네, 주세요 (ne, juseyo), which means "yes, please give it to me".

intro: "You're welcome" in Korean is most often 아니에요 (anieyo), which literally means "it's not (anything)". The textbook phrase 천만에요 (cheonmaneyo) is correct, but in daily life Koreans usually brush off thanks in a humbler way.

ways.note: The most natural everyday reply to thank you. Like saying "oh, not at all".
The textbook "you're welcome". Correct, but it can sound a little stiff in casual conversation.
"It's nothing." Humble and friendly.
"It's fine." Often added after 아니에요.
"Nah, it's nothing" to a friend or younger person.
Short for "what for?", a casual "don't mention it" between friends.

examples.context: A friend thanks you for buying lunch
A stranger thanks you for holding the door
An older neighbor thanks you for help

tips: Koreans tend to deflect thanks rather than accept it. Saying 아니에요 shows modesty, which is why it is more common than 천만에요.
Do not confuse 아니에요 here with "no". In this situation it means "it was nothing", not a refusal.
Sometimes people reply with a small nod, a smile, or a simple 네 (ne). That is fine too.

faq.q: Do Koreans actually say cheonmaneyo?
faq.a: They know it and it is correct, but in daily conversation 아니에요 (anieyo) or 별거 아니에요 (byeolgeo anieyo) is much more common.

faq.q: What is a casual way to say you're welcome in Korean?
faq.a: With friends, say 아니야 (aniya) or 뭘 (mwol). Both mean something like "don't mention it".

intro: "Yes" in Korean is 네 (ne), the polite yes you can use with anyone. 예 (ye) is a slightly more formal version, and with close friends you can say 응 (eung).

ways.note: The everyday polite yes. Safe with everyone.
A slightly more formal yes. Common in workplaces, the military, or when speaking to elders.
"Yeah" for close friends, partners and younger people.
A very relaxed "yeah" or "uh-huh" between close friends.
"Sure" or "okay" when agreeing to a suggestion.
"That's right." Use it to confirm something is correct.

examples.context: Confirming an order on the phone
A teacher calls your name in class
A friend asks if you have eaten

tips: 네 is also used to show you are listening, like "uh-huh", and 네? with a rising tone means "pardon?" or "what?".
Be careful with negative questions. If someone asks 안 먹었어요? ("You didn't eat?"), answering 네 means "Right, I didn't eat". Korean yes agrees with the statement.
네 sounds close to "neh". Some people hear it as "deh" because Korean ㄴ is soft.

faq.q: Is yes in Korean ne or ye?
faq.a: Both. 네 (ne) is the everyday polite yes, and 예 (ye) is a little more formal. You can use 네 almost everywhere.

faq.q: Why do Koreans say ne so often?
faq.a: 네 is used not only for yes but also to show you are listening and to acknowledge what someone said, so you hear it many times in a conversation.

intro: "No" in Korean is 아니요 (aniyo), the polite no you can use with anyone. With friends you can just say 아니 (ani), and in speech 아니요 is often shortened to 아뇨 (anyo).

ways.note: The standard polite no. Safe with everyone.
A shorter spoken form of 아니요. Very common in conversation.
"No" or "nope" to friends and younger people.
"No, it isn't" or "not at all". Used to deny something or to brush off thanks.
"No thanks, I'm fine." The polite way to turn down an offer.
"I don't want to." A strong, direct refusal between close people.

examples.context: Turning down a plastic bag at a store
A friend asks if you are upset
Correcting someone who guessed your nationality

tips: To refuse food, gifts or offers politely, Koreans often say 괜찮아요 rather than a plain no.
With negative questions, Korean no disagrees with the statement. If someone asks 안 바빠요? ("You're not busy?"), answering 아니요 means "No, I am busy".
You may see 아니오 on forms, but when you answer someone, the correct spelling is 아니요.

faq.q: What is the difference between aniyo and anieyo?
faq.a: 아니요 (aniyo) is the answer word "no". 아니에요 (anieyo) means "it is not" and is used to deny a fact, like 제 거 아니에요 ("it's not mine"), or to reply to thanks.

faq.q: How do you say "no thank you" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 괜찮아요 (gwaenchanayo), which means "I'm fine". You can add 아니요 before it: 아니요, 괜찮아요.

intro: "Okay" in Korean is 알겠어요 (algesseoyo) when you mean "okay, got it", and with friends you can say 알았어 (arasseo). For "it's okay" or "I'm okay", Koreans use 괜찮아요 (gwaenchanayo) instead.

ways.note: "Okay, I understand" when agreeing to a request or instruction.
"Understood." Used at work, with customers, or with elders.
"Okay, got it" to friends, partners and younger people.
"Sounds good" when agreeing to a plan.
"Okay" or "sure" to a friend's suggestion.
"It's okay" or "I'm okay". Also used as a question: 괜찮아요? ("Are you okay?")

examples.context: Your manager gives you a task
A friend suggests meeting at seven
Someone trips in front of you

tips: Koreans do say 오케이 (okei) in casual speech, and in texts you will see ㅇㅋ. It is fine with friends but sounds too casual for elders or work.
알겠어요 and 괜찮아요 are both "okay" in English but not interchangeable. 알겠어요 means "I got it", while 괜찮아요 means "it's fine" or "I'm fine".
알았어요 (arasseoyo) is also common and polite, but 알겠어요 can sound a little softer.

faq.q: Do Koreans say okay?
faq.a: Yes, 오케이 (okei) is used casually, especially by younger people. In polite situations, 알겠어요 (algesseoyo) or 네 (ne) is better.

faq.q: How do you ask "are you okay?" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 괜찮아요? (gwaenchanayo?) with a rising tone. To a friend, 괜찮아? (gwaenchana?).

intro: "I don't know" in Korean is 모르겠어요 (moreugesseoyo), a polite and soft way to say it. With friends you can say 몰라 (molla).

ways.note: Polite and gentle. Sounds like "I'm not sure". The best choice for most situations.
"I'm not really sure." Even softer and very common.
For work, customers, or speaking to someone much older.
A plain "I don't know". Polite, but can sound a bit blunt depending on tone.
"Dunno" to friends. Said sharply, it can sound like "I don't care".
"Well..." or "Hmm, I'm not sure" when you need time to think.

examples.context: A tourist asks you for directions
A friend asks what you want to eat
Your boss asks about a schedule

tips: 모르겠어요 sounds softer than 몰라요 because the -겠- part makes it feel like "I can't say" rather than a flat "I don't know".
몰라 is very common between friends, but in an argument it can sound dismissive, like "whatever".
The base verb is 모르다 (to not know). Korean has a separate verb for not knowing, so you do not need a word for "not".

faq.q: What is the difference between molla and moreugesseoyo?
faq.a: 몰라 (molla) is casual and short. 모르겠어요 (moreugesseoyo) is polite and softer, so use it with anyone you are not close to.

faq.q: How do you say "I'm not sure" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 잘 모르겠어요 (jal moreugesseoyo). It is polite and very natural.

intro: "I understand" in Korean is 알겠어요 (algesseoyo) when you mean "got it" after an instruction or explanation. When you mean you understand someone's feelings or a difficult idea, Koreans use 이해해요 (ihaehaeyo).

ways.note: "Got it" or "I see". The everyday way to show you understood.
"Understood." Used at work, with customers, or with elders.
"Got it" to friends and younger people.
"I understood (it)." For an explanation, lesson or idea.
"I understand" in the sense of empathy, like "I get why you feel that way".
"I know what you mean."

examples.context: Your teacher explains a grammar point
A friend tells you why they are upset
Your manager explains a new rule

tips: 알다 means "to know", and 알겠어요 is how Koreans say "got it". 이해하다 means "to understand" in a deeper sense, such as understanding a concept or a person.
To show you are following someone's explanation, Koreans often just say 네 or 아, 네 ("ah, yes") as they listen.
In casual speech, 네 (your) is often pronounced 니 (ni) so it does not sound like 네 (yes).

faq.q: What is the difference between algesseoyo and ihaehaeyo?
faq.a: 알겠어요 (algesseoyo) means "got it" and is used for instructions and information. 이해해요 (ihaehaeyo) means you understand an idea or someone's situation.

faq.q: What does arasseo mean?
faq.a: 알았어 (arasseo) is a casual "okay, got it". You will hear it a lot between friends and in dramas.

intro: "I don't understand" in Korean is 이해가 안 돼요 (ihaega an dwaeyo), a polite way to say something does not make sense to you. If you simply did not catch what someone said, 못 알아들었어요 (mot aradeureosseoyo) is more natural.

ways.note: "I don't understand (it)." For an idea, explanation or situation that does not make sense.
The formal version, for work or speaking to elders.
To friends. Can also mean "I can't believe it" when something seems unreasonable.
"I didn't catch that." When someone spoke too fast or you did not hear the words.
"What does it mean?" Asked as a question about a word or phrase.
"I'm not sure." A gentle way to say you don't follow.

examples.context: Asking your teacher for help in class
Someone speaks to you very quickly
Seeing a new slang word online

tips: Use 이해가 안 돼요 for ideas, and 못 알아들었어요 for words you did not hear or catch. Language learners usually need the second one more.
이해가 안 돼 can also express disbelief, like "I just don't get why she did that". You will hear this often in dramas.
Koreans are usually happy to repeat. Adding 천천히 말해 주세요 (please speak slowly) helps a lot.

faq.q: How do you say "I don't understand Korean"?
faq.a: Say 한국어 잘 못해요 (hangugeo jal motaeyo), "I don't speak Korean well". This is the most natural way to explain.

faq.q: How do you ask what a word means in Korean?
faq.a: Say the word and then 무슨 뜻이에요? (museun tteusieyo?), "what does it mean?"

intro: "Wait" in Korean is 잠깐만요 (jamkkanmanyo), a polite "just a moment". With friends you can say 잠깐만 (jamkkanman), and to ask someone to wait for you, use 기다려 주세요 (gidaryeo juseyo).

ways.note: "Just a moment." Polite and useful almost anywhere.
"Wait" or "hold on" to friends.
Same meaning as 잠깐만요 but a little more formal. Common from shop and phone staff.
"Please wait (for me)." When you need someone to wait a while.
"Please wait a moment." Very common in restaurants, shops and on the phone.
"Wait!" A direct command. Fine with close friends but can sound bossy.

examples.context: A friend starts walking off without you
A restaurant server asks you to wait
Looking for something while on the phone
examples.en: Hold on, I'm looking for it now.

tips: 잠깐 and 잠시 both mean "a short moment". 잠시 sounds a little more formal, which is why staff and announcements use it.
기다려 on its own is an order. To someone older or a stranger, always say 기다려 주세요.
잠깐만요 is also handy for squeezing past people, much like "excuse me".

faq.q: What is the difference between jamkkanman and gidaryeo?
faq.a: 잠깐만 (jamkkanman) means "just a moment" or "hold on". 기다려 (gidaryeo) is the verb "wait" used as a command, so it is stronger.

faq.q: How do you say "wait for me" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 기다려 줘 (gidaryeo jwo) to a friend, or 기다려 주세요 (gidaryeo juseyo) politely.

intro: "What's your name?" in Korean is 이름이 뭐예요? (ireumi mwoyeyo?), a polite question you can ask most people your age. For someone older or a customer, use the honorific 성함이 어떻게 되세요? (seonghami eotteoke doeseyo?).

ways.note: The standard polite question. Good for classmates, new friends and people around your age.
Softer and more respectful. Literally "how does your name go?"
Very respectful, using the honorific word for name. Used with elders and by staff with customers.
To children or people clearly younger than you.
An even more relaxed version, dropping the particle.

examples.context: Meeting a new classmate
A hotel clerk checking you in
Talking to a child at the park

tips: Koreans avoid using "you" with people they just met, so the polite question simply says "name is what?" without a word for "your".
성함 is the honorific word for name. Never use it about yourself. For your own name, always use 이름.
Do not use 너 (you) with adults you do not know well. It is only for close friends and younger people.

faq.q: How do you answer "what's your name" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 제 이름은 ___예요 (je ireumeun ___yeyo) if your name ends in a vowel, or ___이에요 (___ieyo) if it ends in a consonant.

faq.q: What is the most polite way to ask someone's name in Korean?
faq.a: 성함이 어떻게 되세요? (seonghami eotteoke doeseyo?) is the most respectful. Use it with elders, customers and anyone senior.

intro: "My name is" in Korean is 제 이름은 ___예요 (je ireumeun ___yeyo), for example 제 이름은 민지예요 (My name is Minji). A shorter and very common way is 저는 ___예요 (jeoneun ___yeyo), "I am ___".

ways.note: "My name is Minji." Use 예요 after a name ending in a vowel, 이에요 after a consonant.
"I'm Minji." Shorter and very natural for introductions.
"I am called Minji." Formal, good for interviews, presentations and business.
"My name is Minji" in formal speech.
To children or people younger than you.
"I'm Minji." Casual and short.

examples.context: Introducing yourself in class
Starting a job interview
Meeting a friend's friend

tips: Pick the ending by the last sound of your name. A name ending in a vowel takes 예요 (제임스예요, 민지예요). A name ending in a consonant takes 이에요 (수진이에요). The same goes for 라고 and 이라고.
Korean names put the family name first: in 김수진, 김 (Kim) is the family name.
Use 저 and 제 (humble "I" and "my") with anyone you are not close to. 나 and 내 are casual.

faq.q: How do you introduce yourself formally in Korean?
faq.a: Say 안녕하세요, 저는 ___라고 합니다 (annyeonghaseyo, jeoneun ___rago hamnida). Use 이라고 if your name ends in a consonant.

faq.q: Should I say jeoneun or je ireumeun?
faq.a: Both are correct. 저는 ___예요 (I am ___) is shorter and more common in conversation.

intro: "I don't speak Korean" in Korean is 한국어 못해요 (hangugeo motaeyo), which literally means "I can't do Korean". If you know a little, 한국어 잘 못해요 (hangugeo jal motaeyo), "I don't speak Korean well", is more natural and modest.

ways.note: "I can't speak Korean." Clear and polite.
"I don't speak Korean well." The most common thing learners say.
The same meaning, using 한국말, a more conversational word for the Korean language.
Formal, for official or business situations.
To friends or younger people.
"Do you speak English?" Asked as a question to follow up.

examples.context: A stranger asks you for directions
examples.en: Sorry, I don't speak Korean well.

examples.context: Asking a shop clerk for help
examples.en: Do you happen to speak English?

examples.context: Telling a Korean friend about your level

tips: Use 못 (can't), not 안 (don't). 한국어 안 해요 would sound like you choose not to speak Korean.
Koreans are often delighted when foreigners try, and may say 한국어 잘하시네요 ("you speak Korean well!") after only a few words.
혹시 (hoksi), "by any chance", makes a question like 영어 하세요? sound softer and more polite.

faq.q: How do you say "I speak a little Korean"?
faq.a: Say 한국어 조금 해요 (hangugeo jogeum haeyo), "I speak Korean a little".

faq.q: How do you ask "do you speak English?" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 영어 하세요? (yeongeo haseyo?), or more softly, 혹시 영어 하세요? (hoksi yeongeo haseyo?).

intro: "I'm learning Korean" in Korean is 한국어 배우고 있어요 (hangugeo baeugo isseoyo), a polite sentence you can say to anyone. To a friend you can drop the 요: 한국어 배우고 있어 (hangugeo baeugo isseo).

ways.note: "I'm learning Korean." The most useful version.
Formal, good for a self-introduction in class or at work.
To friends and younger people.
"I'm studying Korean." Very common, especially if you study with books or classes.
"I'm in the middle of studying Korean." Natural and friendly.
"I study Korean." Simple present tense.

examples.context: Telling someone why your Korean is basic
Explaining how you study
examples.en: I study Korean while watching dramas.

examples.context: Chatting with a Korean friend

tips: 배우다 means "to learn" and 공부하다 means "to study". Both work here. 공부하다 suggests books and homework, while 배우다 is more general.
한국어 and 한국말 both mean the Korean language. 한국어 is a little more formal, and 한국말 is common in everyday speech.
Koreans usually react warmly to this sentence, so it is a great conversation starter.

faq.q: What is the difference between hangugeo and hangungmal?
faq.a: Both mean the Korean language. 한국어 (hangugeo) sounds slightly more formal or academic, while 한국말 (hangungmal) is everyday speech.

faq.q: How do you say "my Korean is not good"?
faq.a: Say 한국어 잘 못해요 (hangugeo jal motaeyo), "I don't speak Korean well".

intro: "Speak slowly" in Korean is 천천히 말해 주세요 (cheoncheonhi malhae juseyo), a polite "please speak slowly". To someone older, you can use the honorific 천천히 말씀해 주세요 (cheoncheonhi malsseumhae juseyo).

ways.note: "Please speak slowly." Polite and useful almost anywhere.
More respectful, using the honorific verb for speak. Good for elders and staff.
"Could you speak a bit more slowly?" Extra soft and polite, asked as a question.
To a friend or younger person.
"Please say it again."
"Please say it one more time."

examples.context: A shopkeeper explains something quickly
Missing a word on the phone
examples.en: Could you say that once more?

examples.context: A Korean friend talks too fast
examples.en: That's too fast. Talk slowly for me.

tips: 말씀 is the honorific word for speech. Use 말씀해 주세요 with older people, teachers and in formal settings.
Starting with 죄송한데 (sorry, but) or 좀 (a bit) makes the request sound gentler.
천천히 is pronounced "cheon-cheon-hi". The ㅎ is often very light, so it can sound like "cheon-cheo-ni".

faq.q: How do you say "can you repeat that" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 다시 말해 주세요 (dasi malhae juseyo), "please say it again", or 한 번 더 말해 주세요 (han beon deo malhae juseyo), "once more, please".

faq.q: What does cheoncheonhi mean?
faq.a: 천천히 (cheoncheonhi) means "slowly". You can use it with other verbs too, like 천천히 드세요 (cheoncheonhi deuseyo), "eat slowly, take your time".

intro: "Help" in Korean is 도와주세요 (dowajuseyo), which means "please help me". In a real emergency people shout 살려 주세요 (sallyeo juseyo), "save me".

ways.note: "Please help me." For everyday help and emergencies.
"Save me!" or "Help!" Only for real danger.
"Help me" to a friend or younger person.
"Could you help me?" A very soft, polite request, asked as a question.
"I need help."
"Can I help you?" Offering help, asked as a question.

examples.context: Calling for help after an accident
Offering to carry someone's luggage
Asking a friend for help with homework

tips: In South Korea, call 112 for the police and 119 for fire or an ambulance.
살려 주세요 literally means "please keep me alive", so it is only for real emergencies. For everyday help, use 도와주세요.
When offering help, Koreans use the humble form 도와드릴까요 toward the person they are helping, which shows respect.

faq.q: What do you shout for help in Korea?
faq.a: Shout 도와주세요! (dowajuseyo!) or, in serious danger, 살려 주세요! (sallyeo juseyo!).

faq.q: How do you say "Can I help you?" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 도와드릴까요? (dowadeurilkkayo?). Shop staff may also ask 뭐 찾으세요? (mwo chajeuseyo?), "what are you looking for?"

intro: "I miss you" in Korean is 보고 싶어 (bogo sipeo), or 보고 싶어요 (bogo sipeoyo) when you want to be polite. Literally it means "I want to see you," which is exactly how Koreans express missing someone.

ways.note: To a partner, close friend or family member. This is the one you hear most in dramas and texts.
Polite and still warm. Good for someone older, like a grandparent or teacher, or anyone you are not close with yet.
Formal. Used in speeches, letters or when addressing a crowd, like an idol speaking to fans.
"I miss you so much." 너무 (neomu) adds strong feeling.
"I long for you." Deeper and more nostalgic, often for someone far away, someone who has passed away, or a place or time.

examples.context: Texting a partner at night
Calling a grandmother
A friend who moved abroad

tips: 보고 싶다 literally means "want to see." Koreans use it for people they miss, but in other sentences it can simply mean wanting to watch something, like 영화 보고 싶어 (I want to see a movie).
Write it with a space: 보고 싶어, not 보고싶어. Many Koreans skip the space in texts, but the spaced version is correct. In speech it sounds like "bo-go si-peo."
The natural reply is 나도 보고 싶어 (nado bogo sipeo), "I miss you too," or 저도 보고 싶어요 (jeodo bogo sipeoyo) to be polite.

faq.q: How do you say "I miss you too" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 나도 보고 싶어 (nado bogo sipeo) casually, or 저도 보고 싶어요 (jeodo bogo sipeoyo) politely.

faq.q: What does bogo sipeo mean?
faq.a: 보고 싶어 (bogo sipeo) means "I miss you." Word for word it is "I want to see you."

faq.q: Is 그리워요 the same as 보고 싶어요?
faq.a: Both express missing someone, but 그리워요 (geuriwoyo) is more nostalgic and poetic. For everyday texts and calls, 보고 싶어 is what Koreans say.

intro: "I'm happy" in Korean is 행복해 (haengbokhae), or 행복해요 (haengbokhaeyo) to be polite. For a lighter "I'm glad" or "I'm in a good mood," Koreans often say 기뻐요 (gippeoyo) or 기분 좋아 (gibun joa).

ways.note: Deep, warm happiness. To a partner, close friend or family.
The safe polite form for most people you talk to.
Formal. Common in speeches, interviews and award acceptance.
"I'm glad" or "I'm happy" about a specific piece of good news. Casual form: 기뻐 (gippeo).
"I'm in a good mood." Very common for everyday happiness, like a sunny day or good food.
"I'm excited" or "this is fun." Lively, upbeat happiness.

examples.context: On a date with a partner
Hearing good news
Eating a favorite meal

tips: 행복하다 is a big, heartfelt word. For small everyday moments Koreans more often say 좋아 (joa, "it's good"), 기분 좋아 (gibun joa) or 신나 (sinna).
기쁘다 (gippeuda) is happiness about something that happened, like passing a test. 행복하다 (haengbokhada) is a general state of happiness with your life or the moment.
Pronunciation: 행복해 sounds like "haeng-bo-kae." The ㄱ and ㅎ blend into a k sound.

faq.q: How do you say "I'm so happy" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 너무 행복해 (neomu haengbokhae) casually, or 너무 행복해요 (neomu haengbokhaeyo) politely.

faq.q: What is the difference between 행복해 and 기뻐?
faq.a: 행복해 is a deeper, general happiness. 기뻐 is gladness about a specific event, like good news.

intro: "I'm sad" in Korean is 슬퍼 (seulpeo), or 슬퍼요 (seulpeoyo) to be polite. When you are upset because something went wrong, Koreans often say 속상해 (soksanghae) instead.

ways.note: To friends and family. Use it for sadness about a sad event, story or goodbye.
The polite form for most people.
Formal and quite stiff. Mostly heard in speeches or announcements.
"I'm upset" or "I feel bad." Hurt and frustrated feelings when something goes wrong. Very common in conversation.
"I'm feeling down" or "I'm blue." Can also mean depressed, so it sounds heavier than 슬퍼.

examples.context: Watching a sad drama
A friend is moving away
Missing out on concert tickets

tips: 슬프다 is for real sadness: a sad movie, a goodbye, a loss. For everyday disappointment, like a canceled plan or a bad test score, 속상해 sounds more natural.
In texts, Koreans show sadness with ㅠㅠ or ㅜㅜ, which look like crying eyes.
슬퍼 can mean both "I'm sad" and "it's sad." Context tells you which.

faq.q: How do you say "don't be sad" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 슬퍼하지 마 (seulpeohaji ma) casually, or 슬퍼하지 마세요 (seulpeohaji maseyo) politely.

faq.q: What does ㅠㅠ mean in Korean texts?
faq.a: ㅠㅠ (yuyu) looks like tears streaming from two eyes. It shows sadness or being touched, like a crying emoji.

intro: "I'm tired" in Korean is 피곤해 (pigonhae), or 피곤해요 (pigonhaeyo) to be polite. Koreans also say 힘들어 (himdeureo) when they are worn out from something hard.

ways.note: Physically tired. To friends and family.
The polite form, fine with coworkers or people you just met.
Formal. Rare in daily talk.
"It's hard" or "I'm worn out." Used for physical and emotional tiredness. Polite: 힘들어요 (himdeureoyo).
"I'm exhausted" or "I'm drained," after a long stretch of effort.

examples.context: Coming home after work
Telling a coworker
After a long, stressful week

tips: 피곤하다 is tired in the body. 힘들다 is broader: something is hard, tiring or stressful. Koreans say 힘들어 a lot, even about a long day.
If you are tired because you want to sleep, use 졸려 (jollyeo), "I'm sleepy."
When someone looks tired after work, Koreans often say 수고했어 (sugohaesseo), "you worked hard."

faq.q: How do you ask "Are you tired?" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 피곤해? (pigonhae?) casually or 피곤해요? (pigonhaeyo?) politely, with a rising tone.

faq.q: What is the difference between 피곤해 and 졸려?
faq.a: 피곤해 means tired or worn out. 졸려 means sleepy, when your eyes are closing.

intro: "I'm hungry" in Korean is 배고파 (baegopa), or 배고파요 (baegopayo) to be polite. Literally it means "my stomach is empty."

ways.note: To friends and family. One of the most common things Koreans say.
Polite. Good for most people.
The same meaning with the subject marker 가 written in. Slightly fuller and very natural.
Formal. Heard in the military or on TV, rarely in daily life.
"I'm a little peckish." A light hunger, like wanting a snack.

examples.context: Right before lunch
Telling a host or older relative
Late at night

tips: 배 means stomach and 고프다 means empty or hungry. 배고파 is often written as one word, and 배가 고파 adds the subject marker.
Food is social in Korea. A friend may greet you with 밥 먹었어? (bap meogeosseo?), "Did you eat?", which is really a way of saying hello.
Pronunciation: 배고파 sounds like "bae-go-pa."

faq.q: How do you ask "Are you hungry?" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 배고파? (baegopa?) casually or 배고파요? (baegopayo?) politely.

faq.q: How do you say "I'm thirsty" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 목말라 (mongmalla) casually or 목말라요 (mongmallayo) politely.

intro: "I'm bored" in Korean is 심심해 (simsimhae), or 심심해요 (simsimhaeyo) to be polite. If something is boring, like a class or a movie, use 지루해 (jiruhae) instead.

ways.note: "I'm bored, I have nothing to do." To friends and family.
Polite. Fine with most people.
Formal. Rarely used, since being bored is not a formal topic.
"It's boring" or "it's dragging." About something tedious, like a long lecture or a slow movie.
Slang for "no fun" or "boring," from 노 (no) plus 잼 (fun). Used about people, shows or jokes.

examples.context: Stuck at home on a rainy day
Sitting in a long lecture
Telling a friend about your weekend

tips: 심심하다 is how you feel when you have nothing to do. 지루하다 describes something that is tedious. Mixing them up is a common learner mistake.
심심해 is also a light way to start a chat. Texting a friend 심심해 often means "Want to hang out?"
Pronunciation: 심심해 sounds like "shim-shim-hae."

faq.q: What is the difference between 심심해 and 지루해?
faq.a: 심심해 means you are bored because there is nothing to do. 지루해 means something is boring or tedious.

faq.q: What does 노잼 mean?
faq.a: 노잼 (nojam) is slang for "no fun" or "boring." Its opposite is 꿀잼 (kkuljaem), "super fun."

intro: "I'm angry" in Korean is 화났어 (hwanasseo), or 화났어요 (hwanasseoyo) to be polite. Koreans use this past-tense form because it means "I got angry and still am."

ways.note: "I'm angry" or "I'm mad." To friends, family or a partner.
Polite. Also common as a question: 화났어요? "Are you angry?"
Formal. Sounds stiff, used in speeches or written statements.
"I'm annoyed" or "this is so annoying." Mild irritation, used all the time.
Slang, close to "I'm so pissed off." Literally "I'm getting heated." Only with close friends.

examples.context: A friend is late again
Stuck in traffic
Checking on a partner

tips: 화 means anger and 나다 means to arise. 화났어 is the most natural way to say you are angry now.
짜증나 is much lighter than 화났어. Use it for small annoyances like slow Wi-Fi, a long line or a bad day.
Be careful with 열받아 and similar slang. They are fine with close friends but rude toward anyone older or in a polite setting.

faq.q: How do you say "Don't be angry" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 화내지 마 (hwanaeji ma) casually, or 화내지 마세요 (hwanaeji maseyo) politely.

faq.q: Why is "I'm angry" in the past tense in Korean?
faq.a: 화났어 literally means "I got angry." Korean uses this form to describe the state you are in now, so it is the natural way to say "I'm angry."

intro: "I'm sick" in Korean is 아파 (apa), or 아파요 (apayo) to be polite. The same word also means "it hurts," so Koreans use it for feeling ill and for pain.

ways.note: To friends and family. "I'm sick" or "I'm not well."
Polite. The one to use with a teacher, boss or doctor.
Formal. Rare in daily conversation.
"I don't feel well," literally "my body is not good." A gentle way to say you are unwell.
"I caught a cold." Polite: 감기 걸렸어요 (gamgi geollyeosseoyo).

examples.context: Calling in sick to work
Telling a friend
Texting family

tips: 아프다 means both "to be sick" and "to hurt." To be specific, put a body part in front: 머리가 아파 (meoriga apa), "I have a headache."
Koreans say 병원 (byeongwon) for any doctor's office or clinic, not only big hospitals. 병원 가 봐 (byeongwon ga bwa) means "Go see a doctor."
Pronunciation: 아파 sounds like "ah-pa," with a clear p sound.

faq.q: How do you say "Get well soon" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 빨리 나아 (ppalli naa) to a friend, or 빨리 나으세요 (ppalli naeuseyo) politely.

faq.q: How do you ask "Are you sick?" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 아파? (apa?) casually or 아파요? (apayo?) politely.

intro: "I'm scared" in Korean is 무서워 (museowo), or 무서워요 (museowoyo) to be polite. The same word also means "it's scary," so context tells you which.

ways.note: To friends and family. "I'm scared" or "it's scary."
Polite. Fine with most people.
Formal. Rare in conversation.
"I'm scared" or "I'm afraid," often before doing something. Casual.
"You scared me!" or "What a fright!" When something suddenly startles you.
A startled cry, like "Oh my gosh!" Literally "Mom!" Said on reflex when frightened.

examples.context: Watching a horror movie
On a roller coaster
A friend sneaks up behind you

tips: 무서워 can mean "I'm scared" or "it's scary." 이 영화 무서워 (i yeonghwa museowo) means "This movie is scary."
깜짝이야 and 엄마야 are reactions to a sudden shock. 무서워 is for fear that lasts, like a dark street or a horror film.
Pronunciation: 무서워 sounds like "moo-saw-wuh."

faq.q: How do you say "Don't be scared" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 무서워하지 마 (museowohaji ma) or 겁먹지 마 (geommeokji ma) to a friend.

faq.q: How do you say "It's scary" in Korean?
faq.a: Use the same word: 무서워 (museowo) or 무서워요 (museowoyo).

intro: "I'm fine" in Korean is 괜찮아 (gwaenchana), or 괜찮아요 (gwaenchanayo) to be polite. If someone asks how you have been, answer 잘 지내요 (jal jinaeyo), "I'm doing well."

ways.note: "I'm okay" or "I'm fine." To friends and family.
Polite. Also means "It's okay" or "No, thank you."
Formal. Good with a boss, a customer or in a formal setting.
"I'm doing well." The answer to 잘 지냈어요? (jal jinaesseoyo?), "How have you been?"
Casual version of "I'm doing well," to friends.

examples.context: A friend asks after you trip
Someone asks how you have been
Politely declining more food

tips: 괜찮아요 is very flexible: "I'm fine," "It's okay," "Are you okay?" with a rising tone, and "No, thank you."
Koreans do not say "How are you?" every day the way English speakers do. 잘 지냈어요? is for when you have not seen someone in a while, and 잘 지내요 is the usual answer.
Pronunciation: the ㅎ in 괜찮아 is silent, so it sounds like "gwaen-cha-na."

faq.q: How do you ask "Are you okay?" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 괜찮아? (gwaenchana?) casually or 괜찮아요? (gwaenchanayo?) politely, with a rising tone.

faq.q: How do you say "I'm fine, and you?" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 잘 지내요 (jal jinaeyo), then add the person's name with 씨는요? (ssineunyo?), as in "Minji 씨는요?" Among friends, 너는? (neoneun?) works.

intro: "It hurts" in Korean is 아파 (apa), or 아파요 (apayo) to be polite. To say where it hurts, put the body part first: 머리가 아파요 (meoriga apayo), "My head hurts."

ways.note: "It hurts" or "I'm in pain." To friends and family.
Polite. Use it with a doctor, pharmacist or anyone older.
Formal. Rare in daily speech.
"Ouch!" A reflex cry when something suddenly hurts.
"It hurts here." Very useful at a clinic, while pointing.
"I have a headache," literally "my head hurts."

examples.context: At the doctor's office
Stubbing a toe
After a long day

tips: The pattern is body part + 가 or 이 + 아파요. For example, 배가 아파요 (baega apayo) means "My stomach hurts" and 목이 아파요 (mogi apayo) means "My throat hurts."
아프다 also works for emotional pain. 마음이 아파 (maeumi apa) means "My heart hurts" or "It breaks my heart."
For a quick "ouch," Koreans say 아야 (aya) or just 아 (a).

faq.q: How do you say "Ouch" in Korean?
faq.a: Koreans say 아야 (aya) or a short 아 (a) when something suddenly hurts.

faq.q: How do you say "My heart hurts" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 마음이 아파 (maeumi apa). It is used for sadness and sympathy, not a medical problem.

intro: "I'm full" in Korean is 배불러 (baebulleo), or 배불러요 (baebulleoyo) to be polite. It comes from 배 (stomach) and 부르다 (to be full).

ways.note: To friends and family after a good meal.
Polite. Useful when a host offers you more food.
Formal. Rare in daily life.
The same meaning with the subject marker 가. Very natural.
"I ate a lot." A soft way to turn down more food.

examples.context: After a big barbecue dinner
A host offers seconds
Thanking a grandmother after dinner

tips: Korean hosts, especially grandmothers, often keep offering food. Saying 배불러요 with a smile, maybe more than once, is a polite way to decline.
After a meal, it is good manners to say 잘 먹었습니다 (jal meogeosseumnida), "I ate well, thank you."
부르다 is irregular, so 배부르다 becomes 배불러 with a double ㄹ. It sounds like "bae-bul-leo."

faq.q: How do you ask "Are you full?" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 배불러? (baebulleo?) casually or 배불러요? (baebulleoyo?) politely.

faq.q: What do Koreans say after eating?
faq.a: They say 잘 먹었습니다 (jal meogeosseumnida), or 잘 먹었어요 (jal meogeosseoyo), to thank whoever cooked or paid.

intro: "It's cold" in Korean is 추워 (chuwo), or 추워요 (chuwoyo) to be polite. It also means "I'm cold." For cold things like water or ice, Koreans use 차가워 (chagawo) instead.

ways.note: Cold weather, or "I'm cold." To friends and family.
Polite. Fine with most people.
Formal. Heard in weather reports or speeches.
Cold to the touch: water, drinks, hands, ice. Polite: 차가워요 (chagawoyo).
"It's chilly." A cool, crisp feeling, often in fall or early spring.

examples.context: Stepping outside in winter
Touching water in the sink
An autumn evening walk

tips: Use 춥다 for weather and for how your body feels. Use 차갑다 for objects that are cold to the touch. 물이 추워 (the water is cold) is a common learner mistake.
추워 can mean "it's cold" or "I'm cold." Korean usually drops the subject, so both come out the same.
Korean winters are harsh, so you will hear 추워 constantly from December to February.

faq.q: How do you ask "Are you cold?" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 추워? (chuwo?) casually or 추워요? (chuwoyo?) politely.

faq.q: What is the difference between 추워 and 차가워?
faq.a: 추워 is about weather or feeling cold. 차가워 is about things that are cold to the touch, like a drink or someone's hands.

intro: "It's hot" in Korean is 더워 (deowo), or 더워요 (deowoyo) to be polite. Korean has different words for hot weather, hot things and spicy food.

ways.note: Hot weather, or "I'm hot." To friends and family.
Polite. Fine with most people.
Formal. Heard in weather reports or speeches.
Hot to the touch: soup, coffee, a stove. Polite: 뜨거워요 (tteugeowoyo).
"It's spicy." For spicy food only. Polite: 매워요 (maewoyo).

examples.context: A humid summer day
Sipping soup that is too hot
Trying a spicy dish

tips: Use 덥다 for weather and body heat, 뜨겁다 for things that are hot to the touch, and 맵다 for spicy food. English uses "hot" for all three.
Korean summers are hot and humid, so 더워 죽겠어 (deowo jukgesseo), "I'm dying of heat," is a very common exaggeration.
더워 sounds like "duh-wuh."

faq.q: How do you say "It's spicy" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 매워 (maewo) casually or 매워요 (maewoyo) politely.

faq.q: How do you ask "Are you hot?" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 더워? (deowo?) casually or 더워요? (deowoyo?) politely.

intro: "I'm sleepy" in Korean is 졸려 (jollyeo), or 졸려요 (jollyeoyo) to be polite. Koreans also say 잠 와 (jam wa), literally "sleep is coming."

ways.note: To friends and family when your eyes are closing.
Polite. Fine with most people.
Formal. Rare in daily life.
"I'm getting sleepy," literally "sleep is coming." Very casual and common.
"I want to sleep." Polite: 자고 싶어요 (jago sipeoyo).

examples.context: Studying late at night
Back at work after lunch
examples.en: I ate lunch and now I'm sleepy.

examples.context: Texting a partner at night

tips: 졸리다 means sleepy. 피곤하다 means tired. You can be tired without being sleepy, and Koreans keep the two apart.
When you head to bed, say 잘게 (jalge), "I'm going to sleep." The other person might answer 잘 자 (jal ja), "Sleep well."
Pronunciation: 졸려 sounds like "jol-lyuh," with a long l sound.

faq.q: What is the difference between 졸려 and 피곤해?
faq.a: 졸려 means sleepy. 피곤해 means tired or worn out, even if you are not ready to sleep.

faq.q: How do you say "I'm going to sleep" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 잘게 (jalge) to a friend, or 잘게요 (jalgeyo) to be polite.

intro: "I'm nervous" in Korean is 긴장돼 (ginjangdwae), or 긴장돼요 (ginjangdwaeyo) to be polite. For nervous excitement, like before a date or a concert, Koreans often say 떨려 (tteollyeo).

ways.note: "I'm nervous" or "I'm tense." Before an exam, interview or performance.
Polite. Fine with most people.
Formal. Often heard from contestants or idols on stage.
"I'm shaking" or "I have butterflies." Nervous excitement. Polite: 떨려요 (tteollyeoyo).
"I'm worried." Anxious about how something will turn out. Polite: 걱정돼요 (geokjeongdwaeyo).

examples.context: Right before an exam
Waiting for a first date
Waiting for test results

tips: 떨려 literally means "I'm trembling." Koreans use it for exciting nerves, like meeting your idol or confessing your feelings.
To calm someone, say 긴장하지 마 (ginjanghaji ma), "Don't be nervous," or cheer them on with 화이팅 (hwaiting).
Pronunciation: 긴장돼 sounds like "gin-jang-dwae."

faq.q: How do you say "Don't be nervous" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 긴장하지 마 (ginjanghaji ma) to a friend, or 긴장하지 마세요 (ginjanghaji maseyo) politely.

faq.q: What does 떨려 mean?
faq.a: 떨려 (tteollyeo) means "I'm trembling." It is how Koreans say they feel nervous and excited at the same time.

intro: "I love you" in Korean is 사랑해요 (saranghaeyo), or 사랑해 (saranghae) when you say it to a partner, a close friend or family. Both come from the verb 사랑하다 (saranghada), "to love". The only difference is how polite you are being.

ways.note: To a partner, close friend or family. This is the one you hear most in K-dramas between couples.
Polite but still warm. Good for parents, grandparents, or anyone you would normally speak politely to.
Formal and a little grand. Idols say it to fans on stage, and people use it in speeches or cards.
"I love you so much." 너무 (neomu) adds feeling. Use it with a partner or family.
"I love you a lot." A gentle, common way to end a phone call or text with someone close.

examples.context: Saying goodbye to Mom on the phone
Texting a partner before bed
An idol speaking to fans at a concert

tips: Koreans usually drop the words "I" and "you". 사랑해 on its own already means "I love you". Adding 나는 너를 (naneun neoreul) is grammatically fine but sounds stiff, like reading from a textbook.

사랑해 carries real weight between couples, so people do not say it on a first date. If you have a crush, 좋아해 (joahae, "I like you") is the usual first step. With parents and grandparents, saying 사랑해요 is common and always welcome.
Pronounce it sa-rang-hae, with the "hae" sounding like "heh". In 사랑해요 the ending sounds like "heh-yo".

faq.q: What does saranghae mean?
faq.a: Saranghae (사랑해) means "I love you" in casual Korean. It is what couples, close friends and family say to each other.

faq.q: Should I say saranghae or saranghaeyo?
faq.a: Use 사랑해 (saranghae) with a partner, close friends and people younger than you. Use 사랑해요 (saranghaeyo) when you want to stay polite, for example with parents-in-law or older relatives.

faq.q: How do you write I love you in Korean?
faq.a: It is written 사랑해 in Hangul (casual) or 사랑해요 (polite). The formal version is 사랑합니다.

intro: "I like you" in Korean is 좋아해요 (joahaeyo), or 좋아해 (joahae) when you speak casually. It comes from 좋아하다 (joahada), "to like", and it is the classic way to confess a crush.

ways.note: To a friend or crush your own age or younger. The standard casual confession.
Polite. Use it with someone you do not speak casually to yet, such as an older classmate or a coworker.
Formal and very serious. It can sound like a dramatic, nervous confession.
"I like you." Adding 너 (neo, "you") makes it clear you mean the person, not something else.
Literally "You are good (to me)". A soft, natural way to say you like someone. In speech 네가 often sounds like 니가 (niga).

examples.context: Confessing to a friend after class
Confessing to an older student
Answering "What do you like about me?"

tips: In Korean dating culture, a confession is called 고백 (gobaek). It usually starts with 좋아해, not 사랑해. 사랑해 comes later, once you are already a couple.
좋아해 can also mean liking a friend, food or a hobby, so context matters. If you want to be clear it is romantic, people add 진짜 (jinjja, "really") or follow with 사귈래? ("Will you go out with me?").
Watch the particles: 너를 좋아해 (I like you, with 좋아하다) but 네가 좋아 (with 좋다). Both are correct, they just use different verbs.

faq.q: What is the difference between joahae and saranghae?
faq.a: 좋아해 (joahae) means "I like you" and is used for crushes and early dating. 사랑해 (saranghae) means "I love you" and is saved for deeper feelings.

faq.q: How do you confess to someone in Korean?
faq.a: The simplest confession is 좋아해 (joahae) or, politely, 좋아해요 (joahaeyo). Many people then ask 나랑 사귈래? (narang sagwillae?), "Will you go out with me?"

intro: "I love you too" in Korean is 나도 사랑해 (nado saranghae). 나도 means "me too", so you are literally saying "I also love (you)". To be polite, say 저도 사랑해요 (jeodo saranghaeyo).

ways.note: The natural reply to a partner, close friend or younger family member.
Polite. 저 (jeo) is the humble word for "I". Good for parents-in-law, grandparents or older relatives.
Formal. You will hear idols say this back to fans.
"I love you a lot too." Warmer than the basic reply.
Just "Me too." Very common as a quick, sweet reply between couples.

examples.context: Replying to a partner's good night text
Replying to Grandma
Hugging a partner at the airport
examples.en: I love you a lot too.

tips: The small word 도 (do) means "too" or "also" and sticks to the word before it. 나도 is "me too" and 저도 is the polite "me too".
Match the other person's politeness. If they said 사랑해, answer 나도 사랑해. If they said 사랑해요, answer 저도 사랑해요.

faq.q: What does nado saranghae mean?
faq.a: 나도 사랑해 (nado saranghae) means "I love you too" in casual Korean.

faq.q: Can I just say nado?
faq.a: Yes. Between people who are close, 나도 (nado, "me too") on its own is a natural reply to 사랑해.

intro: "You are beautiful" in Korean is usually 예뻐요 (yeppeoyo), or 예뻐 (yeppeo) when you speak casually. It comes from 예쁘다 (yeppeuda), "pretty", which Koreans use every day for "beautiful". There is also 아름다워요 (areumdawoyo), which sounds more poetic.

ways.note: To a partner or close friend. The everyday word for pretty or beautiful.
Polite. Fine for complimenting someone you do not know well.
"You're really beautiful." 정말 (jeongmal) means "really".
An exclamation, like "Wow, you're so pretty!" said in the moment.
"Beautiful" in a more poetic way. Used for scenery, voices, a bride, or in songs and letters.

examples.context: Seeing a partner dressed up for a date
Complimenting a friend's new hairstyle
Complimenting a bride at a wedding

tips: Korean usually leaves out "you are". 예뻐 alone means "(You're) pretty". Add 너 (neo, "you") only if you need to be clear who you mean.
예쁘다 is used for people, clothes, places and things. 아름답다 is more literary, so 아름다워 to a partner can sound like a line from a romance novel. That can be sweet, but 예뻐 is what people say day to day.
For men, people normally say 잘생겼어 (jalsaenggyeosseo, "handsome") or 멋있어 (meosisseo, "cool") instead of 예뻐.

faq.q: What does yeppeo mean?
faq.a: 예뻐 (yeppeo) means "pretty" or "beautiful" in casual Korean. It is often used on its own to mean "You're pretty".

faq.q: What is the difference between yeppeoyo and areumdawoyo?
faq.a: 예뻐요 is the everyday word for pretty or beautiful. 아름다워요 is more elegant and poetic, and is often used for scenery, music or a person's heart.

intro: "You are cute" in Korean is 귀여워요 (gwiyeowoyo), or 귀여워 (gwiyeowo) when you speak casually. It comes from 귀엽다 (gwiyeopda), "to be cute". Koreans use it a lot, for babies, pets, friends and partners.

ways.note: To a partner, friend, child or pet. The most common way.
Polite. Good for complimenting someone's baby or pet, or an idol in a comment.
"So cute!" The reaction you will hear everywhere.
An exclamation in the moment, like "You're seriously cute!"

examples.context: Seeing a friend's baby
Teasing a partner who is pouting
Commenting politely on a coworker's puppy photo

tips: 귀엽다 changes its ㅂ to 워 when conjugated: 귀엽다 becomes 귀여워. You will see the same pattern in 고마워 and 추워.
Calling a grown man cute is a normal compliment in Korea, not an insult. Many people find it sweeter than "handsome". Acting cute on purpose is called 애교 (aegyo).

faq.q: What does gwiyeowo mean?
faq.a: 귀여워 (gwiyeowo) means "cute" or "You're cute" in casual Korean.

faq.q: Is it okay to call a Korean man cute?
faq.a: Yes. 귀여워 is a common, affectionate compliment for men too, especially between couples and friends.

intro: "You are handsome" in Korean is 잘생겼어요 (jalsaenggyeosseoyo), or 잘생겼어 (jalsaenggyeosseo) when you speak casually. It comes from 잘생기다 (jalsaenggida), literally "well formed". Another favorite compliment is 멋있어요 (meosisseoyo), "You're cool".

ways.note: To a partner or friend. Talks about someone's face and looks.
Polite. Fine for someone you do not know well, or an actor at a fan meeting.
An exclamation, like "Wow, you're so handsome!"
"You're cool" or "You look great." About style, attitude or what someone did, not just their face.
Polite version of 멋있어.

examples.context: Fan meeting an actor
Seeing a boyfriend in a suit
Praising a coworker's presentation

tips: 잘생기다 is used in the past tense form 잘생겼어 even when you mean right now. Think of it as "(you) came out handsome". Saying 잘생겨 sounds wrong to Koreans.
멋있다 is broader than handsome. You can say it about a man, a woman, an outfit, a car or a brave act. 잘생기다 is mostly about a man's face. For women, 예쁘다 (pretty) is the usual word.

faq.q: What does jalsaenggyeosseo mean?
faq.a: 잘생겼어 (jalsaenggyeosseo) means "(You're) handsome" or "good-looking" in casual Korean.

faq.q: What is the difference between jalsaenggyeosseo and meosisseo?
faq.a: 잘생겼어 is about good looks. 멋있어 means cool or impressive, and can describe style, personality or actions.

intro: "My love" in Korean is 내 사랑 (nae sarang). 내 means "my" and 사랑 means "love". Couples also use pet names like 자기야 (jagiya) and, once married, 여보 (yeobo).

ways.note: Sweet and a little dramatic. Common in texts, letters and songs.
"Honey" or "babe". The pet name dating couples use most.
"Honey" between married couples. Used with both casual and polite speech.
"My love" in a more poetic, written style. Found in letters, poems and lyrics.

examples.context: Ending a good night text
Calling a boyfriend or girlfriend
A wife asking her husband

tips: 내 사랑 is lovely in writing, but many couples feel shy saying it out loud every day. In daily speech, 자기야 is much more common.
여보 is for married couples. Dating couples who call each other 여보 are being playful.

faq.q: What does nae sarang mean?
faq.a: 내 사랑 (nae sarang) means "my love". It is a term of endearment used between partners.

faq.q: What do Korean couples call each other?
faq.a: Dating couples often say 자기야 (jagiya). Married couples say 여보 (yeobo). A woman may also call an older boyfriend 오빠 (oppa).

intro: "Honey" as a pet name in Korean is 자기야 (jagiya), used between dating couples. Married couples say 여보 (yeobo). If you mean the food, honey is 꿀 (kkul).

ways.note: "Honey" or "babe" when calling your partner. The 야 is added when you call out to someone.
The same pet name without 야, used in the middle of a sentence, like "Did honey eat?"
"Honey" between husband and wife.
"Baby". A cute pet name some couples use. 애기 is the spoken form of 아기 (baby).
Honey the food, the sweet thing bees make.

examples.context: Greeting a partner
A husband calling his wife
Asking for honey at a cafe

tips: 자기 also means "oneself" in other sentences, so do not be surprised to see it outside romance. As a pet name, use it only with your partner. Calling a friend 자기야 sounds odd.
Korean has no exact word for honey as a casual term for strangers, like a waiter saying "Here you go, honey". Those uses do not translate.

faq.q: What does jagiya mean?
faq.a: 자기야 (jagiya) means "honey" or "babe". Dating couples use it to call each other.

faq.q: What is the difference between jagiya and yeobo?
faq.a: 자기야 is used mostly by dating couples. 여보 is used between married couples.

faq.q: How do you say honey the food in Korean?
faq.a: Honey the food is 꿀 (kkul).

intro: "Boyfriend" in Korean is 남자 친구 (namja chingu), literally "male friend". Online it is usually written without the space, 남자친구, and shortened to 남친 (namchin) in casual talk.

ways.note: The standard word. Fine in any situation.
The short, casual form. Very common among friends and online.
"Lover" or "partner". Works for a boyfriend or girlfriend and sounds a bit more serious.
What a woman often calls a boyfriend who is older than her. It also means "older brother".

examples.context: Introducing a boyfriend to a friend's parents
A friend asking
Texting her boyfriend

tips: 남자 친구 always means a romantic boyfriend. For a male friend who is just a friend, Koreans say 친구 (chingu), or jokingly 남사친 (namsachin), short for 남자 사람 친구, "a male human friend".
In dictionaries the word is spaced as 남자 친구, but you will see 남자친구 everywhere online. Both are understood.

faq.q: What does namchin mean?
faq.a: 남친 (namchin) is the short, casual form of 남자 친구 (namja chingu), "boyfriend".

faq.q: Why do Korean girls call their boyfriend oppa?
faq.a: 오빠 (oppa) is what a woman calls an older brother or an older man she is close to. Many women keep using it for an older boyfriend.

intro: "Girlfriend" in Korean is 여자 친구 (yeoja chingu), literally "female friend". Online it is usually written without the space, 여자친구, and shortened to 여친 (yeochin) in casual talk.

ways.note: The standard word. Fine in any situation.
The short, casual form. Very common among friends and online.
"Lover" or "partner". Works for a girlfriend or boyfriend and sounds a bit more serious.

examples.context: A friend asking politely
Telling a friend about weekend plans
Showing a photo to a close friend

tips: In English, women often call their female friends "girlfriends". In Korean, 여자 친구 always means a romantic partner. For a friend, just say 친구 (chingu), or jokingly 여사친 (yeosachin), short for 여자 사람 친구, "a female human friend".
In dictionaries the word is spaced as 여자 친구, but you will see 여자친구 everywhere online. Both are understood.

faq.q: What does yeochin mean?
faq.a: 여친 (yeochin) is the short, casual form of 여자 친구 (yeoja chingu), "girlfriend".

faq.q: How do I say my female friend without meaning girlfriend?
faq.a: Just say 친구 (chingu), "friend". 여자 친구 would be understood as a romantic girlfriend.

intro: "Kiss" in Korean is 뽀뽀 (ppoppo) for a quick, sweet peck, or 키스 (kiseu) for a romantic kiss. To say "to kiss", add 하다: 뽀뽀하다 (ppoppohada) or 키스하다 (kiseuhada).

ways.note: A light peck. Used between couples, and with children and family. Cute and playful.
A romantic kiss on the lips, from English. More serious than 뽀뽀.
"Give me a kiss." Playful, between partners or to a small child.
A literary word for kiss. You will see it in novels, poems and news, rarely in conversation.

examples.context: Asking a partner for a kiss
Talking about a drama scene
Telling a friend what happened

tips: 뽀뽀 comes from the sound of a little kiss, so it feels cute. Parents ask their kids for a 뽀뽀, and couples use it too. 키스 suggests a real romantic kiss.
Pronounce the ㅃ in 뽀뽀 as a tense p with no puff of air, closer to "bbo-bbo" than "po-po".
Public kissing is less common in Korea than in many Western countries, so a 뽀뽀 in public is usually quick.

faq.q: What is the difference between ppoppo and kiseu?
faq.a: 뽀뽀 (ppoppo) is a quick peck, used with partners, children and family. 키스 (kiseu) is a romantic kiss.

faq.q: How do you say kiss me in Korean?
faq.a: Say 뽀뽀해 줘 (ppoppohae jwo) for a playful "Kiss me", or 키스해 줘 (kiseuhae jwo) for a romantic one.

english: Will you go out with me?

answer.en: Will you go out with me?

intro: "Will you go out with me?" in Korean is 나랑 사귈래? (narang sagwillae?). It comes from 사귀다 (sagwida), "to date" or "to be in a relationship". To ask politely, say 저랑 사귈래요? (jeorang sagwillaeyo?).

ways.note: The classic confession question, to someone your age or younger, or someone you already speak casually with.
Polite. Use it if you still speak politely to the person, for example an older coworker.
"Let's go out." More direct and confident than a question.
Just "Let's date." Short and bold.
A softer, slightly shy way to ask, like "Would you go out with me?"

examples.context: Confessing to a friend
examples.en: Will you go out with me?

examples.context: Confessing to a coworker
examples.en: Will you go out with me?

examples.context: After a few dates going well

tips: 사귀다 means to officially start a relationship, not to go on one date. To ask for a single date, people say something like 주말에 영화 볼래? ("Want to see a movie this weekend?").
Korean dating often starts with a clear confession, called 고백 (gobaek). Many couples count their anniversary from that day and celebrate 100 days, 200 days and so on.
The period of flirting before anyone confesses is called 썸 (sseom).

faq.q: What does sagwija mean?
faq.a: 사귀자 (sagwija) means "Let's go out" or "Let's date". It is a direct casual way to ask someone to be your partner.

faq.q: How do you confess in Korean?
faq.a: A common pattern is 좋아해 ("I like you") followed by 나랑 사귈래? ("Will you go out with me?").

intro: "I need you" in Korean is 네가 필요해 (nega piryohae). It uses 필요하다 (piryohada), "to be needed", so it literally means "You are needed (by me)". Koreans also often say 너 없으면 안 돼 (neo eopseumyeon an dwae), "I can't do without you".

ways.note: To a partner or close friend. In speech, 네가 often sounds like 니가 (niga).
"I can't do without you." Emotional and very natural between couples.
"You're the only one I have." Said to a partner or a loyal friend.
Polite and romantic. You hear it in songs and between older couples. It can sound dramatic in daily life.
"I need help." Use this when you need someone's help rather than the person in a romantic way.

examples.context: Asking a partner not to leave
Making up after a fight
Asking a classmate for help

tips: 필요하다 works differently from English "need". The thing you need takes the subject marker 이/가, so it is 네가 필요해, not 너를 필요해.
