Korean speakers rarely use 당신 (dangsin) for "you" in conversation, since it can sound distant or even rude. Between couples, people usually use the person's name, 자기 or 너.

faq.q: What does nega piryohae mean?
faq.a: 네가 필요해 (nega piryohae) means "I need you" in casual Korean.

faq.q: Why is it 네가 and not 너를?
faq.a: With 필요하다 the needed thing is the grammatical subject, so it takes 가: 네가 필요해.

intro: "Sweet dreams" in Korean is 좋은 꿈 꿔 (joeun kkum kkwo), literally "Dream a good dream". To be polite, say 좋은 꿈 꾸세요 (joeun kkum kkuseyo). Most people pair it with 잘 자 (jal ja), "Sleep well".

ways.note: To a partner, friend or child at bedtime.
Polite. Good for someone older or someone you do not know well.
"Sleep well" or "Good night". What Koreans say most at bedtime.
Polite "Sleep well". Fine for friends you speak politely to, not for elders.
"Sleep tight." 꿀잠 means "honey sleep", a deep, sweet sleep. Fun and friendly.
"Good night" to parents, grandparents and other elders. Uses the honorific verb for sleeping.

examples.context: Texting a partner at night
Saying good night to a host
Tucking in a friend after a long day

tips: In Korean you 꾸다 (kkuda) a dream, so "to dream" is 꿈을 꾸다. 꿔 is the casual form of 꾸다.
Couples sometimes add 꿈에서 만나 (kkumeseo manna), "See you in my dreams".
To elders, skip 잘 자 and 좋은 꿈 꿔. Say 안녕히 주무세요 instead.

faq.q: How do you say good night and sweet dreams in Korean?
faq.a: Say 잘 자, 좋은 꿈 꿔 (jal ja, joeun kkum kkwo) to someone close. Politely, 잘 자요, 좋은 꿈 꾸세요.

faq.q: What does kkuljam mean?
faq.a: 꿀잠 (kkuljam) means a deep, sweet sleep, literally "honey sleep". 꿀잠 자 means "Sleep tight".

intro: "Happy birthday" in Korean is 생일 축하해요 (saengil chukhahaeyo), which literally means "I congratulate you on your birthday." With close friends you can drop the 요 and say 생일 축하해 (saengil chukhahae). For grandparents and other elders, Koreans use the honorific word 생신 instead of 생일.

ways.note: To friends, younger siblings, or a partner. This is what you will see most in texts and on social media.
The safe everyday choice for coworkers, classmates you are not close to, or anyone you speak politely to.
Formal and a little ceremonial. It is also the line Koreans sing in the birthday song.
For parents, grandparents, and other elders. 생신 is the respectful word for birthday and 드려요 humbly lowers you.
A short slang form of 생일 축하, used only in texts and comments between friends.

examples.context: Texting a friend on their birthday
Writing in a coworker's birthday card
Calling your grandmother on her birthday

tips: 축하 is pronounced more like "chu-ka" because the ㄱ and ㅎ blend into a strong k sound. So 생일 축하해 sounds like "saeng-il chu-ka-hae."
Use 생신 instead of 생일 when the birthday belongs to someone older and respected, like a grandparent, a parent, or a boss. Saying 생일 to them is not rude among family, but 생신 shows extra care.
On their birthday many Koreans eat 미역국 (miyeokguk), a seaweed soup. Asking "미역국 먹었어?" (Did you eat seaweed soup?) is a friendly birthday question.

faq.q: How do you sing happy birthday in Korean?
faq.a: The Korean birthday song uses the same tune as the English one. The words are 생일 축하합니다, 생일 축하합니다, 사랑하는 (name), 생일 축하합니다.

faq.q: How do you say happy birthday to an older person in Korean?
faq.a: Say 생신 축하드려요 (saengsin chukhadeuryeoyo). It uses the honorific word for birthday and a humble verb, so it fits grandparents, parents, and bosses.

faq.q: What do ㅊㅋ and 생축 mean in a birthday text?
faq.a: ㅊㅋ is short for 축하 (congrats), and 생축 is short for 생일 축하 (happy birthday). They are casual texting shortcuts for friends only.

intro: "Congratulations" in Korean is 축하해요 (chukhahaeyo), the polite form that works with almost anyone. Friends just say 축하해 (chukhahae). To say what you are congratulating someone on, put the word for it first, like 결혼 축하해요 (congratulations on your wedding).

ways.note: To friends, younger people, and family members close to you.
The everyday polite form for coworkers, acquaintances, and people you just met.
For speeches, announcements, or congratulating someone in a formal setting.
Very respectful. Use it in cards or messages to a boss, a teacher, or an elder.
Texting shorthand made of the first consonants of 축하. Often doubled as ㅊㅋㅊㅋ.

examples.context: A friend tells you they passed an exam
Writing in a coworker's wedding card
Your manager just got promoted

tips: The pattern is simple: event + 축하해요. Try 졸업 축하해요 (graduation), 생일 축하해요 (birthday), or 취업 축하해요 (getting a job).
축하 sounds like "chu-ka" in real speech, so 축하해요 sounds close to "chu-ka-hae-yo."
When someone congratulates you, answer with 고마워 (gomawo) to a friend or 감사합니다 (gamsahamnida) to anyone else.

faq.q: How do you reply when someone says 축하해요?
faq.a: Just say thank you: 고마워요 (gomawoyo) or 감사합니다 (gamsahamnida). With a friend, 고마워 (gomawo) is enough.

faq.q: What is the difference between 축하해요 and 축하드려요?
faq.a: Both mean congratulations and both are polite. 축하드려요 uses a humble verb, so it sounds more respectful and suits elders, bosses, and teachers.

intro: "Merry Christmas" in Korean is 메리 크리스마스 (meri keuriseumaseu), borrowed straight from English and fine to say to anyone. A more Korean way is 즐거운 크리스마스 보내세요 (jeulgeoun keuriseumaseu bonaeseyo), which means "have a merry Christmas."

ways.note: The most common greeting. It works for friends, coworkers, and cards.
"Have a good Christmas" to a friend, often said when you part before the holiday.
"Have a merry Christmas." Warm and polite for coworkers, teachers, or shop owners you know.
성탄절 is the traditional word for Christmas Day. It sounds a little more classic and is common in cards and at church.
Very formal, for business messages or announcements.

examples.context: Sending a group text to friends
Saying bye to a classmate before winter break
Leaving the office on December 24th

tips: Christmas is a public holiday in Korea, but for many people it is more of a couples' day than a family day. Christmas Eve dates, cake, and lights are a big part of it.
Koreans pronounce 메리 크리스마스 with Korean sounds, roughly "meh-ri keu-ri-seu-ma-seu." Saying it the English way is also understood everywhere.
The verb 보내다 means "to spend (time)." So 잘 보내 and 즐거운 ... 보내세요 work for any holiday: just swap in the holiday's name.

faq.q: Do Koreans celebrate Christmas?
faq.a: Yes. December 25th is a national holiday in Korea. Many people go on dates, meet friends, or eat Christmas cake, and churches hold services.

faq.q: What does 성탄절 mean?
faq.a: 성탄절 (seongtanjeol) is the traditional Korean word for Christmas Day. It is used on calendars, in the news, and in more formal greetings.

intro: "Happy New Year" in Korean is 새해 복 많이 받으세요 (saehae bok mani badeuseyo). It literally means "receive a lot of blessings in the new year." Koreans use it both on January 1st and on Seollal, the Lunar New Year.

ways.note: To friends and younger people. Same wish, casual ending.
The standard greeting for almost everyone, including parents, coworkers, and teachers.
Very formal. Common in speeches, company messages, and on TV.
"Stay healthy in the new year too." A caring extra line often added for parents and grandparents.
The English phrase in Korean letters. Young people use it in texts and posts.

examples.context: Bowing to your grandfather on Seollal
Texting a friend at midnight
A New Year message to your teacher
examples.en: Stay healthy in the new year too.

tips: Korea has two new years: January 1st and Seollal (설날), the Lunar New Year in late January or February. Seollal is the bigger family holiday, and you can use the same greeting for both.
On Seollal, children bow deeply to elders (세배) while saying 새해 복 많이 받으세요, and elders often give them money called 세뱃돈.
많이 is pronounced "ma-ni" because the ㅎ is silent, so the whole phrase sounds like "sae-hae bok ma-ni ba-deu-se-yo."

faq.q: How do you reply to 새해 복 많이 받으세요?
faq.a: Say the same thing back: 새해 복 많이 받으세요. With friends you can say 너도 새해 복 많이 받아 (you too, happy New Year).

faq.q: Can I just say Happy New Year in English to Koreans?
faq.a: Yes, most people will understand and appreciate it. Saying the Korean phrase, especially to older people, shows real effort and is warmly received.

intro: "Cheers" in Korean is 건배 (geonbae), the standard toast when people raise their glasses. Among friends you will also hear 짠 (jjan), the sound of glasses clinking.

ways.note: The standard toast. Works at a dinner with friends, a family meal, or a company party.
A playful "clink!" used with friends. People say 짠 하자 (let's clink) or just 짠.
From English "one shot": finish your glass in one go, like "bottoms up."
"To...!" Someone says a toast like 우리의 건강을 (to our health) and everyone shouts 위하여. Very common at work dinners.

examples.context: Raising your glass at dinner with friends
Clinking glasses with a close friend
A friend dares the table to finish their drinks

tips: When drinking with someone older, turn your head slightly away from them as you drink. It is a small sign of respect.
Do not pour your own drink. Pour for others, and hold the bottle with two hands (or one hand supporting your wrist) when pouring for an elder.
Nobody has to drink if they do not want to. Saying 저는 술 못 마셔요 (I can't drink) is a normal, polite way to pass.

faq.q: What is the difference between 건배 and 짠?
faq.a: 건배 is the standard word for a toast and fits any setting. 짠 is the casual "clink" sound, used mostly among friends.

faq.q: What do Koreans shout at company dinners?
faq.a: Often one person makes a short toast and everyone replies 위하여 (wihayeo), meaning "to that!" 건배 is also common.

intro: "Good luck" in Korean is 행운을 빌어요 (haenguneul bireoyo), which means "I wish you luck." In everyday life, though, Koreans more often say 화이팅 (hwaiting) or 잘 될 거야 (it will go well) before a test or interview.

ways.note: The direct translation of "good luck." It sounds sincere and a bit serious, good for cards and goodbyes.
The same wish to a friend. Still a little dramatic in speech, so it often appears in writing.
The everyday cheer before any challenge. Add the event in front: 시험 화이팅 (good luck on your exam).
"It will go well." Reassuring words for a nervous friend. Polite form: 잘 될 거예요.
"Do well on your test." The usual thing to say to a friend before an exam. Polite form: 시험 잘 보세요.

examples.context: Texting a friend before a job interview
Your little brother is leaving for an exam
Saying goodbye to a coworker who is moving abroad

tips: In speech, 행운을 빌어 can sound like a line from a movie. For a friend facing something hard, 화이팅 or 잘 될 거야 feels more natural.
Before the big college entrance exam (수능), Koreans give sticky 엿 (taffy) and 찹쌀떡 (rice cakes) because 붙다 means both "to stick" and "to pass."
Many people avoid seaweed soup (미역국) before an exam, because it is slippery and 미끄러지다 (to slip) is slang for failing.

faq.q: How do you say good luck on your exam in Korean?
faq.a: Say 시험 잘 봐 (siheom jal bwa) to a friend or 시험 잘 보세요 (siheom jal boseyo) politely. 시험 화이팅 also works.

faq.q: Is 화이팅 the same as good luck?
faq.a: Not exactly, but it is used in the same moments. 화이팅 means something like "you can do it" or "go for it" and is the most common thing to say before a challenge.

intro: "Good job" in Korean is 잘했어요 (jalhaesseoyo), which literally means "you did well." With friends and kids you say 잘했어 (jalhaesseo). After a long day of work, Koreans also say 수고했어요 (sugohaesseoyo), "you worked hard."

ways.note: To friends, kids, and younger people. Often said with 진짜 (really) or 너무 (so) in front.
Polite praise for someone around your age or younger. It can sound like grading if said to a boss.
"You worked hard." Said at the end of a task or workday to thank someone for their effort.
The formal version, heard at the end of meetings, shifts, and events.
"That's amazing." Praise for an impressive result rather than effort.

examples.context: Your friend nailed a performance
A teammate finished their presentation
Packing up at the end of a workday

tips: Be careful praising people above you with 잘했어요. It can sound like you are judging their work. To a boss or elder, 수고하셨습니다 or a specific compliment like 발표 정말 좋았어요 (the presentation was really good) is safer.
수고했어요 is one of the most useful phrases in Korean workplaces. Coworkers say it to each other when leaving, after a project, or after any shared effort.
잘했어 is said in one smooth breath: "jal-hae-sseo."

faq.q: What does 수고했어요 mean?
faq.a: It means "you worked hard" or "thanks for your effort." Koreans use it at the end of work or after someone finishes a task.

faq.q: Can I say 잘했어요 to my boss?
faq.a: It is better not to. Praising a superior's performance can sound a bit presumptuous. Say 수고하셨습니다 (sugohasyeotseumnida) instead.

answer.en: Thank you for the meal (I ate well)

intro: "Thank you for the meal" in Korean is 잘 먹었습니다 (jal meogeotseumnida), said after eating. Before you start eating, Koreans say 잘 먹겠습니다 (jal meokgetseumnida), "I will eat well." Both thank the person who cooked or paid.

ways.note: After the meal. Say it to the host, the person who paid, or the restaurant owner as you leave.
A softer polite version after eating, good for friends' parents or coworkers.
To a friend who treated you or cooked for you.
Before eating. Say it when the food arrives, especially if someone else is paying or cooked it.
A friendlier way to say the same thing before eating. Casual form: 잘 먹을게.

examples.context: Leaving a small restaurant
Your mom puts dinner on the table
A friend paid for dinner
examples.en: Thanks so much for dinner today.

tips: Remember the timing: 겠 (will) is for before eating and 었 (did) is for after. Mixing them up is a common learner mistake, but people will still understand you.
Even when you pay for yourself, saying 잘 먹었습니다 to the owner on the way out of a small restaurant is polite and makes people smile.
In real speech the endings sound like "meo-geot-sseum-ni-da" and "meok-get-sseum-ni-da." The ㅂ in 습니다 sounds like m.

faq.q: What do Koreans say before eating?
faq.a: They say 잘 먹겠습니다 (jal meokgetseumnida), meaning "I will eat well." It thanks whoever prepared or paid for the meal.

faq.q: How should the host reply to 잘 먹겠습니다?
faq.a: Common replies are 맛있게 드세요 (enjoy your meal) or 많이 드세요 (eat a lot). With friends, 많이 먹어 is enough.

intro: "Enjoy your meal" in Korean is 맛있게 드세요 (masitge deuseyo), literally "please eat deliciously." Hosts and grandparents also love to say 많이 드세요 (mani deuseyo), "eat a lot."

ways.note: The standard phrase. Servers, hosts, and friends' parents all say it. 드세요 is the respectful "please eat."
To a friend, a partner, or a younger sibling.
"Eat a lot." A warm, hospitable way to say enjoy, very common from hosts.
What parents and grandparents say to kids, and friends say to each other.
Formal. You may hear it in hotels or at formal events.

examples.context: A server sets down your food
Grandma fills your bowl again
Serving food to a guest's grandmother

tips: Use 드세요, not 먹어요, when telling someone older or a guest to eat. 드시다 is the respectful verb for eating.
The usual exchange goes like this: the host says 맛있게 드세요, and the guest answers 잘 먹겠습니다 (thank you for the food).
맛있게 sounds like "ma-sit-ge" with a tense g, close to "ma-shit-kke" in fast speech.

faq.q: How do you reply to 맛있게 드세요?
faq.a: Say 잘 먹겠습니다 (jal meokgetseumnida) or simply 감사합니다 (thank you).

faq.q: Is there a Korean word for bon appetit?
faq.a: There is no single word. 맛있게 드세요 (enjoy your meal) and 많이 드세요 (eat a lot) do the same job.

intro: "Get well soon" in Korean is 빨리 나으세요 (ppalli naeuseyo), meaning "please get better quickly." To a friend, say 빨리 나아 (ppalli naa). Koreans also often say 아프지 마 (apeuji ma), "don't be sick."

ways.note: To friends and family. You can swap 빨리 for 얼른 (eolleun), which also means "quickly."
The standard polite wish for coworkers, teachers, and acquaintances.
"Don't be sick." An affectionate line for a friend, partner, or child.
"Take good care of your health." Common for someone recovering at home or after surgery.
"I wish you a speedy recovery." Formal, used in cards, flowers, and messages to elders or bosses.

examples.context: Texting a friend who caught a cold
Your partner is sick in bed
Your teacher is out sick

tips: Watch the spelling. The verb is 낫다 (to get better), and its ㅅ drops before a vowel: 나아, 나으세요. Writing 낳으세요 means "please give birth," a common typo even among Koreans.
아프지 마 sounds a little like a command, but it is caring. You will hear it a lot in dramas between couples and close friends.
When visiting someone in the hospital, Koreans often bring a box of drinks or fruit along with their wishes.

faq.q: How do you write get well soon in a card in Korean?
faq.a: For a friend, 빨리 나아! works. For an elder or boss, write 빠른 쾌유를 빕니다 (I wish you a speedy recovery) for a formal, respectful tone.

faq.q: What does 아프지 마 mean?
faq.a: It means "don't be sick" or "don't get hurt." It is a caring, casual phrase said to someone close.

intro: "Happy Chuseok" in Korean is 즐거운 추석 보내세요 (jeulgeoun chuseok bonaeseyo), meaning "have a happy Chuseok." With friends, 추석 잘 보내 (chuseok jal bonae) is the easy casual version.

ways.note: The standard holiday wish for coworkers, teachers, neighbors, and friends' parents.
"Have a good Chuseok." What friends say before everyone heads to their hometowns.
The same simple wish in polite form.
"Have an abundant Hangawi." 한가위 is the native Korean name for Chuseok. You will see this on cards, banners, and gift boxes.
Formal, for business messages and greetings to clients.

examples.context: Saying bye to a classmate before the holiday
Leaving the office before the long weekend
A holiday text to your Korean teacher

tips: Chuseok is the autumn harvest holiday, held on the 15th day of the 8th lunar month, so it usually falls in September or early October. It lasts three days, and many people travel to their hometowns.
Families hold memorial rites for ancestors (차례), visit graves, and make 송편 (songpyeon), half-moon rice cakes. Gift sets of fruit, meat, or Spam are a big tradition.
A traditional saying goes 더도 말고 덜도 말고 한가위만 같아라: "no more, no less, may every day be like Hangawi." It is a nice line to add to a card.

faq.q: Is Chuseok Korean Thanksgiving?
faq.a: It is often called that in English because it is a harvest festival centered on family and food. It also includes honoring ancestors, which makes it different from American Thanksgiving.

faq.q: What is the difference between 추석 and 한가위?
faq.a: They are the same holiday. 추석 comes from Chinese characters, while 한가위 is the native Korean name and sounds more poetic.

intro: "You can do it" in Korean is 할 수 있어 (hal su isseo), literally "(you) can do (it)." Politely, say 할 수 있어요 (hal su isseoyo). Koreans also cheer each other on with 힘내 (himnae) and 화이팅 (hwaiting).

ways.note: To friends and family before a challenge. Adding 넌 (you) makes it stronger: 넌 할 수 있어.
The same encouragement for coworkers, classmates, or anyone you speak politely to.
"Cheer up" or "stay strong." Best when someone is tired, stressed, or going through a hard time.
The polite "stay strong." Fans often write it to idols and actors.
The all-purpose cheer, from English "fighting." Use it before games, exams, work, anything.

examples.context: Your friend is nervous before a race
A friend is pulling an all-nighter
examples.en: Hang in there a little longer!

examples.context: Cheering for your team

tips: 할 수 있다 is the basic "can do" pattern: verb stem + ㄹ 수 있다. Once you know it, you can say 갈 수 있어 (I can go) or 먹을 수 있어 (I can eat it).
The dictionary spelling is 파이팅, but 화이팅 is just as common in everyday writing. Both are pronounced close to "hwa-i-ting" or "pa-i-ting."
힘내 is for when someone is struggling, and 화이팅 is for when someone is about to start something. 할 수 있어 fits both.

faq.q: What does hwaiting mean in Korean?
faq.a: 화이팅 comes from the English word "fighting" and means "go for it" or "you can do it." Koreans say it to cheer people on before any challenge.

faq.q: What is the difference between 힘내 and 화이팅?
faq.a: 힘내 means "find your strength" and comforts someone who is tired or having a hard time. 화이팅 is a cheerful push before a challenge.

intro: "Mom" in Korean is 엄마 (eomma), the warm, everyday word children and adults use with their own mother. In more formal or respectful situations Koreans say 어머니 (eomeoni), and for someone else's mother or a mother-in-law they say 어머님 (eomeonim).

ways.note: The everyday word for your own mom, used by kids and adults alike. Use it when talking to her or about her with friends.
"Mother." More respectful and grown-up. Used when speaking formally about your mother, in letters and speeches, and by some adult sons when talking to their mom.
The honorific form. Used for someone else's mother, a friend's mom, or your mother-in-law. Not usually used for your own mom.
"My mom." Koreans say 우리 (our) rather than 내 (my) when talking about family members.

examples.context: Calling out when you get home
Asking politely about a friend's mother
Talking about your family

tips: Koreans almost always say 우리 엄마 ("our mom") instead of 내 엄마 ("my mom"), even when they are an only child. Saying 내 엄마 sounds odd or overly possessive.

엄마 is not just for children. Many adults keep calling their mother 엄마 their whole life. 어머니 sounds more formal and is common in speeches, writing and when a grown man speaks respectfully about his mother.
When you meet a friend's mother, greet her as 어머님 (eomeonim), not 엄마. Using 엄마 for someone else's mom would sound strange.

faq.q: What is the difference between 엄마 and 어머니?
faq.a: Both mean mother. 엄마 is the warm, casual word like "mom," while 어머니 is more formal and respectful, like "mother."

faq.q: How do you say "I love you, Mom" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 엄마 사랑해 (eomma saranghae) casually, or 엄마 사랑해요 (eomma saranghaeyo) to sound a little more polite and sweet.

faq.q: Does Korea have Mother's Day?
faq.a: Korea celebrates Parents' Day, 어버이날 (eobeoinal), on May 8 for both mothers and fathers. People often give carnations and say thank you to their parents.

intro: "Dad" in Korean is 아빠 (appa), the everyday word for your own father. In formal or respectful situations Koreans say 아버지 (abeoji), and for someone else's father or a father-in-law they say 아버님 (abeonim).

ways.note: The everyday word for your own dad. Kids use it, and many adults, especially daughters, keep using it.
"Father." More respectful and grown-up. Common in formal speech, writing, and when adult sons talk to or about their father.
The honorific form for someone else's father, a friend's dad, or your father-in-law.
"My dad." Koreans say 우리 (our) instead of 내 (my) for family members.

examples.context: Asking on the phone when he will be home
Asking politely about someone's father
examples.en: Is your father in good health?

examples.context: Telling a friend about your dad

tips: Use 우리 아빠 ("our dad") when talking about your father. 내 아빠 ("my dad") sounds unnatural to Koreans.
Many grown men switch from 아빠 to 아버지 as they get older, while many women keep saying 아빠. Both are normal, and 아버지 is the safe choice in formal settings.
When you meet a friend's or partner's father, call him 아버님 (abeonim). It shows respect and is what Koreans actually say.

faq.q: What is the difference between 아빠 and 아버지?
faq.a: Both mean father. 아빠 is the casual, affectionate "dad," while 아버지 is the respectful "father" used in more formal situations.

faq.q: How do you say "I love you, Dad" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 아빠 사랑해 (appa saranghae) casually, or 아빠 사랑해요 (appa saranghaeyo) to sound a little more polite.

faq.q: Does Korea have Father's Day?
faq.a: Not separately. Korea celebrates Parents' Day, 어버이날 (eobeoinal), on May 8 for both parents.

intro: "Older brother" in Korean is 오빠 (oppa) if you are female and 형 (hyung) if you are male. Korean has no single word for "brother": the word depends on whether the speaker is a woman or a man, and both words are also used for close older men who are not family.

ways.note: Used by women and girls for an older brother, and also for older male friends or a boyfriend.
Used by men and boys for an older brother, and also for older male friends, teammates or coworkers they are close to.
"My actual older brother" (said by a woman). Used to make clear you mean a blood relative, since 오빠 is also used for friends and boyfriends.
A respectful version of 형, used by men for an older man they respect. It is also a sister-in-law term in some families.
An old-fashioned, very respectful form of 오빠. You mostly hear it in historical dramas or as a joke.

examples.context: A girl asking her brother where he is going
A boy complaining to his older brother
A man talking about his family
examples.en: My older brother is a soldier.

tips: The speaker's gender decides the word, not the brother's. A woman says 오빠 and a man says 형. A man saying 오빠 sounds like a joke.
Koreans use 오빠 and 형 for older people who are not family at all: a close older friend, a senior at school, or (for 오빠) a boyfriend. That is why fans call male idols 오빠.
You usually call your older brother 오빠 or 형 directly, not by his name. Calling an older sibling by name can sound rude.

faq.q: Can a guy say oppa?
faq.a: Not normally. Men say 형 (hyung) for an older brother or older male friend. A man saying 오빠 is usually joking.

faq.q: Does oppa only mean brother?
faq.a: No. Women also use 오빠 for older male friends and boyfriends. To say you mean a real brother, use 친오빠 (chinoppa).

faq.q: How do you say "brother" without knowing who is older?
faq.a: The general word for brothers is 형제 (hyeongje), and for a younger brother it is 남동생 (namdongsaeng). In everyday speech Koreans almost always specify older or younger.

intro: "Older sister" in Korean is 언니 (unnie) if you are female and 누나 (noona) if you are male. The word depends on the speaker's gender, and both are also used for close older women who are not family.

ways.note: Used by women and girls for an older sister, and also for older female friends or coworkers they are close to.
Used by men and boys for an older sister, and also for older female friends.
"My actual older sister" (said by a woman). Makes clear you mean a blood relative.
"My actual older sister" (said by a man).
A respectful form of 누나, used by men for an older woman. It sounds formal or playful today.

examples.context: A woman asking her sister's opinion while shopping
A boy thanking his older sister
A man introducing his family politely
examples.en: My older sister is a nurse.

tips: A woman says 언니 and a man says 누나. It depends on who is speaking, not on the sister.
Women in Korea often call a friendly older woman 언니, and some use it for female staff in shops and restaurants. It feels warm and friendly.
언니 is usually romanized as "unnie" by fans, but the Revised Romanization is "eonni." Both are pronounced the same.

faq.q: What is the difference between unnie and noona?
faq.a: Both mean older sister. Women say 언니 (unnie) and men say 누나 (noona).

faq.q: Can I call an older friend unnie?
faq.a: Yes, if you are a woman and you are close. Koreans commonly call older female friends 언니 instead of using their name.

faq.q: How do you say "my sister" in Korean?
faq.a: A woman says 우리 언니 for an older sister, a man says 우리 누나, and anyone says 여동생 (yeodongsaeng) for a younger sister.

intro: "Younger sibling" in Korean is 동생 (dongsaeng), and it works for both boys and girls no matter who is speaking. To be specific, say 남동생 (namdongsaeng) for a younger brother and 여동생 (yeodongsaeng) for a younger sister.

ways.note: Any younger sibling. Also used for a younger friend you treat like family.
Younger brother. 남 means male.
Younger sister. 여 means female.
The youngest in a family or group. K-pop fans know it as the youngest member of a band.

examples.context: Introducing your younger sibling
Talking about your family
Asking about someone's sister
examples.en: How old is your younger sister?

tips: Unlike 오빠, 언니, 형 and 누나, the word 동생 is not used to call your sibling. Older siblings just call a younger one by name.
동생 is the same no matter if the speaker is male or female, which makes it easier than the words for older siblings.
Koreans also call a younger friend 동생 when describing the relationship, for example 친한 동생 (a younger friend I'm close to).

faq.q: How do you say "little brother" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 남동생 (namdongsaeng). In casual talk many people just say 동생 when it is clear.

faq.q: How do you say "little sister" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 여동생 (yeodongsaeng).

faq.q: Do I call my younger sibling dongsaeng?
faq.a: Usually not to their face. Koreans call younger siblings by their name and use 동생 when talking about them.

intro: "Grandma" in Korean is 할머니 (halmeoni). It works for your own grandmother and is also a polite way to address any elderly woman. Koreans often add 친 or 외 to say whether she is on the father's or mother's side.

ways.note: Grandma or grandmother. Use it for your own grandmother or any elderly woman.
Grandmother on your father's side.
Grandmother on your mother's side.
An extra-respectful form, used for someone else's grandmother.
A dialect word from the Gyeongsang region (Busan, Daegu). Warm and folksy.

examples.context: Calling your grandmother
Telling a friend your weekend plan
examples.en: I'm going to my grandma's house.

examples.context: Inviting your grandmother to eat

tips: With grandparents, Koreans use honorific words: 진지 instead of 밥 for a meal, 댁 instead of 집 for a home, and 드시다 instead of 먹다 for eating.
Strangers will call an elderly woman 할머니 too, for example on the bus or at a market. It is polite, not an insult.
In casual talk, people often skip 친 and 외 and just say 할머니. The prefixes come up when you need to be clear.

faq.q: What does oehalmeoni mean?
faq.a: 외할머니 (oehalmeoni) is your mother's mother. 외 refers to the mother's side of the family.

faq.q: Can I call any old woman halmeoni?
faq.a: Yes. Koreans politely call elderly women 할머니 even if they are not related.

faq.q: How do you say "I love you, Grandma" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 할머니 사랑해요 (halmeoni saranghaeyo).

intro: "Grandpa" in Korean is 할아버지 (harabeoji). It is used for your own grandfather and also as a polite way to address any elderly man. Add 친 for your father's side and 외 for your mother's side.

ways.note: Grandpa or grandfather. Also used for any elderly man.
Grandfather on your father's side.
Grandfather on your mother's side.
An extra-respectful form, used for someone else's grandfather.
A dialect word from the Gyeongsang region. Warm and folksy.

examples.context: Saying good night to your grandfather
Talking about your grandfather
Wishing him a happy birthday

tips: Use honorific words with grandparents: 생신 instead of 생일 for birthday, 주무시다 instead of 자다 for sleep. It shows real respect.
할아버지 is pronounced "ha-ra-beo-ji" because the ㄹ sound links into the next syllable.
Koreans politely call any elderly man 할아버지, so you will hear it on the street and in shops.

faq.q: What does oeharabeoji mean?
faq.a: 외할아버지 (oeharabeoji) is your mother's father.

faq.q: Why is it spelled harabeoji and not halabeoji?
faq.a: When ㄹ comes before a vowel it sounds like a light r, so 할아버지 sounds like "harabeoji."

faq.q: How do I say good night to my grandpa in Korean?
faq.a: Say 할아버지 안녕히 주무세요 (harabeoji annyeonghi jumuseyo). It is the respectful way to say good night to elders.

intro: "Friend" in Korean is 친구 (chingu). In Korea it usually means someone your own age, while friends who are older or younger are often called by words like 언니, 오빠, 형, 누나 or 동생.

ways.note: Friend. The everyday word, mostly for people the same age as you.
A polite way to say "your friend" or someone else's friend, especially when speaking to elders.
Slang for a male friend who is just a friend, not a boyfriend. Short for 남자 사람 친구.
Slang for a female friend who is just a friend, not a girlfriend.
"Same age." Koreans say 우리 동갑이에요 (we're the same age) when becoming friends.

examples.context: Introducing someone
Telling someone what you did
examples.en: I hung out with a friend.

examples.context: Asking someone to be friends

tips: Age matters for friendship in Korea. 친구 is mainly for people born in the same year. With someone even a year older, you would usually call them 언니, 오빠, 형 or 누나.
Two people often become friends after finding out they are the same age and saying 우리 친구 하자 (let's be friends), then switching to casual speech.
남사친 and 여사친 are handy words to make clear a friend is not a romantic partner, which comes up a lot in Korean dramas.

faq.q: Can I call an older person chingu?
faq.a: You can describe them as a friend, but you would usually address them as 언니, 오빠, 형, 누나 or 선배 rather than by name or as 친구.

faq.q: How do you say "my friend" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 제 친구 (je chingu) politely or 내 친구 (nae chingu) casually.

faq.q: What does yeosachin mean?
faq.a: 여사친 means a female friend who is only a friend, as opposed to 여친 (girlfriend).

intro: "Best friend" in Korean is 절친 (jeolchin), short for 절친한 친구 (a very close friend). Younger people also say 베프 (bepeu), from the English "best friend."

ways.note: The most common word for a best friend or very close friend.
Short for 베스트 프렌드 (best friend). Popular with teens and young adults.
A close pal you are always with, often a friend from school days.
Slang for a "real friend," someone so close you can be completely yourself.
A childhood friend, someone you played with when you were little.

examples.context: Introducing your best friend
Reminding a friend how close you are
Talking about a trip
examples.en: I went on a trip with my best friend.

tips: 절친 is a safe, natural choice in any situation. 베프 and 찐친 sound younger and more playful.
Korean friendships are often tied to age and school year, so a best friend is usually someone born in the same year.
Koreans often say 친한 친구 (chinhan chingu), "close friend," when they mean a good friend but not necessarily the very best one.

faq.q: What does jeolchin mean?
faq.a: 절친 is short for 절친한 친구, meaning a very close friend or best friend.

faq.q: Do Koreans say BFF?
faq.a: Not usually. They say 베프 (bepeu) for best friend, or 절친 (jeolchin).

faq.q: What is the difference between 절친 and 친한 친구?
faq.a: 친한 친구 means a close friend. 절친 is stronger and is closer to "best friend."

intro: "Teacher" in Korean is 선생님 (seonsaengnim). Students use it both to talk about a teacher and to call them directly, and the respectful ending 님 is always included.

ways.note: The standard way to say and address a teacher. Also used for doctors and other respected professionals.
A friendly, shortened form students use with teachers they are close to, like "teach." Common in schools and online classes.
Professor. Used at university instead of 선생님.
The word without 님. Fine in writing or job titles, but calling a teacher just 선생 to their face is rude.

examples.context: Raising your hand in class
A student thanking a teacher after class
Introducing your Korean teacher

tips: In Korea you do not call a teacher by their first name. Say 선생님 alone, or their family name plus 선생님, like 김 선생님 (Teacher Kim).
선생님 is also a respectful title for doctors, artists and other experts, so you will hear it in hospitals too.
쌤 is friendly but casual. Use 선생님 until a teacher seems happy with the shorter form.

faq.q: What does ssaem mean?
faq.a: 쌤 is a casual, shortened form of 선생님 (teacher) used by students.

faq.q: Can I call my teacher by name in Korean?
faq.a: Not by their first name. Use 선생님, or their family name plus 선생님, like 박 선생님.

faq.q: What do you call a professor in Korean?
faq.a: 교수님 (gyosunim).

intro: "Family" in Korean is 가족 (gajok). To say "my family," Koreans say 우리 가족 (uri gajok), and you may also hear 식구 (sikgu), a warm word for the people who live and eat together.

ways.note: The standard word for family.
"My family," literally "our family." The natural way to talk about your own family.
Family members who live together, literally "mouths to eat." Also used warmly for close teams or pets.
Household or home. Used in more formal or written contexts, like 가정의 달 (family month).
"Your family" in a polite, respectful way.

examples.context: Describing your family
examples.en: There are five people in my family.

examples.context: Talking about your evening
examples.en: I have dinner with my family.

examples.context: A warm wish at the end of a letter
examples.en: I hope your whole family stays healthy.

tips: Koreans say 우리 가족 ("our family") even when speaking only about their own. 내 가족 sounds unnatural in most situations.
식구 has a homey feeling. Coworkers or a close team might say 우리는 한 식구야, "we're one family."
May is called 가정의 달 (family month) in Korea, with Children's Day on May 5 and Parents' Day on May 8.

faq.q: How do you say "my family" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 우리 가족 (uri gajok), literally "our family."

faq.q: What is the difference between 가족 and 식구?
faq.a: 가족 is the general word for family. 식구 means the people who live and eat together, and it sounds warmer and more everyday.

faq.q: How do you ask how many people are in someone's family?
faq.a: Ask 가족이 몇 명이에요? (gajogi myeot myeongieyo?), "How many people are in your family?"

intro: "Baby" in Korean is 아기 (agi) when you mean an actual infant or newborn. If you mean "baby" as a pet name for a partner, Koreans usually say 자기야 (jagiya), and some couples say 애기야 (aegiya).

ways.note: Newborn or infant meaning. The standard word for a baby.
Both meanings. A very common spoken form of 아기 for a real baby, and also a cute pet name for a partner, like "babe."
Newborn meaning. What people say when talking directly to a baby or a small child, like "little one."
Newborn meaning. Specifically a newborn baby, only days or weeks old.
Pet name meaning. The most common way couples call each other "baby" or "honey."

examples.context: Whispering in a quiet room (infant)
Talking to a little child (infant)
Texting your partner (pet name)

tips: For a real baby, use 아기. For your boyfriend or girlfriend, 아기 sounds odd, so use 자기야 or the cute spoken form 애기야.
아기 is the standard spelling. 애기 is how many people actually say it in everyday speech, and couples like it as a pet name.
Some couples also say 베이비 (beibi), borrowed from English, but it usually sounds playful or jokey.

faq.q: How do you call your boyfriend or girlfriend "baby" in Korean?
faq.a: The most common pet name is 자기야 (jagiya). Some couples use 애기야 (aegiya), which sounds extra cute.

faq.q: Is it 아기 or 애기?
faq.a: 아기 is the standard spelling for a baby. 애기 is a very common spoken form and is also used as a pet name.

faq.q: How do you say "newborn" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 갓난아기 (gannanagi) or 신생아 (sinsaenga), which is the more medical word.

intro: "Oh my god" in Korean is usually 세상에 (sesange), which literally means "in the world" and works with anyone. In everyday speech you will also hear short exclamations like 어머 (eomeo), 헐 (heol) and 아이고 (aigo), each with its own feel.

ways.note: The closest match to "oh my god". Safe with anyone, for good or bad surprises.
A quick gasp, like "oh my!" Heard more often from women, but anyone can use it.
Young, slangy "OMG" or "what?!" for shock or disbelief. Keep it to friends.
A sigh of surprise, worry or tiredness, like "oh dear". Very common with older people.
"OMG, amazing!" for exciting surprises. Casual slang.
"Good heavens." Sounds dramatic or old-fashioned, more common in books and subtitles.

examples.context: Seeing a messy room

chips.g: oh my god (lit. in the world)

examples.en: Oh my god, what is this?

examples.context: Seeing a cute dress in a shop
examples.en: Oh my god, it's so pretty!

examples.context: Hearing shocking news from a friend

tips: Koreans do not usually translate "oh my god" word for word. They reach for a short sound instead: 세상에 for real astonishment, 어머 for a little gasp, 헐 for "wait, what?", and 아이고 when something is tiring or worrying.
You will sometimes hear the English "oh my god" said as 오 마이 갓 (o mai gat), usually as a joke. It is fine with friends but sounds playful, not sincere.
헐 and 대박 are slang. With teachers, bosses or older strangers, 세상에 or a polite reaction like 정말요? (jeongmallyo, "really?") is safer.

faq.q: What does 세상에 mean literally?
faq.a: 세상 means "the world" and 에 means "in", so 세상에 is literally "in the world". It is used like "oh my god" or "good grief".

faq.q: Is 어머 only for girls?
faq.a: It is heard more from women, and some men avoid it for that reason, but it is not wrong for anyone to say. Men often say 헐 or 와 (wa) instead.

faq.q: How do Koreans write OMG in texts?
faq.a: 헐 and 대박 are the most common. People also type ㄷㄷ, a short form of 덜덜, the sound of shaking, for "that's scary" or "wow".

intro: "Really?" in Korean is 진짜? (jinjja?) with friends, or 진짜요? (jinjjayo?) when you need to be polite. 정말? (jeongmal?) means the same thing and sounds a little softer.

ways.note: The everyday "really?" with friends. Also means "really" or "so" inside a sentence.
Add 요 to make it polite for coworkers, shop staff or anyone older.
Same meaning as 진짜, a bit softer and more standard. Also used in writing.
Polite and gentle. Pronounced "jeongmallyo", with a double L sound.
"Is that so?" when said with a rising tone. Polite version: 그래요? (geuraeyo?).

examples.context: A friend says they never knew a secret
A coworker shares good news
Tasting food at a friend's parents' house

tips: Your voice does the work. Said with a rising tone, 진짜? is a question ("really?"). Said flat inside a sentence, 진짜 just means "really" or "very", as in 진짜 좋아 (jinjja joa, "I really like it").
진짜 is more casual and spoken. 정말 is a touch softer and is the one you will see in writing. In polite speech, both work with 요.
To an older person, a bare 진짜? can sound too familiar. Adding 요 is a small change that makes a big difference.

faq.q: What is the difference between 진짜 and 정말?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. 진짜 is more casual and common in speech, while 정말 sounds slightly softer and more standard.

faq.q: How do I say "really?" politely?
faq.a: Say 진짜요? (jinjjayo?) or 정말요? (jeongmallyo?). 그래요? (geuraeyo?), "is that so?", is also polite and very common.

intro: "Wow" in Korean is 와 (wa), and you can stretch it out as 와~ for more feeling. 우와 (uwa) is a bigger, cuter wow, and 대박 (daebak) is the slangy "that's amazing".

ways.note: The basic wow. Works with anyone, in any situation.
A bigger, more excited wow. Sounds a little cute or childlike.
"Amazing!" or "no way!" Casual slang, very common with friends.
"That's cool!" Said about something or someone impressive. Polite: 멋있어요 (meosisseoyo).
A shocked wow, closer to "whoa, what?" Young people's slang.

examples.context: Seeing a beautiful view
Looking out the window in winter
Reacting politely to a coworker's news

tips: Koreans often stretch 와 into a long "waaa" when they are really impressed. In texts you will see it written 와~ or 와아.
대박 is the go-to word for "awesome" among friends, but it is slang. With your boss or an older stranger, a simple 와 or 와, 멋있어요 is better.

faq.q: What is the difference between 와 and 우와?
faq.a: Both mean "wow". 우와 is louder and more excited, and it can sound a little cute, the way a child would say it.

faq.q: Can I say 대박 to older people?
faq.a: It is slang, so it can sound too casual. Many people use it lightly with friendly coworkers, but 와 is the safer choice.

intro: "What?" in Korean is 뭐? (mwo?) with friends, but when you just didn't hear someone, the polite and safe choice is 네? (ne?). For "what is it?" you say 뭐야? (mwoya?) casually or 뭐예요? (mwoyeyo?) politely.

ways.note: Said with a rising tone, "Pardon?" or "Sorry?" The safest way to say what when you didn't catch something.
A blunt "What?" Fine with friends, rude to elders or strangers.
"What did you say?" Can sound shocked or annoyed depending on tone.
Polite "What did you say?" Careful: a sharp tone makes it sound like "Excuse me?!"
"What is it?" or "What the...?" for surprise or annoyance.
Polite "What is it?" Use it to ask about a thing.

examples.context: Pointing at a dish in a restaurant
A friend mumbles something surprising
Asking a friend about dinner
examples.en: What do you want to eat?

tips: If you didn't hear something, don't say 뭐? to a teacher, boss or older person. It sounds like a rude "Huh?" Say 네? with a rising tone instead.
뭐 is the spoken form of 무엇 (mueot), the textbook word for "what". You will see 무엇 in writing and formal speech, but people almost always say 뭐 out loud.
Before a noun, "what" becomes 무슨 (museun): 무슨 일이에요? (museun irieyo?) means "What's going on?"

faq.q: How do I say "what?" politely when I didn't hear?
faq.a: Say 네? (ne?) with a rising tone, or 네? 다시 한번 말씀해 주세요 (ne? dasi hanbeon malsseumhae juseyo), "Sorry? Could you say that again, please?"

faq.q: What does 뭐야 mean?
faq.a: 뭐야 means "what is it?" or "what the...?" It is casual and often shows surprise or annoyance, so keep it to friends.

intro: "Why?" in Korean is 왜? (wae?) with friends and 왜요? (waeyo?) in polite speech. To ask "What's wrong?" you can say 왜 그래? (wae geurae?).

ways.note: The basic "why?" with friends and family. Also starts longer questions.
Polite "why?" Keep your tone soft, or it can sound like you are challenging the person.
"What's wrong?" or "Why are you acting like that?" Tone decides if it is caring or annoyed.
Polite and respectful "What's the matter?" Good for older people.
"How come?" Sounds a bit more serious or written.

examples.context: Comforting a friend in tears
Asking a friend who skipped a meetup
A close friend is acting strange
examples.en: Why are you being like this?

tips: A sharp 왜요? to a teacher or boss can sound like "Why should I?" If you are asking an older person what is wrong, 왜 그러세요? or 무슨 일 있으세요? (museun il isseuseyo?) sounds kinder.
왜 also answers someone calling your name. If a friend says your name, replying 왜? just means "Yeah? What's up?", not "why?"

faq.q: How do you say "because" in Korean?
faq.a: The word is 왜냐하면 (waenyahamyeon), often shortened to 왜냐면 (waenyamyeon). It usually starts the answer to a why question.

faq.q: Is 왜요 rude?
faq.a: No, it is polite. But a flat or sharp tone can make it sound defensive, so say it gently with people you respect.

intro: "Of course" in Korean is 물론이죠 (mullonijyo) in polite speech or 당연하지 (dangyeonhaji) with friends. 그럼 (geureom) and 그럼요 (geureomyo) are warm, everyday ways to say "sure, of course".

ways.note: A friendly, polite "of course" for coworkers, customers or new people.
"Of course!" or "Obviously!" with friends. Can sound teasing, like "duh".
Polite version of 당연하지. Confident and warm.
"Sure!" or "Of course!" Very natural with friends and family. It can also mean "then".
A soft, kind "of course". Older people use it a lot.
Formal "of course" for work, customer service or speeches.

examples.context: A friend asks if you want to come along
Reassuring a worried customer
A coworker asks for a hand

tips: 당연하지 literally means "it's obvious". Said warmly it is lovely, but said flatly it can sound like "obviously, duh". Smile when you say it.
그럼 has two jobs. As a reply it means "of course", and at the start of a sentence it means "then" or "in that case".

faq.q: What is the difference between 물론 and 당연?
faq.a: 물론 means "of course" and 당연 means "natural, obvious". 물론이죠 sounds friendly and polite, while 당연하지 is more casual and can be playful.

faq.q: How do I say "of course not"?
faq.a: Say 당연히 아니지 (dangyeonhi aniji) with friends, or 물론 아니죠 (mullon anijyo) politely.

intro: "Me too" in Korean is 저도요 (jeodoyo) in polite speech and 나도 (nado) with friends. The little word 도 (do) means "too" or "also", and you can stick it onto almost anything.

ways.note: With friends, partners and younger people. Short and very common.
Polite "me too" with 저, the humble word for "I". Use it with anyone older or new.
"Same here" or "I feel the same".
Polite "Same here". Good when agreeing with a feeling.
"It's the same for me." Formal, for work or speeches.

examples.context: Replying to a partner
A coworker says they are hungry
Agreeing with a tired coworker

tips: Match 나 with casual speech and 저 with polite speech. You will hear 나도요 now and then, but 저도요 is the correct polite form.
도 works on anything: 커피도 (keopido) is "coffee too", 오늘도 (oneuldo) is "today too". Once you know it, you will hear it everywhere.
In cute texting you may see 나두 (nadu) instead of 나도. It means the same thing, just softer.

faq.q: How do I say "I love you too" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 나도 사랑해 (nado saranghae) casually or 저도 사랑해요 (jeodo saranghaeyo) politely.

faq.q: How do I say "me neither"?
faq.a: Korean uses 도 for both. If someone says they don't like something, 나도 (nado) or 저도요 (jeodoyo) also means "me neither".

intro: "No way" in Korean is 말도 안 돼 (maldo an dwae), which literally means "it doesn't even make sense". If you mean "absolutely not" as a refusal, say 절대 안 돼 (jeoldae an dwae) instead.

ways.note: "No way!" or "That's ridiculous!" for disbelief. Very common.
Polite version for coworkers or older people.
"No way... surely not?" When you can't believe something might be true.
Slangy "No way!" or "What?!" with friends.
"Unbelievable" or "That's absurd". Shows you are shocked and a bit annoyed.
"No way" as a firm refusal: "absolutely not". Polite: 절대 안 돼요.

examples.context: Hearing a friend won the lottery
Finding out the sale ended
Refusing a risky idea

tips: English "no way" has two meanings, and Korean splits them. Disbelief is 말도 안 돼 or 설마. Refusal is 절대 안 돼 or just 안 돼 (an dwae, "you can't").
말도 안 돼 is spelled with a space between 안 and 돼. A common spelling mistake is 안 되 or 안돼; the standard form is 안 돼.

faq.q: What does 설마 mean?
faq.a: 설마 means "surely not" or "no way, don't tell me". It is used when you suspect something bad or surprising might be true.

faq.q: Is 말도 안 돼 rude?
faq.a: No, it is just casual. Add 요 (말도 안 돼요) for people you should be polite to.

intro: "Awesome" in Korean is most often 대박 (daebak), the go-to slang for anything amazing. For "the best" say 최고 (choego), and for "cool" say 멋있어 (meosisseo).

ways.note: "Awesome!" or "Amazing!" The most common reaction among friends.
"The best!" Often with a thumbs up. Fine with anyone.
Polite "It's the best" or "You're the best".
"Cool!" or "Looks great!" Polite: 멋있어요 (meosisseoyo).
Cute slang for "the best", as in 짱이야 (jjangiya). A little old-school now.
"Killer!" or "Amazing!" Strong praise, casual.

examples.context: Listening to a new song
A friend brings you snacks
Seeing a coworker's new photos

tips: 대박 originally meant a big jackpot. Today it is used for any big surprise, and sometimes even for bad ones, like 대박, 늦었다 (daebak, neujeotda, "oh no, I'm so late").
With people you should be polite to, 최고예요 or 멋있어요 sound warmer and more natural than slang.

faq.q: What does daebak mean?
faq.a: 대박 (daebak) means "awesome", "amazing" or "wow". It is casual slang used for exciting news, great food, a great performance and more.

faq.q: How do I say "you're awesome"?
faq.a: Say 너 최고야 (neo choegoya) to a friend, or 최고예요 (choegoyeyo) politely.

intro: "Crazy" in Korean is based on the verb 미치다 (michida), so "that's crazy" is 미쳤다 (michyeotda) and "are you crazy?" is 미쳤어? (michyeosseo?). Be careful: about a song or a view it is fun slang, but aimed at a person it can be quite rude.

ways.note: "That's insane!" about a thing, often as praise: a song, a goal, a view. Fine with friends. Not for elders or work.
"Are you crazy?" at a person. Close friends say it jokingly. To strangers, older people, parents, teachers or a boss it is rude, even with 요 added.
"It's no joke", meaning crazy good or crazy hard. Not rude at all. Polite: 장난 아니에요.
"That's crazy, no way." A safe way to show disbelief. Polite: 말도 안 돼요.
"Have you lost your mind?" Harsh and angry. Never to anyone older or anyone you need to respect.
"Are you in your right mind?" Very harsh, said in real anger. Never to elders, teachers or a boss.

examples.context: Hearing a great new song
Joking with a close friend who did something reckless
Seeing a long line at a restaurant

tips: How rude is it? 미쳤다 about a thing is everyday slang, fine among peers. 미쳤어? at a person is rude except between close friends who are joking. 정신 나갔어 and 제정신이야 are harsh and sound like a real fight. None of these belong with parents, grandparents, teachers, a boss, customers or older strangers.
미친 (michin, "crazy") before a noun can be praise, as in 미친 노래 (michin norae, "an insane song"). But 미친 put in front of a word for a person turns into a real insult. Do not use it about people.
If you are not sure, use 대박 (daebak) or 장난 아니다 instead. They show the same excitement with no risk of offending.

faq.q: Is 미쳤어 rude?
faq.a: It depends on who hears it. Between close friends joking around it is normal. To anyone older, to a stranger, or to someone you should respect, it is rude and can sound like an insult.

faq.q: Can I say 미쳤다 about something good?
faq.a: Yes. Young Koreans often say 미쳤다 about an amazing song, dance or meal. It is casual slang, so keep it to friends.

intro: "Shut up" in Korean is 닥쳐 (dakchyeo), but it is one of the rudest everyday words you can say, so most learners should use 조용히 해 (joyonghi hae), "be quiet", instead. In polite situations, say 조용히 해 주세요 (joyonghi hae juseyo), "please be quiet".

ways.note: "Be quiet." Blunt but not offensive. Fine with friends or younger siblings, too bossy for elders.
"Please be quiet." The only safe version for strangers, customers or older people.
"Stop it." Blunt but not a swear word. Used with friends and family.
"You're so loud!" Used like a teasing "shut up" between friends or siblings. Rude to anyone older.
"Shut your mouth." Rude and harsh. Never to elders, teachers, a boss or strangers.
"Shut up!" Very rude and aggressive, the word you hear in drama fights. Never say it to parents, elders, teachers, a boss, customers or strangers.

examples.context: Asking people in a library to keep it down
Teasing a little brother
A friend keeps teasing you

tips: From mildest to rudest: 조용히 해 주세요 (polite), 조용히 해 and 그만해 (blunt), 시끄러워 (teasing, rude to elders), 입 다물어 (rude), 닥쳐 (very rude). The last two can start a real fight.

Even very close friends only say 닥쳐 jokingly, and plenty of people find it offensive even then. Never say it, even as a joke, to parents, grandparents, teachers, a boss, customers or anyone older or unfamiliar.
If you just want quiet, asking softly works best in Korea: 조금만 조용히 해 주세요 (jogeumman joyonghi hae juseyo) means "Please be a little quieter."

faq.q: How rude is 닥쳐?
faq.a: Very rude. It is like an angry "shut up!" and is used in fights. It is never acceptable with elders, teachers, a boss or strangers.

faq.q: How do I politely ask someone to be quiet?
faq.a: Say 조용히 해 주세요 (joyonghi hae juseyo), or more softly, 조금만 조용히 해 주세요 (jogeumman joyonghi hae juseyo).

intro: "Stupid" in Korean is most often 바보 (babo), which is mild and often said with affection, like "silly" or "dummy". 멍청해 (meongcheonghae) is a stronger "stupid" that can really hurt when you aim it at someone.

ways.note: "Silly" or "dummy". Mild, often playful between couples and friends. Still never call a parent, teacher or older person 바보.
"That's silly" or "I feel stupid". Safe when you say it about yourself.
"Stupid" or "dumb". Rude when said about a person. Never to elders, teachers, a boss or strangers.
"Idiot." A real insult. Only between very close friends joking, and never to anyone older.
"Pathetic." Cold and hurtful, even more than calling someone stupid. Avoid it with people.
"A foolish idea." 어리석다 (eoriseokda) is a serious, bookish word, usually about a decision or idea rather than a person.

examples.context: After forgetting your keys
Gently correcting a partner
Discussing a plan at work

tips: How rude is it? 바보 is mild and often sweet between couples or friends. 멍청이 and 멍청해 are real insults when aimed at someone. 한심해 is cold and hurtful. None of these should ever be said to parents, grandparents, teachers, a boss, customers or older people, not even as a joke.
Saying these words about yourself is fine and common: 나 바보야 (na baboya) means "I'm such a dummy."
Dramas also use much stronger insults than these. They are offensive, so this page leaves them out. If you hear a word in a fight scene, assume it is not safe to repeat.

faq.q: Is 바보 rude?
faq.a: Usually not very. Between friends or couples it is playful, like "silly". But calling an older person 바보 is disrespectful.

faq.q: What is the difference between 바보 and 멍청이?
faq.a: 바보 is mild and often affectionate. 멍청이 is stronger and sounds like a real insult, closer to "idiot".

intro: "Funny" in Korean is 웃겨 (utgyeo) with friends and 웃겨요 (utgyeoyo) politely, from the verb 웃기다 (utgida), "to make someone laugh". If you mean "fun" rather than "makes me laugh", use 재미있어 (jaemiisseo).

ways.note: "That's funny" or "You're funny." Something that makes you laugh.
Polite "It's funny." Fine with coworkers and new people.
"It's fun" or "It's interesting." Short for 재미있어. Use for movies, games, people.
Polite "It's fun" or "It's interesting."
Slang for "super fun" or "hilarious". Literally "honey fun".
Texting laughter, like "lol" or "haha". The more ㅋ, the funnier.

examples.context: Laughing at a friend's joke
Talking about a movie
Sharing a video with a friend

tips: 웃기다 means something makes you laugh. 재미있다 means something is fun or interesting. A boring lecture is not 재미있어, and a great board game is 재미있어 even if nobody laughs.
Careful with tone: 웃기네 (utgine) said flatly is sarcastic, like "That's ridiculous" or "Don't make me laugh." Said with a smile, it is just "that's funny".
In texts Koreans laugh with ㅋㅋㅋ (from the sound "keu") or ㅎㅎ (a softer "hehe").

faq.q: What is the difference between 웃기다 and 재미있다?
faq.a: 웃기다 is "funny, makes me laugh". 재미있다 is "fun or interesting". A comedy is both; a good mystery novel is 재미있다 but not 웃기다.

faq.q: How do Koreans say "lol"?
faq.a: They type ㅋㅋㅋ (kekeke) or ㅎㅎ (hehe). More ㅋ means more laughter.

intro: "Don't worry" in Korean is 걱정하지 마세요 (geokjeonghaji maseyo) in polite speech and 걱정 마 (geokjeong ma) with friends. Adding 괜찮아 (gwaenchana), "it's okay", makes it extra comforting.

ways.note: Short and warm "Don't worry" for friends, partners and family.
The full casual form. Sounds a little more sincere.
Short polite version, natural with anyone.
The standard polite "Don't worry". Safe with anyone older or new.
"It's okay." Often said together with 걱정 마. Polite: 괜찮아요.
Formal, for customer service, announcements or work.

examples.context: Offering to handle a task
Comforting someone after a small accident
Calling home before a trip

tips: The pattern -지 마 (-ji ma) means "don't". Once you know 걱정하지 마, you can also say 울지 마 (ulji ma, "don't cry") and 가지 마 (gaji ma, "don't go").
Koreans often pair comfort words together: 걱정 마, 괜찮아 ("don't worry, it's okay") or 걱정 마, 잘될 거야 (geokjeong ma, jaldoel geoya, "don't worry, it'll work out").

faq.q: How do I say "don't worry about it" when someone apologizes?
faq.a: Say 괜찮아요 (gwaenchanayo), "it's okay", or 신경 쓰지 마세요 (singyeong sseuji maseyo), "don't worry about it".

faq.q: What is the difference between 걱정 마 and 걱정하지 마?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. 걱정 마 is shorter and more casual; 걱정하지 마 is the full form and sounds a bit more careful.

intro: "Delicious" in Korean is 맛있어요 (masisseoyo), the polite way to say a food tastes good. With friends you can drop the ending and just say 맛있어 (masisseo). It is one of the most useful words you can learn before a trip to Korea.

ways.note: The safe default for restaurant staff, hosts and anyone you don't know well.
With friends, family or younger people. Say it with a question tone to ask "Is it good?"
The plain form. People blurt it out to themselves right after the first bite, so it works in any company as an exclamation.
Very polite and a little stiff. Good for complimenting a meal at a business dinner or on camera.
Slang for "super tasty". Common online and among young friends, but the first part comes from a vulgar word, so keep it away from elders.

examples.context: Complimenting the food at a restaurant
Taking the first bite of street food
Asking a friend about their dish

tips: The ㅆ at the end of 맛있 links into the next syllable, so 맛있어요 sounds like "ma-shi-sseo-yo". You will also hear "ma-di-sseo-yo", and both are accepted.
The opposite is 맛없어요 (madeopseoyo), "it doesn't taste good". Koreans rarely say this to a cook's face. If you didn't love something, a gentle 괜찮아요 (gwaenchanayo, "it's okay") is kinder.
Before a meal people say 잘 먹겠습니다 (jal meokgesseumnida) and after it 잘 먹었습니다 (jal meogeosseumnida). Adding 맛있었어요 (masisseosseoyo, "it was delicious") when you pay makes restaurant owners smile.

faq.q: How do you pronounce 맛있어요?
faq.a: Say "ma-shi-sseo-yo", with a slightly stronger ss sound. The romanization is masisseoyo.

faq.q: How do you say "it was delicious" in Korean?
faq.a: Use the past tense: 맛있었어요 (masisseosseoyo). It is a nice thing to say when you leave a restaurant or finish a meal someone cooked.

faq.q: What does 존맛 mean?
faq.a: 존맛 (jonmat) is slang for "really, really tasty". It is very casual and a bit crude, so use it only with close friends.

intro: "How much" in Korean is 얼마예요? (eolmayeyo?), which means "How much is it?" Point at something and add 이거 (igeo, "this") to ask about a specific item. It works in shops, markets, taxis and cafes.

ways.note: The everyday way to ask a price. Polite enough for any shop.
"How much is this?" Point at the item as you say it.
"How much is it all together?" Useful at a market stall when you buy several things.
With friends, for example asking what they paid for something.
Very formal. You will hear it in textbooks and announcements more than in shops.

examples.context: Pointing at an item in a market
Paying for several things at a stall
examples.en: How much is it all together?

examples.context: Asking a friend about a bag they like

tips: The correct spelling is 얼마예요, not 얼마에요. After a word ending in a vowel, "is" becomes 예요. Many Koreans misspell it too, so don't worry if you see both.
Prices are said with Sino-Korean numbers plus 원 (won): 천 원 (cheon won) is 1,000 won and 만 원 (man won) is 10,000 won. If the number is too fast, ask the seller to show you on a calculator or phone.
In traditional markets a little bargaining is sometimes fine. You can try 좀 깎아 주세요 (jom kkakka juseyo, "a small discount, please"). In shops and department stores prices are fixed.

faq.q: Is it 얼마예요 or 얼마에요?
faq.a: 얼마예요 is the correct spelling. 얼마에요 is a very common mistake, even among native speakers.

faq.q: How do you ask for a discount in Korean?
faq.a: Say 좀 깎아 주세요 (jom kkakka juseyo). It is most natural at street markets, not in chain stores.

intro: "Where is the bathroom?" in Korean is 화장실 어디예요? (hwajangsil eodiyeyo?). 화장실 means bathroom or restroom, and 어디예요 means "where is it". It is short, polite and works anywhere.

ways.note: The everyday version. Polite enough for staff in restaurants, shops and stations.
The same question with the subject marker 이 added. Slightly more complete, same politeness.
Literally "Where is the bathroom located?" Just as common as 어디예요.
For friends, for example at a friend's apartment or a party.
Very formal. Fine, but it can sound stiff in everyday places.

examples.context: Asking a server in a restaurant
Looking for a restroom in a shopping mall
Visiting a friend's apartment

tips: To get a staff member's attention first, say 저기요 (jeogiyo), which works like "excuse me". Then ask your question.
Public restrooms in Korea are usually free, and subway stations almost always have one. Look for 남 (men) and 여 (women) on the doors, or the signs 남자 and 여자.
화장실 is pronounced "hwa-jang-shil". If you add the subject marker it becomes 화장실이, which sounds like "hwa-jang-shi-ri".

faq.q: How do you say bathroom in Korean?
faq.a: Bathroom or restroom is 화장실 (hwajangsil). The same word is used for homes and public places.

faq.q: What do 남 and 여 mean on restroom doors?
faq.a: 남 means men and 여 means women. They are short for 남자 (namja) and 여자 (yeoja).

intro: "Water" in Korean is 물 (mul). To ask for some, say 물 좀 주세요 (mul jom juseyo), "Some water, please." It is one of the first words worth learning for eating out in Korea.

ways.note: The basic word for water. You can say it on its own with a questioning look and be understood.
"Some water, please." 좀 softens the request and makes it sound friendlier.
The same request to a friend or family member.
Bottled mineral water, the word you see in convenience stores.
Cold water. Warm water is 따뜻한 물 (ttatteutan mul).

examples.context: Asking a server at a restaurant
Staff at a casual restaurant
Shopping at a convenience store

tips: Water is free in Korean restaurants. In many casual places it is self-service, and you will see a sign reading 물은 셀프 ("water is self-service") near a water machine and cups.
The ㄹ at the end of 물 sits between an English l and r. Keep it light and short so it doesn't sound like "mool-uh".
Korean tap water is treated and considered safe, but many people still drink filtered or bottled water at home.

faq.q: Is water free at Korean restaurants?
faq.a: Yes. It is almost always free, though you may need to fetch it yourself from a water dispenser.

faq.q: How do you say cold water in Korean?
faq.a: Cold water is 찬물 (chanmul). You can also say 시원한 물 (siwonhan mul), "nice cool water".

intro: "Check, please" in Korean is 계산해 주세요 (gyesanhae juseyo), which literally means "please calculate it for me". In most Korean restaurants you say it at the counter rather than at your table.

ways.note: The standard way to ask to pay. Works in any restaurant, cafe or shop.
"I'll pay now." Common when you walk up to the counter.
A quick, everyday way to say "the bill for here, please".
"I'll pay." Use it to offer to pay for someone else.
"It's on me." Casual slang between friends, from 쏘다, "to shoot".

examples.context: At the counter after a meal
Offering to pay for a coworker
Treating friends to dinner

tips: In most Korean restaurants you don't wait for a bill at the table. When you're done, take the receipt from your table (if there is one) to the counter near the door and pay there.
Tipping is not expected in Korea. A warm 잘 먹었습니다 (jal meogeosseumnida, "I ate well") on the way out is the thank-you.
To split the bill, say 따로 계산해 주세요 (ttaro gyesanhae juseyo), "please charge us separately". Koreans also use the word 더치페이 (deochipei) for going Dutch.

faq.q: Do you tip in Korean restaurants?
faq.a: No. Tipping is not part of Korean culture, and the price on the menu is what you pay.

faq.q: How do you ask to split the bill in Korean?
faq.a: Say 따로 계산해 주세요 (ttaro gyesanhae juseyo). Staff are used to it, especially with younger customers.

intro: "This one, please" in Korean is 이거 주세요 (igeo juseyo). 이거 means "this" and 주세요 means "please give me". Point at a menu picture or an item, say it, and you can order almost anything in Korea.

ways.note: The most useful ordering phrase. Polite and simple.
"One of these, please." Change the number for more.
"I'll take this one." Natural when choosing between options.
"I'll go with this." Common when ordering food or picking a size or color.
For friends and family only. Too blunt for shop staff.

examples.context: Ordering at a street food stall
Choosing from a cafe menu
Asking your sibling for a snack

tips: Korean has three "this/that" words: 이거 (igeo) for something near you, 그거 (geugeo) for something near the listener, and 저거 (jeogeo) for something far from both of you.
With counters, the numbers shorten: 한 개 (han gae, one), 두 개 (du gae, two), 세 개 (se gae, three). 하나 becomes 한 before the counter.
Pointing at a menu photo is completely normal in Korea, so don't feel shy about it.

faq.q: What is the difference between 이거, 그거 and 저거?
faq.a: 이거 is "this" near you, 그거 is "that" near the person you're talking to, and 저거 is "that over there".

faq.q: How do you say "two of these, please" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 이거 두 개 주세요 (igeo du gae juseyo).

intro: "Let's eat" in Korean is 밥 먹자 (bap meokja) with friends, or 같이 먹어요 (gachi meogeoyo) when you need to be polite. 밥 means rice, but here it just means a meal.

ways.note: "Let's eat." The everyday way between friends, partners and family.
Just "let's eat". Often said when the food arrives.
"Let's eat together." Polite and friendly for coworkers or new acquaintances.
"Let's go eat." For heading out to a restaurant with friends.
"Let's go have a meal." 식사 is a politer word for a meal, good with people older than you.
Used by someone speaking to a group, like a boss to a team. Avoid it with elders, since it can sound bossy.

examples.context: Calling a friend over when the food arrives
Inviting a coworker to lunch
Making late-night plans with friends

tips: 언제 밥 한번 먹자 (eonje bap hanbeon meokja), "let's grab a meal sometime", is often a friendly way to say goodbye rather than a real plan. If someone sets a date, then it's real.
밥 먹었어? (bap meogeosseo?, "did you eat?") is used almost like "how are you?" between friends and family.
Before eating, people say 잘 먹겠습니다 (jal meokgesseumnida), especially when someone else is paying or cooked.

faq.q: What does 밥 한번 먹자 mean?
faq.a: It means "let's eat together sometime". It is often a polite way to keep in touch rather than a firm invitation.

faq.q: How do you say "let's eat" to someone older?
faq.a: Say 식사하러 가요 (siksahareo gayo), "let's go have a meal". At work, 식사하러 가시죠 (siksahareo gasijyo) is even more respectful.

intro: "Let's go" in Korean is 가자 (gaja) with friends and 가요 (gayo) when you want to be polite. Add 같이 (gachi, "together") to sound warmer.

ways.note: The everyday "let's go" between friends, siblings and partners.
Polite "let's go". The same word can also mean "I'm going" or "are you going?", so tone and context matter.
"Let's go together." Friendly and polite.
Said to a group, like a guide to a tour group. To one older person it can sound like an order.
"Departure!" People shout it when a trip or drive starts, like "off we go".
Internet slang, a stretched-out 가자 full of hype, like "let's gooo". Only with friends.

examples.context: Leaving for the bus with a friend
Walking to a cafe with a classmate
Ending a long night out

tips: 가요 does a lot of work: "let's go", "I'm going" and "are you going?" all sound like 가요. Koreans tell them apart by tone and situation.
가즈아 (gajeua) became popular online as a fun, over-the-top cheer. You'll see it in comments and fan chants, but it's not something to say to a teacher.
To invite someone older politely, 같이 가실래요? (gachi gasillaeyo?, "would you like to go together?") is softer than 갑시다.

faq.q: What does 가즈아 mean?
faq.a: It's playful slang for 가자, "let's go", stretched out for excitement. Think "let's gooo!"

faq.q: How do you say "let's go" politely in Korean?
faq.a: Say 가요 (gayo) or 같이 가요 (gachi gayo). For someone much older, 같이 가실래요? is even more polite.

intro: "Hurry up" in Korean is 빨리 (ppalli), which means "quickly". Add a verb to say what to do fast, like 빨리 와 (ppalli wa, "come quickly"). To be polite, use 서둘러 주세요 (seodulleo juseyo).

ways.note: "Quick!" or "Hurry!" on its own. Too blunt for strangers or elders.
"Hurry up and come." For a friend who is running late.
"Quick, quick!" Doubling it adds urgency. It is also the name for Korea's fast-paced culture.
"Hurry!" From 서두르다, to hurry.
"Please hurry." Polite enough for a taxi driver or staff, but use it only when it's really needed.

examples.context: Texting a friend who is late
Waiting for your sibling to get ready
Running late in a taxi

tips: 빨리빨리 (ppalli-ppalli) culture describes how fast things move in Korea, from food delivery to internet speed. You'll hear the phrase a lot.
The opposite is 천천히 (cheoncheonhi), "slowly". 천천히 하세요 (cheoncheonhi haseyo) means "take your time", a kind thing to say.
빨리 starts with a tense ㅃ sound. Say it like a sharp "bb" with no puff of air: "ppal-li".

faq.q: What is 빨리빨리 culture?
faq.a: It's a common way to describe Korea's love of speed and efficiency, from quick service to fast public transport.

faq.q: How do you say "slow down" or "take your time" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 천천히 (cheoncheonhi), "slowly". 천천히 하세요 (cheoncheonhi haseyo) means "take your time".

intro: "Be careful" in Korean is 조심하세요 (josimhaseyo), or 조심해 (josimhae) with friends. Put a word in front to say what to watch out for, like 계단 조심하세요 ("watch the stairs").

ways.note: The standard polite "be careful". Fine for strangers, coworkers and elders.
For friends, partners, family and kids.
Very formal. You'll mostly see it on signs and hear it in announcements.
"Get home safely." A caring way to say goodbye.
"Get home safely", literally "go in carefully". Very common when parting at night.
"Drive safely."

examples.context: Warning a guest about steep stairs
Saying goodbye after dinner
A friend reaches toward a hot pan

tips: 조심히 들어가세요 is said all the time when friends or coworkers split up at night. It isn't a warning, just a warm "get home safe".
To warn about something specific, put the thing first: 차 조심해 (cha josimhae, "watch out for cars"), 감기 조심하세요 (gamgi josimhaseyo, "don't catch a cold").
For a sudden "watch out!", Koreans often shout 조심해! or simply 위험해! (wiheomhae!, "it's dangerous!").

faq.q: What does 조심히 들어가세요 mean?
faq.a: It means "get home safely". People say it when parting, especially at night.

faq.q: What is the difference between 조심해 and 조심하세요?
faq.a: 조심해 is casual, for friends and family. 조심하세요 is polite, for strangers and people older than you.

intro: "I'm home" in Korean is 다녀왔습니다 (danyeowatseumnida), literally "I have been out and come back". Kids say it to their parents every day when they walk in. With friends or roommates, 나 왔어 (na wasseo) is enough.

ways.note: What you say walking into your family home, especially to parents or grandparents.
A slightly softer polite version, common in many families.
To a partner, sibling or roommate.
"I'm here" or "I'm back". Very casual and very common.
"I've arrived home." What you text someone who asked you to let them know you got home.

examples.context: Walking in after school
Coming home to your roommate
Texting a friend after a night out

tips: Leaving and coming home come as a pair: 다녀오겠습니다 (danyeoogesseumnida, "I'll be back") when you head out, and 다녀왔습니다 when you return.
Family usually answers with 왔어? (wasseo?, "you're back?"), 다녀왔어? or 어서 와 (eoseo wa, "welcome back").
Friends often say 집에 도착하면 연락해 (jibe dochakamyeon yeollakae), "text me when you get home". Answer with 집에 도착했어 (jibe dochakaesseo).

faq.q: What do you say back when someone says 다녀왔습니다?
faq.a: Common replies are 왔어? (wasseo?), 다녀왔어? (danyeowasseo?) or 어서 와 (eoseo wa), all meaning roughly "welcome back".

faq.q: What do Koreans say when leaving the house?
faq.a: They say 다녀오겠습니다 (danyeoogesseumnida), "I'll go and come back". Family replies 잘 다녀와 (jal danyeowa), "have a good day".

intro: "It's okay" in Korean is 괜찮아요 (gwaenchanayo), or 괜찮아 (gwaenchana) with friends. It can mean "it's fine", "I'm okay", "no thanks", or, as a question, "are you okay?"

ways.note: The everyday polite form. Works with strangers, staff and elders.
With friends and family. Said gently, it's a comforting "it's okay".
Formal and a little stiff. Common at work or with customers.
"It's nothing." A modest reply when someone thanks you or apologizes for something small.
"Never mind" or "forget it". It can sound cold or annoyed, so use it with care.

examples.context: Someone apologizes for bumping into you
A friend trips on the sidewalk
Turning down a second helping

tips: The ㅎ in 괜찮아요 is silent, so it sounds like "gwen-cha-na-yo".
괜찮아요 is a polite way to say "no thanks". If a shop clerk offers a bag or a server offers more food, 괜찮아요 with a small smile declines it nicely.
Ask 괜찮아요? with a rising tone to check on someone: "Are you okay?"

faq.q: Can 괜찮아요 mean "no thank you"?
faq.a: Yes. It's one of the most common ways to politely turn something down in Korean.

faq.q: How do you pronounce 괜찮아?
faq.a: Say "gwen-cha-na". The ㅎ in 찮 is not pronounced.

intro: "I want this" in Korean is 이거 갖고 싶어요 (igeo gatgo sipeoyo), literally "I want to have this". Korean usually says what you want to do with something, so wanting to buy it or eat it uses a different verb.

ways.note: "I want this" in the sense of wanting to own it.
The same with friends or family, like pointing at something in a shop window.
"I want to buy this." Clear and useful while shopping.
"I want to eat this." Point at a menu photo or a dish.
"I'll buy this." What you say to the clerk once you've decided.

examples.context: Looking at a gift with a friend
Asking a clerk in a shop
Pointing at a menu photo

tips: The pattern is verb stem + 고 싶어요: 사고 싶어요 (want to buy), 먹고 싶어요 (want to eat), 가고 싶어요 (want to go).
원해요 (wonhaeyo) also means "want", but it sounds stiff in everyday talk. For things you'd like to have, 갖고 싶어요 is what people really say.
갖고 is said "gat-kko" and 싶어요 is said "shi-peo-yo".

faq.q: Can I say 이거 원해요?
faq.a: It's understandable but sounds unnatural in daily life. Use 이거 갖고 싶어요, or a more specific verb like 사고 싶어요.

faq.q: How do you say "I don't want it" politely?
faq.a: A polite 괜찮아요 (gwaenchanayo, "it's okay, no thanks") is the most natural way to decline.

intro: "Spicy" in Korean is 매워요 (maewoyo), "it's spicy", from the verb 맵다 (maepda). With friends say 매워 (maewo). Before a spicy food trip, it also helps to know how to ask for a milder version.

ways.note: "It's spicy." The polite everyday form.
With friends, often with a gasp. 너무 매워! means "too spicy!"
The dictionary form. People also blurt it out as an exclamation after a spicy bite.
"Spicy" before a noun, as in 매운 음식 (maeun eumsik, spicy food).
"Is it very spicy?" when asked with a rising tone. A smart question before ordering.
"Please make it not spicy." Not every dish can be changed, but it's worth asking.

examples.context: Asking a server before ordering
Ordering tteokbokki
Your first bite of buldak noodles

tips: 맵다 changes shape when you add endings: the ㅂ turns into a 우 sound, so you get 매워요, 매워 and 매운, never 맵어요. 덥다 (hot weather) works the same way: 더워요.
Spicy and hot are different words. 매워요 is spicy, while 뜨거워요 (tteugeowoyo) is hot to the touch.

Many menus list spice levels: 순한맛 (sunhanmat) is mild, and 매운맛 (maeunmat) is the spicy version. If spice is hard for you, ask 안 매운 거 있어요? (an maeun geo isseoyo?, "do you have anything that's not spicy?").

faq.q: How do you say "not spicy" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 안 매워요 (an maewoyo), "it's not spicy". To ask for food without spice, say 안 맵게 해 주세요 (an maepge hae juseyo).

faq.q: Is 매워요 the same as hot?
faq.a: Only for spice. For temperature, use 뜨거워요 (tteugeowoyo) for food or drinks and 더워요 (deowoyo) for weather.

intro: "What are you doing?" in Korean is 뭐 해? (mwo hae?), a casual question for friends and people younger than you. With people you don't know well, add 요 and say 뭐 해요? (mwo haeyo?).

ways.note: The everyday question between friends, family and partners. Very common as a text, like "wyd?" in English.
The polite version for coworkers, classmates you don't know well, or anyone older than you.
Adds respect with the honorific 시. Good for elders, a boss or a customer.
"What are you doing right now?" Stresses what the person is in the middle of.
The polite form of "What are you doing right now?"
"What do you think you're doing?" Often sounds surprised or annoyed, so use it with care.

examples.context: Texting a friend in the evening
Asking a coworker about weekend plans
examples.en: What are you doing on the weekend?

examples.context: Seeing a friend climb on the table
