tips: In texts, 뭐 해? is a friendly way to start a chat, and between people who like each other it can be a small sign of interest. It does not always need a detailed answer.

To answer, say what you are doing plus 고 있어: 밥 먹고 있어 (bap meokgo isseo), "I'm eating". If you are doing nothing special, say 그냥 있어 (geunyang isseo), "Just hanging out". Add 요 to both when speaking politely.
뭐 하는 거야? is not a neutral question. It usually means "What on earth are you doing?" so avoid it unless you really mean that.

faq.q: How do you reply to 뭐 해?
faq.a: Say what you are doing with 고 있어, like 공부하고 있어 (gongbuhago isseo), "I'm studying", or simply 그냥 있어 (geunyang isseo), "Nothing much".

faq.q: What does mwohae mean in a text?
faq.a: 뭐 해 (mwohae) means "What are you doing?" It is a casual check-in, similar to "wyd" or "what's up".

faq.q: Is mwo hae rude?
faq.a: No, but it is casual. Use 뭐 해요? (mwo haeyo?) with people older than you or people you don't know well.

intro: "Where are you?" in Korean is 어디야? (eodiya?), a casual question for friends and family. The polite version is 어디예요? (eodiyeyo?), and on the phone people often say 어디세요? (eodiseyo?).

ways.note: Literally "Where is it?" The standard way to ask a friend where they are.
The polite version for coworkers or people you don't know well.
"Where are you (staying, sitting) right now?" Close in meaning to 어디야.
Respectful and very common on the phone, for example when a delivery driver calls.
Uses the honorific verb 계시다. Use it for parents, grandparents and other elders.
"About where are you?" Asked when someone is on the way and you want to know how close they are.

examples.context: Calling a friend who hasn't shown up
Looking for your mom in the house
Waiting for a coworker to arrive

tips: 어디예요 is written as one word. Because 어디 ends in a vowel, the ending is 예요, not 이에요.
To answer, name the place and add 이야 or 야: 집이야 (jibiya), "I'm home". If you are on your way, say 가고 있어 (gago isseo), "I'm on my way", or 거의 다 왔어 (geoui da wasseo), "I'm almost there".
Use 계세요 only for other people. Never use it about yourself.

faq.q: How do you say "I'm on my way" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 가고 있어 (gago isseo) casually or 가고 있어요 (gago isseoyo) politely.

faq.q: What is the difference between 어디야 and 어디 있어?
faq.a: They mean nearly the same thing. 어디야 is "Where is it (that you are)?" and 어디 있어 is "Where are you staying?" Both are casual.

intro: "Are you okay?" in Korean is 괜찮아? (gwaenchana?), said with a rising tone to a friend or someone younger. To be polite, say 괜찮아요? (gwaenchanayo?), or 괜찮으세요? (gwaenchaneuseyo?) for a stranger or an elder.

ways.note: For friends, family and people younger than you. As a question it rises at the end.
The polite form for coworkers and people you don't know well.
More respectful, with the honorific 시. Good for a stranger who fell or an older person.
Very formal. Heard from staff, in the military or in announcements.
"Are you really okay?" Shows concern when someone says they are fine but you are not sure.

examples.context: A friend looks pale at lunch
A stranger trips on the stairs
Checking on a coworker after bad news

tips: The question and the answer use the same word. With a rising tone 괜찮아? is "Are you okay?", and with a falling tone 괜찮아 is "I'm okay".
To answer, say 응, 괜찮아 (eung, gwaenchana) to a friend or 네, 괜찮아요 (ne, gwaenchanayo) politely. If you are not okay, 아니, 좀 아파 (ani, jom apa) means "No, it hurts a bit" or "I feel a bit sick".
괜찮아요 is also a polite way to say "No, thank you." If a shop worker offers a bag and you say 괜찮아요, you are turning it down.

faq.q: How do you answer "are you okay" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 네, 괜찮아요 (ne, gwaenchanayo), "Yes, I'm okay", or 응, 괜찮아 (eung, gwaenchana) to a friend.

faq.q: Does gwaenchana also mean "it's okay"?
faq.a: Yes. 괜찮아 can mean "Are you okay?", "I'm okay" or "It's okay", depending on tone and situation.

intro: "Where are you from?" in Korean is 어디에서 왔어요? (eodieseo wasseoyo?), literally "Where did you come from?" To sound more respectful, say 어디에서 오셨어요? (eodieseo osyeosseoyo?).

ways.note: The standard polite question. Safe with most people around your age.
Adds the honorific 시, so it sounds warmer and more respectful. Good for elders and customers.
For friends and younger people. 어디서 is the short spoken form of 어디에서.
"Which country are you from?" Clear and common, though it can feel a little direct.
"Where is your hometown?" Asks about the town you grew up in, often used between Koreans.

examples.context: Chatting with a new classmate
Meeting a friend's friend at a party
A taxi driver making small talk

tips: To answer, say the country plus 에서 왔어요: 미국에서 왔어요 (migugeseo wasseoyo), "I'm from America". You can also say 미국 사람이에요 (miguk saramieyo), "I'm American".
Koreans use the past tense here because the question really asks "Where did you come from?" Do not change it to the present tense.
If you live in Korea, people may follow up with 한국에 언제 왔어요? (hanguge eonje wasseoyo?), "When did you come to Korea?"

faq.q: How do you say "I'm from America" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 미국에서 왔어요 (migugeseo wasseoyo). For the UK it is 영국에서 왔어요 (yeonggugeseo wasseoyo).

faq.q: What is the difference between 어디에서 and 어디서?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. 어디서 is the shorter form that people use more in speech.

intro: "How old are you?" in Korean is 몇 살이에요? (myeot sarieyo?), literally "How many years is it?" Koreans ask this often because age decides how people speak to each other.

ways.note: The standard polite question for people around your age.
For children and close friends. It sounds rude to an adult you just met.
Softer and more respectful. Literally "How does your age go?"
Uses the honorific word for age. Only for elders, such as someone's grandparents.
"What year were you born?" A common way young adults compare ages.

examples.context: Getting to know a language exchange partner
Talking to a child at a family gathering
Asking a new coworker politely
examples.en: Excuse me, but how old are you?

tips: Asking age is normal in Korea, not rude. It tells people whether to use polite speech and what to call each other, like 오빠 (oppa) or 언니 (eonni).
To answer, use native Korean numbers with 살: 스무 살이에요 (seumu sarieyo), "I'm 20", or 스물다섯 살이에요 (seumuldaseot sarieyo), "I'm 25".
Since June 2023, official documents in Korea use international age. You may still hear older ways of counting in daily life, which is why people sometimes ask your birth year instead.

faq.q: How do you answer "how old are you" in Korean?
faq.a: Use a native Korean number plus 살이에요, for example 스물두 살이에요 (seumuldu sarieyo), "I'm 22".

faq.q: Is it rude to ask someone's age in Korea?
faq.a: No, it is common. Just use the polite form, and use 연세 (yeonse) for elders.

intro: "What time is it?" in Korean is 지금 몇 시예요? (jigeum myeot siyeyo?), literally "Now, how many o'clock is it?" With friends, say 몇 시야? (myeot siya?).

ways.note: The most natural polite question. 지금 means "now".
The same question without "now". Also used to ask what time something starts.
For friends and family.
A softer polite form, a bit like "What time is it now, I wonder?" Good for asking a stranger.

examples.context: Asking a stranger at a bus stop
examples.en: Excuse me, what time is it now?

examples.context: Asking a classmate before the bell
Waking up late on a lazy Sunday

tips: To answer, use native Korean numbers for the hour and Sino-Korean numbers for minutes: 세 시 십 분 (se si sip bun), "3:10". 반 (ban) means "half", so 세 시 반 (se si ban) is "3:30".
A common spelling mistake is 몇 시에요. Because 시 ends in a vowel, the correct ending is 예요.
몇 시 is pronounced close to "myeot ssi" because the ㅅ becomes tense after 몇.

faq.q: How do you say 3:30 in Korean?
faq.a: Say 세 시 반 (se si ban) or 세 시 삼십 분 (se si samsip bun).

faq.q: Why are hours and minutes counted differently?
faq.a: Hours use native Korean numbers (한 시, 두 시) and minutes use Sino-Korean numbers (일 분, 이 분). It is simply the rule, and you get used to it quickly.

intro: "Did you eat?" in Korean is 밥 먹었어? (bap meogeosseo?), a casual question for friends and family. It is less about food and more a warm way of saying "How are you doing?"

ways.note: "Have you eaten?" The everyday check-in between friends, partners and family.
The polite version for coworkers or people you don't know well.
Respectful, using 식사 (meal) and the honorific 시. Good for a boss, a teacher or an older neighbor.
Very respectful, with honorific words for both "meal" and "eat". Used for grandparents and elders.
"Did you at least eat?" A caring question when someone has had a hard or busy day.

examples.context: Checking on a friend after a long day
examples.en: Did you at least eat today?

examples.context: Visiting grandma in the evening
Greeting your manager after lunch

tips: Koreans ask this as a greeting, the way English speakers say "How's it going?" It is not always an invitation to eat together.
To answer, say 응, 먹었어 (eung, meogeosseo), "Yeah, I ate", or 아직 (ajik), "Not yet". Politely, 네, 먹었어요 (ne, meogeosseoyo). You can ask back with 너는? (neoneun?), "What about you?"
밥 means cooked rice, but here it means any meal. You do not need to have eaten rice to say yes.

faq.q: What does bap meogeosseo mean?
faq.a: 밥 먹었어? (bap meogeosseo?) means "Did you eat?" It is a friendly check-in that shows you care.

faq.q: How do you answer "did you eat" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 네, 먹었어요 (ne, meogeosseoyo) politely or 응, 먹었어 (eung, meogeosseo) to a friend. If you haven't, say 아직 안 먹었어요 (ajik an meogeosseoyo), "I haven't eaten yet".

intro: "What is this?" in Korean is 이게 뭐예요? (ige mwoyeyo?), a polite question you can use with anyone. With friends, say 이게 뭐야? (ige mwoya?).

ways.note: The standard polite question. 이게 is short for 이것이, "this (thing)".
Very common in speech, for example pointing at something in a market or on a menu.
For friends and family. Depending on tone, it can also mean "What is this?!" in surprise or annoyance.
"And what is this one?" Used when you have already asked about something else.
Textbook formal Korean. Correct, but it sounds stiff in daily conversation.

examples.context: Pointing at a side dish in a restaurant
Asking about a second item at a market
Opening a surprise gift from a friend

tips: Korean has three words for "this" and "that": 이거 (this, near me), 그거 (that, near you) and 저거 (that, over there). So "What is that?" is 저게 뭐예요? (jeoge mwoyeyo?) or 그게 뭐예요? (geuge mwoyeyo?).
The answer uses the name plus 이에요 or 예요: 이건 김치예요 (igeon gimchiyeyo), "This is kimchi". If you don't know, say 잘 모르겠어요 (jal moreugesseoyo), "I'm not sure".
이게 뭐야! with a sharp tone means something like "What is this mess?" Say it gently if you are just curious.

faq.q: What is the difference between 이거 and 이게?
faq.a: 이거 is "this" and 이게 is "this" with the subject marker. In the question "What is this?" both are common and natural.

faq.q: How do you say "What is that?" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 저게 뭐예요? (jeoge mwoyeyo?) for something far away, or 그게 뭐예요? (geuge mwoyeyo?) for something near the other person.

intro: "Do you speak English?" in Korean is 영어 할 줄 아세요? (yeongeo hal jul aseyo?), literally "Do you know how to do English?" A shorter, friendly option is 혹시 영어 하세요? (hoksi yeongeo haseyo?).

ways.note: Polite and respectful. Safe with strangers, staff and elders.
"By any chance, do you speak English?" 혹시 makes it softer and less pushy.
Short and polite. Literally "Do you do English?"
"Can you speak English?" Correct and common, a little more direct.
For friends and younger people.
"Can you speak English?" in casual speech.

examples.context: Asking a shop worker for help
examples.en: Do you speak English, by any chance?

examples.context: Asking a stranger for directions
Asking a new friend's younger cousin

tips: Korean usually says "do" a language rather than "speak" it, so 영어 해요 (yeongeo haeyo) means "I speak English".
Common answers are 조금요 (jogeumyo), "A little", 네, 조금 해요 (ne, jogeum haeyo), "Yes, a little", or 아니요, 못 해요 (aniyo, mot haeyo), "No, I can't".
Many Koreans study English in school but feel shy speaking it. Starting with 혹시 and a smile, and trying a little Korean first, makes the question feel friendlier.

faq.q: How do you say "I don't speak Korean" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 한국어 못 해요 (hangugeo mot haeyo), or 한국어 잘 못 해요 (hangugeo jal mot haeyo), "I don't speak Korean well".

faq.q: What does 영어 할 줄 아세요 mean literally?
faq.a: It means "Do you know how to do English?" 할 줄 알다 is a common way to say you know how to do something.

intro: "Can you help me?" in Korean is 도와주실 수 있어요? (dowajusil su isseoyo?), a polite question for strangers and staff. To simply ask "Please help me", say 도와주세요 (dowajuseyo).

ways.note: "Could you help me?" Polite and respectful, good for strangers and shop staff.
"Please help me." A request rather than a question. Also what you shout in an emergency.
"Would you help me a little?" Very polite and soft.
"Will you help me?" A gentle casual request to a friend or younger sibling.
"Help me." Direct, for close friends and family.

examples.context: Asking a stranger at a ticket machine
Carrying boxes with a friend
examples.en: Will you help me with this?

examples.context: In an emergency on the street

tips: 좀 (jom) softens a request, a bit like "please" or "a little". Adding it makes almost any request sound nicer.
People usually answer 네, 물론이죠 (ne, mullonijyo), "Yes, of course", or 뭐 도와드릴까요? (mwo dowadeurilkkayo?), "What can I help you with?"
In a real emergency in Korea, call 112 for the police or 119 for fire and ambulance.

faq.q: What is the difference between 도와주세요 and 도와주실 수 있어요?
faq.a: 도와주세요 is a request, "Please help me". 도와주실 수 있어요? is a question, "Could you help me?", which feels a little softer.

faq.q: How do you say "Can I help you?" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 도와드릴까요? (dowadeurilkkayo?), a humble and polite offer of help.

intro: "Where do you live?" in Korean is 어디 살아요? (eodi sarayo?), a polite everyday question. For someone older, say 어디 사세요? (eodi saseyo?).

ways.note: The common polite question. The particle 에 is usually dropped in speech.
The full form with 에 (in, at). Same meaning, a little more careful.
Respectful, with the honorific 시. Good for elders, a teacher or a customer.
For friends and younger people.
"Where is your home?" Often asked when deciding who lives near whom, for example after a dinner.
The casual version of "Where's your place?"

examples.context: Small talk with a new coworker
Asking a friend after a late dinner
Chatting with your teacher

tips: To answer, name the city or neighborhood plus 에 살아요: 서울에 살아요 (seoure sarayo), "I live in Seoul". Koreans usually answer with an area, not a full address.
When a friend asks 집이 어디야? late at night, they may be thinking about how you'll get home or offering to share a ride.
살다 (to live) loses its ㄹ before 세요, so the honorific form is 사세요, not 살세요.

faq.q: How do you say "I live in Seoul" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 서울에 살아요 (seoure sarayo), or 서울 살아요 (seoul sarayo) in relaxed speech.

faq.q: Is it rude to ask where someone lives in Korea?
faq.a: No, asking the area or neighborhood is normal small talk. Asking for an exact address would feel too personal.

intro: "What do you mean?" in Korean is 무슨 말이에요? (museun marieyo?), literally "What words is that?" To ask what a word means, say 무슨 뜻이에요? (museun tteusieyo?).

ways.note: The polite question when you don't understand what someone means.
For friends and family.
"What do you mean by that?" Can sound surprised or upset, depending on tone.
"What does it mean?" Best for asking about a word or phrase.
The casual "What does it mean?"
Very respectful, using the honorific word for words. Good for a boss, a teacher or an elder.

examples.context: A friend says something confusing
examples.en: What do you mean by that?

examples.context: Asking a tutor about a new word
Your boss gives a surprising instruction

tips: 말 (mal) is what someone said, and 뜻 (tteut) is the meaning of a word. Use 무슨 말이에요? in conversation and 무슨 뜻이에요? for vocabulary.
If you simply didn't hear, 네? (ne?) with a rising tone means "Pardon?" You can also ask 다시 말해 주세요 (dasi malhae juseyo), "Please say it again".
When someone asks you this, explain again starting with 그러니까 (geureonikka), "I mean" or "So".

faq.q: What is the difference between 무슨 말 and 무슨 뜻?
faq.a: 무슨 말이에요? asks what a person means, and 무슨 뜻이에요? asks what a word or phrase means.

faq.q: Is 그게 무슨 말이야 rude?
faq.a: Not always, but it often sounds surprised or annoyed. A calm 무슨 말이에요? is safer.

english: How do you say this in Korean?

answer.en: How do you say this in Korean?

intro: "How do you say this" in Korean is 이거 한국어로 뭐라고 해요? (igeo hangugeoro mworago haeyo?), literally "What do you call this in Korean?" It is one of the most useful questions for learners.

ways.note: The natural polite question. Point at the thing or show the English word.
The same question without "this". Say the English word first, then ask.
"What do you call this?" For friends.
"What's this in Korean?" Short and casual.
"How do I say this in Korean?" Closer to the English, and also correct.
"How do you read this?" Use it when you see written Korean and want the pronunciation.

examples.context: Pointing at an umbrella during a language exchange
examples.en: How do you say this in Korean?

examples.context: Asking a Korean friend about a snack
Looking at a sign on the street

tips: The answer usually comes back as ___(이)라고 해요, "It's called ___". For example, 우산이라고 해요 (usanirago haeyo), "It's called 우산 (umbrella)".
To ask about English instead, change 한국어로 to 영어로 (yeongeoro): 이거 영어로 뭐라고 해요?
After you get the answer, repeating it with 맞아요? (majayo?), "Is that right?", is a good way to check your pronunciation.

faq.q: How do you ask "How do you say ___ in Korean?"
faq.a: Say the English word, then ask 한국어로 뭐라고 해요? (hangugeoro mworago haeyo?). For example, "Umbrella", 한국어로 뭐라고 해요?

faq.q: What does 뭐라고 mean?
faq.a: 뭐라고 is "what" plus the quoting particle 라고, so 뭐라고 해요? means "What do you call it?" On its own, 뭐라고? also means "What did you say?"

intro: "Who are you?" in Korean is 누구세요? (nuguseyo?), a polite question you can use when someone knocks on the door or calls you. With a child or close friend, say 누구야? (nuguya?).

ways.note: Polite and respectful. What Koreans say when someone rings the doorbell or calls from an unknown number.
"Excuse me, but who are you?" Softer, for when a stranger approaches you.
"Who is it?" Usually about someone else, like a person in a photo.
For children, friends, or asking a friend about someone else.
"Who are you?!" Blunt and often rude. Heard in dramas when a stranger shows up, but avoid it in real life.

examples.context: A stranger walks into your office
examples.en: Excuse me, but who are you?

examples.context: Looking at a friend's group photo
A child meets a new babysitter

tips: Korean politely avoids saying "you" to people it doesn't know, so 누구세요? has no word for "you" at all. Adding 너 (you) makes it sound blunt.
To answer, give your name plus 예요 or 이에요: 저 민지예요 (jeo minjiyeyo), "It's me, Minji". At the door, a delivery driver might say 택배예요 (taekbaeyeyo), "Delivery".
On the phone, Koreans start with 여보세요 (yeoboseyo), "Hello", and then may ask 누구세요?

faq.q: What does nuguseyo mean?
faq.a: 누구세요? (nuguseyo?) means "Who is it?" or "Who are you?" It is polite and very common at the door and on the phone.

faq.q: Is 너 누구야 rude?
faq.a: Yes, it is blunt and can sound hostile to an adult. Use 누구세요? instead.

intro: "What do you want?" in Korean is 원하는 게 뭐예요? (wonhaneun ge mwoyeyo?), literally "What is the thing you want?" In daily life, Koreans more often name the want, like 뭐 먹고 싶어요? (mwo meokgo sipeoyo?), "What do you want to eat?"

ways.note: The direct question. Polite, but it can sound serious, like in a negotiation.
"What is it you want?" Common in drama confrontations, so it can sound intense.
"What do you want to eat?" The everyday question when choosing food.
"What do you want (to have)?" Used for gifts and things.
"What can I get you?" What staff say in a cafe or shop.
"What?" or "Why?" The short reply when a friend calls your name. It can sound curt.

examples.context: Planning a friend's birthday
examples.en: What do you want for your birthday?

examples.context: A barista greeting a customer
A tense talk with a rival

tips: English "What do you want?" covers many situations, but Korean usually names the action: 먹고 싶어 (want to eat), 마시고 싶어 (want to drink), 갖고 싶어 (want to have).
To answer, say the thing plus 주세요 (juseyo) at a shop, like 아메리카노 주세요 (amerikano juseyo), "An americano, please". With a friend, say 떡볶이 먹고 싶어 (tteokbokki meokgo sipeo), "I want to eat tteokbokki".
Saying 원하는 게 뭐야? to a friend over a small thing can sound like a challenge. For everyday choices, use the specific questions above.

faq.q: How do you say "What do you want to eat?" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 뭐 먹고 싶어요? (mwo meokgo sipeoyo?) politely or 뭐 먹고 싶어? (mwo meokgo sipeo?) casually.

faq.q: How do you say "I want this" in Korean?
faq.a: In a shop, say 이거 주세요 (igeo juseyo), "This, please". To say you want to have it, 이거 갖고 싶어요 (igeo gatgo sipeoyo).

intro: "Is it good?" in Korean is 좋아요? (joayo?), a polite question you can use for almost anything. For food, Koreans ask 맛있어요? (masisseoyo?), "Is it tasty?"

ways.note: "Is it good?" or "Do you like it?" Works for places, products, movies and plans.
The casual version for friends and family.
"Is it delicious?" The question to ask about food.
"Is it tasty?" Casual, for friends and family.
"How is it?" An open question that invites a fuller answer.
"Is it okay?" or "Is it decent?" Asks whether something is good enough.

examples.context: Watching a friend try a new snack
Asking a coworker about a movie
A friend just bought a new phone

tips: To answer, say 네, 좋아요 (ne, joayo), "Yes, it's good", or 진짜 맛있어요 (jinjja masisseoyo), "It's really tasty". If not, 별로예요 (byeolloyeyo), "Not really", is a mild way to say so.
좋아요 can also mean "I like it" or "Sounds good", so 좋아요? can mean "Do you like it?" depending on the situation.
The ㅎ in 좋 is silent before a vowel, so 좋아요 sounds like "jo-a-yo".

faq.q: How do you say "It's good" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 좋아요 (joayo) in general, or 맛있어요 (masisseoyo) for food.

faq.q: How do you say "It's not good" politely?
faq.a: Say 별로예요 (byeolloyeyo), "Not really" or "It's so-so". It is softer than saying 나빠요 (nappayo), "It's bad".

intro: "Good afternoon" in Korean is usually just 안녕하세요 (annyeonghaseyo), the everyday polite hello. Korean has no separate greeting for the afternoon, so the same hello works from morning to night. When you leave someone, you can wish them a good afternoon with 좋은 오후 보내세요 (joeun ohu bonaeseyo).

ways.note: The normal greeting at any time of day. Use it with anyone you don't know well.
Hi. Only for close friends, younger people and children.
Have a good afternoon. Said when parting or at the end of a message, not as a hello.
Did you enjoy your lunch? A very common friendly check-in around early afternoon, especially at work.
Very formal hello for speeches, the military, news broadcasts and formal business settings.

examples.context: Greeting a teacher after lunch
Saying goodbye to a coworker at 2 pm
Small talk with a colleague after lunch

tips: You may see 좋은 오후예요 in textbooks or translation apps, but Koreans almost never say it out loud. A plain 안녕하세요 sounds much more natural.

Koreans often greet each other with a question about food instead of a time-of-day greeting. Around lunch, 점심 드셨어요? (Did you have lunch?) is a warm, normal thing to ask. A simple 네 (yes) is enough as an answer.

faq.q: Is there a Korean word for good afternoon?
faq.a: Not one that people use as a greeting. Koreans say 안녕하세요 (annyeonghaseyo) at any time of day.

faq.q: How do you say have a good afternoon in Korean?
faq.a: Say 좋은 오후 보내세요 (joeun ohu bonaeseyo). It is polite and works when leaving or ending a message.

intro: "Good evening" in Korean is usually just 안녕하세요 (annyeonghaseyo), the same polite hello used all day. There is no special evening greeting in everyday speech. To wish someone a nice evening as you leave, say 좋은 저녁 보내세요 (joeun jeonyeok bonaeseyo).

ways.note: The standard greeting in the evening too. Safe with almost anyone.
Hi. For friends and people younger than you.
Have a good evening. Used when parting or at the end of a message.
Did you have dinner? A caring greeting in the evening. Casual version: 저녁 먹었어? (jeonyeok meogeosseo?)
Very formal hello. TV news anchors often open the evening news with it.

examples.context: Meeting your partner's parents at dinner
Leaving a shop in the evening
Calling an older relative at night

tips: Translation apps may give 좋은 저녁이에요, but it sounds like a translation. Use 안녕하세요 to say hello, and save 좋은 저녁 보내세요 for goodbye.
저녁 means both evening and dinner, so 저녁 드셨어요? is about the meal. Asking if someone has eaten is a common way to show you care.

faq.q: How do you say good evening in Korean?
faq.a: Most Koreans simply say 안녕하세요 (annyeonghaseyo). The very formal 안녕하십니까 (annyeonghasimnikka) is used in speeches and on the news.

faq.q: What does 좋은 저녁 보내세요 mean?
faq.a: It means "Have a good evening." It is polite and said when you are leaving or ending a conversation.

intro: "See you soon" in Korean is 곧 봐요 (got bwayo), a friendly polite way to say goodbye when you will meet again shortly. With close friends, drop the 요 and say 곧 봐 (got bwa). In formal or work settings, use 곧 뵙겠습니다 (got boepgetseumnida).

ways.note: See you soon. Friendly and polite, good for most people.
See you soon, to friends and people younger than you.
Let's meet soon. A little warmer, often used when the meeting is planned.
I will see you soon. Humble and formal, for clients, bosses and elders.
See you one of these days. For when there is no fixed date yet.
See you in a bit, meaning later the same day.

examples.context: Texting a friend after making plans
Saying bye to an old classmate
Ending a work email

tips: 곧 is pronounced with a light final t sound, close to "goht." 봐 sounds like "bwah."
Use 이따 봐 only for later today. For tomorrow, say 내일 봐 (naeil bwa). For an unknown date, 조만간 봐 or 다음에 봐 (daeume bwa, see you next time) is more natural.

faq.q: How do you say see you soon in Korean?
faq.a: Say 곧 봐요 (got bwayo) politely or 곧 봐 (got bwa) to close friends.

faq.q: What is the difference between 곧 봐 and 이따 봐?
faq.a: 곧 봐 means see you soon in general. 이따 봐 means see you later today.

intro: "Welcome home" in Korean is 어서 와 (eoseo wa), a warm "come on in" for family and close friends. In real Korean homes people most often just ask 왔어? (wasseo?), meaning "You're back?" To a parent or older person, say 다녀오셨어요? (danyeoosyeosseoyo?).

ways.note: Come on in, welcome. Warm and casual, for family, partners and friends.
You're home? The most everyday way family members greet each other at the door.
You're back? Literally "Did you go and come back?" Used for someone back from school, work or a trip.
You're here? A polite greeting for an older family member or guest arriving home.
Welcome back. How children greet parents or grandparents coming home.

examples.context: Greeting your mom at the door
Welcoming a partner after a long day
A child greeting dad back from work

tips: The person coming home usually speaks first with 다녀왔습니다 (danyeowatseumnida), "I'm back." Family members answer with 왔어? or 어서 와. See our page on "I'm home" for more.
Koreans often add 수고했어 (sugohaesseo), "you worked hard," when someone comes back from work or school. It is a kind way to say "good job today."

faq.q: What do Koreans say when someone comes home?
faq.a: Usually 왔어? (wasseo?) or 어서 와 (eoseo wa). Children say 다녀오셨어요? (danyeoosyeosseoyo?) to their parents.

faq.q: Is 어서 오세요 used for welcome home?
faq.a: 어서 오세요 (eoseo oseyo) is mainly what shop staff say to customers. At home, the casual 어서 와 is more natural.

intro: "Bye-bye" in Korean is 안녕 (annyeong), the casual word for both hi and bye among friends. Koreans also borrow the English and say 바이바이 (bai bai), which sounds light and cute. With anyone older or in a polite setting, use 안녕히 가세요 (annyeonghi gaseyo) instead.

ways.note: Bye. Also means hi. For friends, younger people and kids.
Bye-bye, borrowed from English. Playful and common among young people.
A cuter, childlike way to say bye-bye. Adults say it to babies or jokingly with friends.
Bye, get home safe. Said to the person who is leaving.
Texting shorthand for 바이바이.
Goodbye, to someone who is leaving. Use with older people, strangers and customers.

examples.context: Leaving a friend after class
Waving off a friend at the station
A toddler leaving grandma's house

tips: Don't use 안녕, 바이바이 or 빠이빠이 with your boss, a teacher or an older stranger. It sounds too casual. Say 안녕히 가세요 if they are leaving, or 안녕히 계세요 (annyeonghi gyeseyo) if you are the one leaving.
Many Koreans wave and say 안녕 twice, 안녕 안녕, which feels friendly and a little cute.

faq.q: Do Koreans say bye-bye?
faq.a: Yes. 바이바이 (bai bai) is common in casual speech, and 빠이빠이 (ppai ppai) is a cuter version used with kids.

faq.q: How do you say bye politely in Korean?
faq.a: Say 안녕히 가세요 (annyeonghi gaseyo) to someone leaving, or 안녕히 계세요 (annyeonghi gyeseyo) when you are the one leaving.

intro: "Have a good weekend" in Korean is 주말 잘 보내세요 (jumal jal bonaeseyo), literally "spend the weekend well." It is the standard polite way to say goodbye on a Friday. With friends, say 주말 잘 보내 (jumal jal bonae).

ways.note: Have a good weekend. The everyday choice for coworkers, teachers and acquaintances.
Have a good weekend, to friends and people younger than you.
Have a nice weekend. Common in messages and emails.
Have a fun weekend. Cheerful, often written in shop posts and group chats.
A very formal version for business emails or announcements.

examples.context: Leaving the office on Friday
Replying to a friend's message
examples.en: You have a good weekend too.

examples.context: Ending a group chat message

tips: If someone says 주말 잘 보내세요 to you, answer 네, 주말 잘 보내세요 (yes, you too) or 감사합니다, 주말 잘 보내세요. Korean has no short "you too," so people simply repeat the phrase.
In messages you will also see 행복한 주말 되세요 (have a happy weekend). It is very common in writing, though some people find 보내세요 more correct.

faq.q: How do you say have a nice weekend in Korean?
faq.a: Say 주말 잘 보내세요 (jumal jal bonaeseyo) or 좋은 주말 보내세요 (joeun jumal bonaeseyo). Both are polite.

faq.q: What does 주말 mean?
faq.a: 주말 (jumal) means weekend.

intro: "I love you so much" in Korean is 너무 사랑해 (neomu saranghae), a casual and heartfelt way to tell a partner, friend or family member how you feel. To an older person or in a polite setting, add 요: 너무 사랑해요 (neomu saranghaeyo). You can also swap 너무 for 정말 (really) or 많이 (a lot).

ways.note: I love you so much. The most natural everyday version.
I really love you. Sincere and a little more serious.
I really, truly love you. Very common in speech and texts.
I love you a lot. Gentle and warm, often said to family.
Polite form, for parents, grandparents or when you want to sound soft.
Formal form, used in speeches, letters or by idols thanking fans.

examples.context: Texting a partner before bed
examples.en: Honey, I love you so much.

examples.context: A card for Mother's Day
Hugging a little sister
examples.en: I really love you a lot.

tips: 너무 originally meant "too much," but today it is normally used to mean "so" or "very." 너무 사랑해 is perfectly natural.
Korean drops "I" and "you" when they are clear, so 사랑해 already means "I love you." Adding 나는 너를 makes it sound stiff, like a textbook.
사랑해 is pronounced "sa-rang-hae," with the last syllable close to "heh."

faq.q: How do you say I love you so much in Korean?
faq.a: Say 너무 사랑해 (neomu saranghae) casually, or 너무 사랑해요 (neomu saranghaeyo) politely.

faq.q: What is the difference between 너무 사랑해 and 정말 사랑해?
faq.a: Both mean you love someone very much. 너무 means "so much," while 정말 means "really" and can sound a bit more sincere or serious.

intro: "I miss you so much" in Korean is 너무 보고 싶어 (neomu bogo sipeo), literally "I want to see you so much." It is casual, for partners, friends and family your age or younger. Politely, say 너무 보고 싶어요 (neomu bogo sipeoyo).

ways.note: I miss you so much. The most common way to say it.
I really miss you. Sincere and heartfelt.
I miss you a lot. Soft and warm.
I miss you to death, like "I miss you like crazy." Dramatic and affectionate.
Polite form, for parents, grandparents, or anyone older.
Formal form, for letters or speeches, such as an idol speaking to fans.

examples.context: Calling a partner in another country
examples.en: Honey, I miss you so much.

examples.context: A video call with grandma
examples.en: Grandma, I miss you a lot.

examples.context: A late-night text to a partner

tips: Korean has no single verb for "miss." 보고 싶어 means "I want to see you," and that is exactly how Koreans say they miss someone.
보고 싶어 is pronounced "bo-go shi-peo." The 시 sounds like "shi."
보고 싶어 죽겠어 is an exaggeration, like English "I'm dying to see you." It is sweet, not dark.

faq.q: How do you say I miss you so much in Korean?
faq.a: Say 너무 보고 싶어 (neomu bogo sipeo), or 너무 보고 싶어요 (neomu bogo sipeoyo) to be polite.

faq.q: How do you reply to 보고 싶어?
faq.a: Say 나도 보고 싶어 (nado bogo sipeo), meaning "I miss you too."

intro: "I love you forever" in Korean is 영원히 사랑해 (yeongwonhi saranghae), using 영원히 (forever) before 사랑해 (I love you). It is casual and romantic. To promise it, say 영원히 사랑할게 (yeongwonhi saranghalge), "I will love you forever."

ways.note: I love you forever. Romantic, for a partner or close family.
I will love you forever. Sounds like a promise to the listener.
I love you for my whole life. Very natural, often said between couples.
I'll always love you, no matter how long. Soft and poetic.
Polite form, for parents, grandparents or anyone older.
Formal form, for wedding speeches, letters or fan messages.

examples.context: Writing in a baby's first-birthday card
examples.en: Our baby, I love you forever.

examples.context: A wedding promise
examples.en: I'll love you for the rest of my life.

examples.context: A note to mom

tips: 영원히 is pronounced close to "yeong-wo-ni" because the h sound is very soft.
영원히 사랑해 is a popular choice for tattoos, rings and engravings. It reads naturally on its own. If you want only the word "forever," use 영원히 (adverb) or 영원 (the noun, eternity).

faq.q: How do you say I will love you forever in Korean?
faq.a: Say 영원히 사랑할게 (yeongwonhi saranghalge). The ending 할게 makes it a promise.

faq.q: Is 영원히 사랑해 good for a tattoo?
faq.a: Yes, it is correct and natural. Write it with the space: 영원히 사랑해.

intro: "Good night, my love" in Korean is 잘 자, 내 사랑 (jal ja, nae sarang). 잘 자 means "sleep well" and 내 사랑 means "my love." Many couples say 잘 자, 자기야 (jal ja, jagiya) instead, which is a little more everyday.

ways.note: Good night, my love. Sweet and a little dramatic, great for texts.
Good night, honey. What many couples actually say.
Good night. Sleep well, to anyone close to you.
Have good dreams, like "sweet dreams." Often said together with 잘 자.
Same with 요. Couples sometimes use it to sound soft and gentle.

examples.context: Last text of the night
Ending a phone call with a partner
Tucking in after a long day

tips: 잘 자 is casual. To parents or elders, say 안녕히 주무세요 (annyeonghi jumuseyo), never 잘 자.
내 사랑 sounds romantic and a little old-fashioned or playful in speech. Couples often use 자기야 day to day and save 내 사랑 for sweet messages.

faq.q: How do you say good night my love in Korean?
faq.a: Say 잘 자, 내 사랑 (jal ja, nae sarang).

faq.q: How do you say sweet dreams in Korean?
faq.a: Say 좋은 꿈 꿔 (joeun kkum kkwo), often after 잘 자.

intro: "You are mine" in Korean is 넌 내 거야 (neon nae geoya), a playful and casual line between couples. You will often see it spelled 내 꺼야 in texts and lyrics, which matches how it sounds. It is only used casually, so there is no natural polite version.

ways.note: You're mine. The standard spelling. 넌 is short for 너는 (you).
The same without the shortening. Sounds a bit slower and more deliberate.
Mine. The spoken spelling of 내 거, very common in texts, captions and songs.
You're my person. Sounds romantic and loyal rather than possessive.
You're my man. For a woman to say to a boyfriend. To a girlfriend: 넌 내 여자야 (neon nae yeojaya).

examples.context: A playful text to a partner
A sweet line on an anniversary
A fan joking about a favorite idol

tips: The correct spelling is 거 (geo), but people pronounce it with a tense sound, so 꺼 (kkeo) is everywhere online. In formal writing use 거.
This line can sound cute or controlling depending on tone. Said with a smile, it is a common couple joke. Fans also say it about their bias, like 오빠는 내 꺼야.

faq.q: Is it 내 거 or 내 꺼?
faq.a: 내 거 is the correct spelling. 내 꺼 is how it sounds and is common in casual texts and song titles.

faq.q: How do you say you are mine in Korean?
faq.a: Say 넌 내 거야 (neon nae geoya). It is casual and best for a partner.

intro: "I love you more" in Korean is 내가 더 사랑해 (naega deo saranghae), literally "I love you more." It is the playful reply couples give when someone says 사랑해. Politely, say 내가 더 사랑해요 (naega deo saranghaeyo), or 제가 더 사랑해요 (jega deo saranghaeyo) to an elder.

ways.note: I love you more. The classic comeback to 사랑해.
I love you even more. Adds 많이 (a lot).
I love you way more. Fun for playful back-and-forth.
Polite and humble, for parents or grandparents. 제가 is the humble "I."
I love you too. The simpler reply if you don't want to compete.

examples.context: Replying to a partner's text
Talking to mom on the phone
Playful back-and-forth with a partner

tips: Use 내가 (naega), not 나는, for "I" here. 가 puts the focus on "I" as the one who loves more.
Couples often go back and forth: 사랑해, 내가 더 사랑해, 아니야 내가 더! It is a well-known cute exchange.

faq.q: How do you say I love you more in Korean?
faq.a: Say 내가 더 사랑해 (naega deo saranghae). Politely, 제가 더 사랑해요 (jega deo saranghaeyo).

faq.q: How do you say I love you too in Korean?
faq.a: Say 나도 사랑해 (nado saranghae).

intro: "Marry me" in Korean is 나랑 결혼해 줘 (narang gyeolhonhae jwo), literally "marry me (for me)." To ask "Will you marry me?" say 나랑 결혼해 줄래? (narang gyeolhonhae jullae?). In a polite or formal proposal, use 저랑 결혼해 주세요 (jeorang gyeolhonhae juseyo).

ways.note: Marry me. Direct and heartfelt, for a partner.
Will you marry me? The most common proposal question.
Please marry me. Polite and earnest, often used in public proposals.
Would you marry me? Very respectful and gentle.
Let's get married. Simple and confident.

examples.context: Proposing with a ring
A proposal at a restaurant
A quiet talk about the future

tips: Koreans call a proposal 프러포즈 (peureopojeu), from English "propose." Many couples are already planning the wedding when it happens, so the proposal is often a surprise event rather than the first question.
줘 and 주세요 add "for me" and make the request softer, like a favor. 결혼해! on its own sounds like an order.

faq.q: How do you say will you marry me in Korean?
faq.a: Say 나랑 결혼해 줄래? (narang gyeolhonhae jullae?) casually, or 저랑 결혼해 주시겠어요? (jeowa gyeolhonhae jusigesseoyo?) politely.

faq.q: What does 결혼 mean?
faq.a: 결혼 (gyeolhon) means marriage. 결혼하다 means to get married.

intro: "Darling" in Korean is 자기야 (jagiya), the most common pet name couples use for each other. Married couples often say 여보 (yeobo) instead. In romantic writing, 내 사랑 (nae sarang), "my love," is also used.

ways.note: Darling, honey. Used by dating and married couples when calling each other.
The same word without the calling ending. Used inside a sentence, like "you" between lovers.
Honey, dear. Mainly between married couples.
My love. Romantic, often in messages and songs.
Baby. A sweet pet name some couples use. Standard spelling is 아기야, but 애기야 is common in speech.
Darling, borrowed from English. Usually said jokingly or for fun.

examples.context: Texting a partner
A wife calling her husband at lunch
A birthday message

tips: 야 is added when you call someone by name. So you call out 자기야, but inside a sentence you say 자기 (for example 자기 뭐 해?).
Don't call friends or coworkers 자기야. It is clearly romantic. Some older women use 자기 with close female friends, but learners should keep it for a partner.

faq.q: What is the difference between 자기야 and 여보?
faq.a: 자기야 is used by dating and married couples. 여보 is mainly for married couples.

faq.q: How do you say darling in Korean?
faq.a: Say 자기야 (jagiya). It is the most common pet name between couples.

intro: The most common way to say "I hate you" in Korean is 미워 (miwo), a sulky, often playful "you're so mean" that couples and friends use when teasing. To say it seriously, Koreans use 네가 싫어 (nega sireo), "I don't like you," which is hurtful. Choose carefully, because tone changes everything.

ways.note: I hate you, in a pouty way. Usually means "you're mean" and is often affectionate.
You, I hate you. The same feeling, pointing at the person.
Polite form, often used cutely, like a girlfriend to her boyfriend or a fan to an idol.
I don't like you, I hate you. Serious and hurtful. Often pronounced 니가 (niga) in speech.
I really hate it, I really hate you. Strong. Can be about a thing or a person.

examples.context: Pouting when a boyfriend teases you
When a friend eats your last snack
A serious fight

tips: 미워 comes from 밉다, "to be hateful or annoying to me." Between couples it is usually loving, like a playful pout. 네가 싫어 is different: it means you truly don't like the person and can really hurt.
증오해 (jeungohae) is a very heavy word for hatred, like "I loathe you." You hear it in dramas, but almost nobody says it in real life.
Never say these to older people or strangers. Even the playful 미워 is for people you are close to.

faq.q: What does 미워 mean?
faq.a: 미워 (miwo) means "I hate you" or "you're mean," but in a sulky, often affectionate way. It is not usually serious.

faq.q: How do you say I hate you seriously in Korean?
faq.a: 네가 싫어 (nega sireo) means "I don't like you" and is hurtful. Use it only if you really mean it.

intro: "I think of you" in Korean is 네 생각해 (ne saenggakhae), literally "I think your thought." Koreans often say 항상 네 생각해 (hangsang ne saenggakhae), "I always think of you," or 네 생각이 나 (ne saenggagi na), "you come to mind." These are casual, for partners and close friends.

ways.note: I think of you. In speech 네 is usually pronounced 니 (ni).
I always think of you. Sweet and common in messages.
You come to mind, I keep thinking of you. Often used when something reminds you of the person.
I think only of you all day. Romantic and a little dramatic.
I'm always thinking of you. Polite, good for parents or anyone older. The "you" is understood.

examples.context: Texting someone you have a crush on
examples.en: Lately I keep thinking of you.

examples.context: A love letter
examples.en: I think only of you all day.

examples.context: A message to parents far away

tips: 네 (your) and 내 (my) sound almost the same in Korean, so people say 니 생각해 to be clear. In writing, keep the correct spelling 네.
To older people, avoid 너 and 네. Leave out "you" and say 항상 생각하고 있어요, or use their title, like 엄마 생각 많이 해요 (I think of you a lot, Mom).

faq.q: How do you say I'm thinking of you in Korean?
faq.a: Say 네 생각하고 있어 (ne saenggakhago isseo) casually, or 항상 생각하고 있어요 (hangsang saenggakhago isseoyo) politely.

faq.q: Why do Koreans say 니 instead of 네?
faq.a: 네 (your) sounds almost the same as 내 (my), so in speech people say 니 to avoid confusion.

intro: "I'm excited" in Korean is 신나 (sinna), the casual way to say you feel fun, upbeat excitement. When you mean you are looking forward to something, Koreans usually say 기대돼 (gidaedwae), and for a fluttery, heart-racing kind of excitement they say 설레 (seolle).

ways.note: Fun, energetic excitement, like at a party, a concert or on a day off. Use with friends and family.
The same feeling with 요 added. Safe with coworkers, teachers and people you just met.
"I'm looking forward to it." The most natural choice for excitement about something coming up, like a trip or a new episode.
Polite version of 기대돼. Very common at work or with older people.
A fluttery, nervous-happy excitement: a first date, the night before a trip, the start of spring. The polite form is 설레요 (seolleyo).
Formal version for speeches, announcements and business messages.

examples.context: Your favorite song comes on at a party
Telling a coworker about your weekend plans
examples.en: I'm really looking forward to the concert.

examples.context: The night before a trip
examples.en: I'm excited because the trip is tomorrow.

tips: Korean splits "excited" into a few feelings. 신나다 is fun and lively, 기대되다 is looking forward to something, and 설레다 is the happy, slightly nervous flutter you get before something special. If you are excited about a future event, 기대돼 is usually the best fit.
Avoid 흥분했어 (heungbunhaesseo) for happy excitement. It means worked up or agitated, and in some contexts it has a sexual meaning, so it can sound very odd.
To say "so excited," add 너무 or 진짜 in front: 너무 신나, 진짜 기대돼. 신나 sounds like "shin-na."

faq.q: What is the difference between 신나 and 설레?
faq.a: 신나 is cheerful, energetic fun, like dancing or a day at an amusement park. 설레 is a fluttery, butterflies-in-your-stomach feeling, often about love or something new.

faq.q: How do you say "I'm so excited to see you" in Korean?
faq.a: You can say 너무 보고 싶었어 (neomu bogo sipeosseo, "I missed you so much") or 만나는 거 너무 기대돼 (mannaneun geo neomu gidaedwae, "I'm so looking forward to meeting you").

intro: "I'm busy" in Korean is 바빠 (bappa) with friends, or 바빠요 (bappayo) to be polite. It comes from the adjective 바쁘다 (bappeuda, "to be busy").

ways.note: The everyday casual form. Use with friends, siblings and people younger than you.
Polite form for coworkers, shop staff, teachers and people you don't know well.
Formal form, used in business settings or when speaking very respectfully.
"I'm a bit busy." Adding 좀 (a bit) softens it and sounds less like you are brushing someone off.
"I'm swamped" or "it's hectic." Literally "I have no mind," for when things are so busy you can't think. Polite: 정신없어요.

examples.context: Texting a friend back quickly
examples.en: I'm a bit busy right now.

examples.context: Catching up with a neighbor
Complaining to a close coworker at lunch

tips: To ask someone if they are busy, say 바빠? (bappa?) to a friend or 바쁘세요? (bappeuseyo?) to someone older or someone you respect. Koreans often ask this before calling or asking a favor.
If you need to say no to a call or plan, a gentle way is 미안, 지금 좀 바빠 (mian, jigeum jom bappa), "Sorry, I'm a bit busy right now." Without 좀 or an apology, a bare 바빠 can sound cold.
The ㅃ in 바빠 is a tense sound, a bit like a sharp "pp" with no puff of air: "ba-ppa."

faq.q: How do you ask "Are you busy?" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 바빠? (bappa?) to a friend and 바쁘세요? (bappeuseyo?) to an older person, a boss or a stranger.

faq.q: What does 정신없어 mean?
faq.a: It literally means "I have no mind or spirit," and people use it to say they are swamped, frazzled or that a place is chaotic.

intro: "I'm lonely" in Korean is 외로워 (oerowo), or 외로워요 (oerowoyo) to be polite. It comes from 외롭다 (oeropda, "to be lonely").

ways.note: The standard way to say you feel lonely. Use with friends, family or a partner.
Polite form for people you are not close to or who are older than you.
Formal form. Rare in conversation, more likely in writing or a speech.
"I'm so lonely." 너무 adds strong emotion.
A quiet, wistful, empty kind of loneliness. Often used about a mood, a season or an empty place. Polite: 쓸쓸해요.

examples.context: Opening up to a close friend
examples.en: I've been a bit lonely lately.

examples.context: Telling a relative you live alone now
examples.en: Being by myself makes me lonely.

examples.context: A caption on a quiet autumn photo
examples.en: It's fall, so I feel a little lonely.

tips: 외롭다 is the general word for lonely. 쓸쓸하다 is more about atmosphere: an empty street, a cold autumn evening, a quiet house. Both can describe how you feel.
A common joking idiom for being single and lonely is 옆구리가 시려 (yeopguriga siryeo), "my side is cold," meaning there is no one next to you.
외 sounds close to "weh," so 외로워 sounds like "weh-ro-wo."

faq.q: What is the difference between 외로워 and 쓸쓸해?
faq.a: 외로워 means you feel lonely and want company. 쓸쓸해 is a more poetic, wistful feeling and is often used for places, seasons or a gloomy mood.

faq.q: How do you say "I'm lonely without you" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 너 없으니까 외로워 (neo eopseunikka oerowo), literally "Since you're not here, I'm lonely."

intro: "I'm stressed" in Korean is 스트레스 받아 (seuteureseu bada), literally "I receive stress." Korean uses the English loanword 스트레스 with the verb 받다 (to receive), and the polite form is 스트레스 받아요 (seuteureseu badayo).

ways.note: The most common way to say you are stressed. Use with friends and family.
Polite form for coworkers, teachers or anyone older.
"I am under stress." Formal, for a work report or a doctor's appointment.
"Stress has piled up." Used when stress has built over days or weeks.
"I'm annoyed" or "this is so annoying." Not the same as stressed, but people often say it in stressful moments.
"I'm going crazy." A strong, dramatic way to say you are at your limit. Only with close friends.

examples.context: Venting to a sibling
Telling your doctor what is going on
Your computer crashes again

tips: You "receive" stress in Korean (스트레스를 받다), and you "untie" it to relieve it (스트레스를 풀다). So "Let's go to karaoke to relieve stress" is 스트레스 풀러 노래방 가자 (seuteureseu pulleo noraebang gaja).
In speech the object particle 를 is usually dropped, so 스트레스 받아 is more natural than 스트레스를 받아 in casual talk.
짜증나 means annoyed or irritated, not stressed. Use it for a moment of frustration and 스트레스 받아 for ongoing pressure.

faq.q: How do you say "stress relief" in Korean?
faq.a: 스트레스 해소 (seuteureseu haeso) is the noun, and 스트레스 풀다 (seuteureseu pulda) is the everyday verb for blowing off steam.

faq.q: Why does Korean say "receive stress"?
faq.a: That is just how the expression works: 받다 means to receive or get, and Koreans use it for stress the same way English uses "get stressed."

intro: "I'm shy" in Korean is 부끄러워 (bukkeureowo), which covers both shy and embarrassed. To describe your personality, as in "I'm a shy person," Koreans usually say 낯을 가려요 (nacheul garyeoyo), meaning you are shy around new people.

ways.note: Shy or embarrassed in the moment, like when someone teases you or stares at you.
Polite form for people you don't know well or who are older.
Bashful or awkward, especially when you get praised or have to perform. Polite: 쑥스러워요.
"I'm shy with strangers." Literally "I'm picky about faces." The usual way to describe a shy personality.
"I'm a shy person," literally "I have a lot of shyness." A gentle, slightly old-fashioned description.

examples.context: A friend shows everyone your old school photo
Introducing yourself at a new job
examples.en: I'm a bit shy with new people.

examples.context: Your teacher praises you in front of the class
examples.en: Hearing that compliment makes me shy.

tips: 부끄럽다 can mean shy, embarrassed or even ashamed, so context decides. If you did something wrong, 부끄러워 can mean "I'm ashamed."
To describe your personality, use 낯을 가리다 ("to be shy with strangers"). 저 낯 많이 가려요 (jeo nat mani garyeoyo, "I'm really shy with new people") is a very natural thing to say when meeting people.
The ㄲ in 부끄러워 is a tense "kk" sound: "boo-kkeu-reo-wo."

faq.q: How do you say "I'm a shy person" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 저는 낯을 많이 가려요 (jeoneun nacheul mani garyeoyo), "I'm very shy with new people." 저는 수줍음이 많아요 (jeoneun sujubeumi manayo) also works.

faq.q: Does 부끄러워 mean shy or embarrassed?
faq.a: Both. It describes the feeling of wanting to hide, so it fits being shy, embarrassed or, in some situations, ashamed.

intro: "I'm proud of you" in Korean is 네가 자랑스러워 (nega jarangseureowo), literally "you are a source of pride (to me)." In everyday life Koreans also show pride with simpler words like 잘했어 (jalhaesseo, "you did well").

ways.note: To a friend, partner, younger sibling or child. 네가 (you) is usually pronounced 니가 (niga) in speech.
Polite form. Koreans usually drop "you" or use the person's title instead, as in 엄마가 자랑스러워요 ("I'm proud of you, Mom").
Formal form for speeches, ceremonies and award messages.
"You did well." The everyday way to praise someone after an achievement. Polite: 잘했어요.
"I'm so proud of you (you've grown up so well)." Only from an older person to a younger one, like a parent to a child.

examples.context: Your best friend just graduated
A parent after a child's piano recital
Your mom finishes her first marathon

tips: The person you are proud of takes the subject marker 이/가, because 자랑스럽다 describes that person as "a pride." So it is 네가 자랑스러워, not 너를 자랑스러워.
The full phrase 자랑스러워 can feel big and emotional in Korean. In daily life, parents, teachers and friends more often say 잘했어 ("you did well") or 수고했어 ("you worked hard").
대견하다 is only used from older to younger. Saying 대견해요 to your boss or parent would sound like you are talking down to them.

faq.q: Can I say "I'm proud of you" to my parents in Korean?
faq.a: Yes. Use the polite form with their title, like 엄마가 자랑스러워요 or 아빠가 자랑스러워요. Avoid 대견해, which is for younger people.

faq.q: What does 대견해 mean?
faq.a: It means you are proud of and touched by how well a younger person has done or grown up. Parents and grandparents often say it to children.

intro: "I feel better" in Korean is 좀 나아졌어 (jom naajyeosseo), "I've gotten a bit better," or 많이 좋아졌어요 (mani joajyeosseoyo) to be polite. For your mood rather than your health, say 기분이 좋아졌어 (gibuni joajyeosseo).

ways.note: "I'm a bit better." Used after being sick or upset. 나아지다 means to get better.
"I'm much better." A very common polite answer when someone asks about your health.
"My mood got better." Use this for feelings, not illness.
"I'm okay now." Simple and reassuring for any situation.
"I have improved a lot." Formal, for a boss or a work message after sick leave.

examples.context: Texting a friend who asked about your cold
examples.en: I took some medicine and feel a bit better.

examples.context: Thanking a coworker who covered for you
examples.en: I'm much better, thanks to you.

examples.context: After a good cry with a friend

tips: Korean separates body and mood. For illness, use 나아졌어 or 좋아졌어. For emotions, add 기분이 ("my mood"): 기분이 좋아졌어 or 기분이 나아졌어.
나았어 (naasseo) means "I've recovered," as in fully healed: 감기 다 나았어 ("my cold is all gone"). 나아졌어 means "I've gotten better," which is safer if you are still a little sick.
Koreans often add 덕분에 ("thanks to you") when someone has helped or checked on them. It sounds warm and grateful.

faq.q: How do you ask "Do you feel better?" in Korean?
faq.a: Ask a friend 좀 나아졌어? (jom naajyeosseo?). To someone older, say 몸은 좀 괜찮으세요? (momeun jom gwaenchaneuseyo?), "Are you feeling okay now?"

faq.q: What is the difference between 나았어 and 나아졌어?
faq.a: 나았어 means you have recovered completely. 나아졌어 means you are getting better but may not be fully well yet.

intro: "I'm worried" in Korean is 걱정돼 (geokjeongdwae), or 걱정돼요 (geokjeongdwaeyo) to be polite. To say who or what you are worried about, put it first with 이/가: 네가 걱정돼 (nega geokjeongdwae), "I'm worried about you."

ways.note: The standard way to say you are worried. Use with friends, family and partners.
Polite form for coworkers, teachers and older people.
Formal form, for business messages, news interviews or speeches.
"I feel anxious" or "I feel uneasy." Less about a specific worry and more about a restless feeling. Polite: 불안해요.
"It's bothering me" or "it's on my mind." For a small worry you can't stop thinking about.

examples.context: Your friend hasn't been eating well
Talking to a teacher before finals
Waiting for a big job interview

tips: When someone gets home late or doesn't answer the phone, Koreans often say 걱정했잖아 (geokjeonghaetjana), "I was worried, you know!" It shows care, even if it sounds like scolding.
To tell someone not to worry, say 걱정하지 마 (geokjeonghaji ma) to a friend, or 걱정하지 마세요 (geokjeonghaji maseyo) politely.
걱정 sounds like "geok-jjeong": the ㅈ after ㄱ becomes tense.

faq.q: How do you say "I was worried about you" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 걱정했어 (geokjeonghaesseo) to a friend or 걱정했어요 (geokjeonghaesseoyo) politely. You can add 네가 or the person's name before it.

faq.q: What is the difference between 걱정돼 and 불안해?
faq.a: 걱정돼 is worry about something specific, like a person or an exam. 불안해 is a general feeling of anxiety or unease.

intro: "I'm jealous" in Korean is 질투 나 (jiltu na) when you mean real jealousy, like in love or rivalry. When you mean "I envy you," as in "you're going to Jeju? I'm so jealous," Koreans say 부러워 (bureowo).

ways.note: Jealousy, especially in relationships. Literally "jealousy comes out." Often written 질투나 in texts.
Polite form of 질투 나.
"I envy you." Used lightly and very often, for someone's trip, new phone or good news.
Polite form of 부러워, safe with coworkers and older people.
Formal form, sometimes used jokingly among friends for extra drama.
A soft, slightly cute word for feeling envious or a little jealous, often used about friends or siblings.

examples.context: Your partner keeps talking about an ex
A coworker says she is going to Jeju Island
A friend texts you a vacation photo

tips: Use 질투 for romantic jealousy or rivalry, and 부러워 for everyday envy. Saying 질투 나 about a friend's vacation can sound more intense than you mean.
질투해? (jiltuhae?), "Are you jealous?", is a classic teasing line between couples. 질투하지 마 (jiltuhaji ma) means "Don't be jealous."
부러워 sounds like "boo-reo-wo." A cheerful 와, 부럽다! (wa, bureopda!) is a very natural reaction to good news.

faq.q: How do you say "Are you jealous?" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 질투해? (jiltuhae?) or 질투 나? (jiltu na?). Both are casual and often used playfully.

faq.q: What is the difference between 질투 나 and 부러워?
faq.a: 질투 나 is jealousy, often about a partner or a rival. 부러워 is envy, wishing you had what someone else has, and it is light and friendly.

intro: "Whatever" in Korean is 아무거나 (amugeona) when you mean "anything is fine," like when choosing food. For the dismissive, eye-rolling "whatever," Koreans say 됐어 (dwaesseo) or 몰라 (molla).

ways.note: "Anything" or "whatever." Use when choosing food, a movie or a place.
"Anything is fine." A polite answer when a boss or older person asks what you want.
"Forget it" or "whatever." Said sharply, it ends a conversation and can sound annoyed.
"I don't know" or "I don't care." Said with a shrug, it works like a dismissive "whatever."
"So what?" Rude and confrontational. Only between close friends as a joke, if at all.

examples.context: A senior coworker asks what you want for lunch
Friends can't decide on dinner
Ending an argument with a sibling

tips: Korean has no single word that covers both meanings of "whatever." 아무거나 is friendly and neutral. 됐어 and 몰라 carry attitude, and the tone of your voice does most of the work.
어쩌라고 is rude. Young people sometimes use the playful slang 어쩔티비 instead, but it is still teasing, so save it for close friends.
With elders, don't just say 아무거나. Add 괜찮아요 or say 저는 다 좋아요 (jeoneun da joayo, "Everything is good for me").

faq.q: How do you say "whatever you want" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 너 하고 싶은 대로 해 (neo hago sipeun daero hae) to a friend, or 원하시는 대로 하세요 (wonhasineun daero haseyo) politely.

faq.q: Is 어쩌라고 rude?
faq.a: Yes. It means "So what do you want me to do about it?" and sounds dismissive and confrontational.

intro: "Never mind" in Korean is usually 아니야 (aniya), literally "no, it's not," said when you take back what you were going to say. Politely, say 아니에요 (anieyo), and to tell someone not to worry about something, say 신경 쓰지 마 (singyeong sseuji ma).

ways.note: "Never mind" or "it's nothing." The most natural way to drop a question or comment.
Polite form, for coworkers, teachers and older people.
"It's nothing." A fuller version when someone asks what you were about to say.
"Forget it." Can sound curt or annoyed, so watch your tone.
"Don't worry about it" or "don't mind it." Literally "don't use your nerves on it."
Polite form of 신경 쓰지 마.

examples.context: You start a question, then remember the answer
A coworker asks what you were about to say
A friend apologizes for forgetting your text
examples.en: Never mind, don't worry about it.

tips: Korean has no fixed phrase for "never mind." The most common choice is a quick 아, 아니야, often with a little laugh.
됐어 can be kind ("no need, it's fine") or cold ("forget it"). If you sound irritated, the other person will hear it as cold.
With older people, 아니에요, 괜찮아요 (anieyo, gwaenchanayo), "No, it's fine," is a gentle and safe way to say never mind.

faq.q: Is 됐어 rude?
faq.a: It depends on tone. Said softly it means "it's fine, no need," but said sharply it means "forget it" and can sound upset.

faq.q: How do you say "never mind" politely in Korean?
faq.a: Say 아니에요 (anieyo) or 아니에요, 괜찮아요 (anieyo, gwaenchanayo), "No, it's fine."

intro: "No problem" in Korean is 문제없어 (munje-eopseo) when you agree to do something, or 문제없어요 (munje-eopseoyo) to be polite. When someone thanks you, Koreans usually answer 괜찮아요 (gwaenchanayo) or 아니에요 (anieyo) instead.

ways.note: "No problem, I can do that." Use with friends when agreeing to a request.
Polite form for coworkers and people you don't know well.
Formal form, common at work when a boss or client asks if something is possible.
"It's fine, don't worry." Use when a friend thanks you or apologizes.
Polite form. A very natural reply to thank-yous and small apologies.
"Of course!" A warm, polite way to agree to a request.

examples.context: A friend asks you to pick them up
Your manager asks if you can finish by Friday
Someone thanks you for holding the door

tips: 문제없어 means "I can handle it." It is not the usual reply to "thank you." For that, Koreans say 아니에요, 괜찮아요 or 별말씀을요 (a polite "don't mention it").
In writing 문제없다 is one word with no space, though you will often see 문제 없어 in casual texts.
Romanizations online vary (munje eopseo, munjeeopseo). It sounds like "moon-jeh up-suh."

faq.q: How do you reply "no problem" to 감사합니다?
faq.a: Say 아니에요 (anieyo) or 괜찮아요 (gwaenchanayo). 문제없어요 sounds odd as a reply to thanks.

faq.q: Is 문제없어 polite?
faq.a: No, it is casual. Add 요 for 문제없어요, or use 문제없습니다 in formal situations.

intro: "Cool" in Korean is 멋있어 (meosisseo) when you mean something or someone looks awesome. For cool weather or a refreshing feeling, the word is 시원해 (siwonhae), and for "cool, sounds good," Koreans just say 좋아 (joa).

ways.note: "That's cool" or "you look cool." For people, outfits, performances and things that impress you.
Polite form, for compliments to people you don't know well.
Very close to 멋있어, often a bit more excited. Polite: 멋져요.
Slang for "the best" or "awesome." Playful and friendly.
Cool in temperature: a breeze, a cold drink, air conditioning. Also "refreshing." Polite: 시원해요.
"Cool, sounds good." Use to agree to a plan.

examples.context: A friend shows you their new jacket
Walking by the river on a summer evening
examples.en: The breeze is nice and cool.

examples.context: Confirming weekend plans

tips: 멋있다 is about style and impressiveness. To call a man handsome and cool you might say 멋있어 or 잘생겼어; 멋있어 also works for women, places and performances.
시원하다 is about a refreshing feeling. Koreans even say it about hot, spicy soup that makes you feel good, which surprises many learners.
There is also the loanword 쿨하다 (kulhada), which describes an easygoing person who doesn't hold grudges, as in 쿨하네 (kulhane), "You're so chill."

faq.q: How do you say "cool" as in the weather?
faq.a: Use 시원해 (siwonhae) for pleasantly cool weather. For chilly, slightly cold weather, use 쌀쌀해 (ssalssalhae).

faq.q: What does 쿨하다 mean?
faq.a: It is a loanword from English "cool" and describes someone relaxed and easygoing, who doesn't fuss or hold grudges.

intro: "Go away" in Korean is 저리 가 (jeori ga), literally "go over there." It is casual and fairly mild, and between friends or siblings it is often playful, but said seriously it is blunt.

ways.note: The mildest common way. Kids and siblings say it all the time, often jokingly.
Polite grammar, but still a blunt request. Use only when you really need someone to leave.
"I want to be alone." A softer, kinder way to ask for space.
"Get out." Used for a room or space, and sounds angry.
"Get lost." Very rude and hurtful. Avoid it with anyone you care about.

examples.context: Your little brother keeps teasing you
After a bad day, to a roommate
Arguing with a sibling

tips: 꺼져 is one of the harshest things you can say to someone's face. It is not a swear word, but it is insulting and can end a friendship.
If a stranger is bothering you, a firm but polite option is 저 좀 내버려 두세요 (jeo jom naebeoryeo duseyo), "Please leave me alone."
저리 가 with a laugh or a whiny tone is affectionate, much like "go away" between friends in English. Tone makes all the difference.

faq.q: Is 꺼져 a swear word?
faq.a: Not technically, but it is very rude, like "get lost" said with anger. It is much stronger than 저리 가.

faq.q: How do you say "leave me alone" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 내버려 둬 (naebeoryeo dwo) casually, or 내버려 두세요 (naebeoryeo duseyo) politely. 혼자 있고 싶어 ("I want to be alone") is gentler.

intro: "Come here" in Korean is 이리 와 (iri wa), the casual way you'd call a friend, a child or a pet. To someone older or a stranger, say 이리 오세요 (iri oseyo) or the even more polite 이쪽으로 오세요 (ijjogeuro oseyo), "please come this way."

ways.note: The standard casual "come here." Used with friends, kids, partners and pets.
Polite form for people you don't know well or older people.
"Please come this way." What staff say when guiding you. Very polite and soft.
"Come here (and see)." Used when you want to show someone something.
A relaxed spoken form of 이리로 와. Very casual, common among friends and family.
"Come over here." Points to a specific spot.

examples.context: Comforting a crying child
examples.en: Come here, let me give you a hug.

examples.context: Showing a friend something on your phone
Restaurant staff guiding you to a table

tips: 와 comes from 오다 (to come). 이리 means "this way" or "here," so 이리 와 is literally "come this way."
Koreans call dogs and cats with 이리 와 too, often in a sing-song voice: 이리 와, 이리 와!
With elders, a bare 이리 오세요 can still feel like an order. Staff and polite speakers prefer 이쪽으로 오세요 or 이쪽으로 오시겠어요? (ijjogeuro osigesseoyo?)

faq.q: How do you say "come here" to a dog in Korean?
faq.a: Say 이리 와 (iri wa). Many people repeat it in a cheerful voice, sometimes with the dog's name first.

faq.q: Is 오세요 polite enough for older people?
faq.a: Yes, 이리 오세요 is polite. 이쪽으로 오세요 sounds even softer and is what you hear in shops and restaurants.

intro: "Stop" in Korean is 그만해 (geumanhae), "stop it," when someone keeps doing something. Politely, say 그만하세요 (geumanhaseyo), and for "don't do that," say 하지 마 (haji ma).

ways.note: "Stop it" or "that's enough." For something already happening, like teasing or nagging.
Polite form. Still firm, so it can sound stern with strangers.
"Don't (do it)." To stop someone before or while they do something.
Polite form of 하지 마. You will see it on signs too.
"Stop!" as in stop moving. For physical motion, like a running child or a car.
"Enough!" A short, sharp word on its own.

examples.context: Your friend keeps tickling you
Asking someone to stop kicking your seat
Your dog runs toward the road

tips: 그만해 stops an action that is already going on. 하지 마 means "don't do it" and can stop something before it starts. 멈춰 is for stopping movement.
Stop signs in Korea say 정지 (jeongji), which means "stop" or "halt."
To soften a request to a stranger, add 좀 and a request ending: 좀 그만해 주세요 (jom geumanhae juseyo), "Could you please stop?"

faq.q: What do stop signs say in Korean?
faq.a: They say 정지 (jeongji), the formal word for stop.

faq.q: Is 하지 마 rude?
faq.a: It is casual, so it is fine with friends and family. With strangers or older people, say 하지 마세요.

answer.en: I don't care / it doesn't matter

intro: "I don't care" in Korean is 상관없어 (sanggwaneopseo), which means "it doesn't matter (to me)" and is usually not rude. For a colder "I don't care," Koreans say 신경 안 써 (singyeong an sseo).

ways.note: "It doesn't matter" or "I don't mind." Friendly and neutral, great for choices.
Polite form, safe with anyone.
"I don't care" or "I don't pay attention to it." Can sound confident or cold depending on tone.
"I'm not interested." Blunt, and can hurt if said about someone's hobby or feelings.
"None of my business" or "not my problem." Rude and dismissive.

examples.context: A friend asks if you want pizza or chicken
Wearing a bold outfit to school
examples.en: I don't care what other people think.

examples.context: Brushing off celebrity gossip
examples.en: I'm not interested in that kind of thing.

tips: 상관없어 is the friendliest choice. When someone asks what you prefer, it simply means "either is fine." Politely, 저는 상관없어요 (jeoneun sanggwaneopseoyo).
알 바 아니야 is hurtful when said to someone who shares a problem with you. It means "that's not my concern."
Be careful with 관심 없어 in dating. Said about a person, it is a clear and blunt rejection.

faq.q: Is 상관없어 rude?
faq.a: No. It usually means "it doesn't matter to me" and is a normal, friendly answer. Only a cold tone makes it sound dismissive.

faq.q: How do you say "I don't care what you think" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 네가 뭐라고 생각하든 상관없어 (nega mworago saenggakhadeun sanggwaneopseo). It is strong, so use it only when you really mean it.

intro: "Good" in Korean is 좋아 (joa), from the adjective 좋다 (jota, "to be good"). Politely, say 좋아요 (joayo), and before a noun, as in "good morning," use 좋은 (joeun).

ways.note: "Good" or "I like it." Also used to agree: "Good, let's do it."
Polite form, used everywhere. On social media, a "like" is also called 좋아요.
Formal form, for business, announcements or sounding very respectful.
The form that goes before a noun: 좋은 사람 (a good person), 좋은 아침 (good morning).
The dictionary form. Also said on its own as an exclamation: "Nice!"
"Good job" or "well done." Use this for praising someone, not 좋아.

examples.context: Stepping outside on a sunny day
Recommending something at a shop
Greeting your roommate

tips: 좋아 means both "it's good" and "I like it." To say you like a person, use 좋아해 (joahae), which comes from the related verb 좋아하다.
For food, Koreans say 맛있어 (masisseo, "delicious") rather than 좋아. For feeling good, say 기분 좋아 (gibun joa).
The ㅎ in 좋 is silent before a vowel, so 좋아 sounds like "jo-a." Before ㄷ it makes a strong "t" sound, so 좋다 sounds like "jo-ta."

faq.q: How do you say "very good" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 정말 좋아요 (jeongmal joayo) or 아주 좋아요 (aju joayo). Casually, 너무 좋아 (neomu joa).

faq.q: How do you say "I'm good" (I'm fine) in Korean?
faq.a: Say 괜찮아요 (gwaenchanayo) or, when asked how you have been, 잘 지내요 (jal jinaeyo).

intro: "Bad" in Korean is 나빠 (nappa), from the adjective 나쁘다 (nappeuda, "to be bad"). In everyday talk, Koreans often soften it to 안 좋아 (an joa, "not good") or 별로야 (byeolloya, "not great").

ways.note: "Bad." Said about a person, it means mean or unkind.
Polite form of 나빠.
The form before a noun: 나쁜 사람 (a bad person), 나쁜 날씨 (bad weather).
"Not good." Softer and very common for weather, health, mood and situations.
Polite form of 안 좋아.
"It's not great" or "meh." A gentle way to say you didn't like something. Polite: 별로예요.

examples.context: Texting a friend after a rough day
A friend eats your last snack, and you tease them
A friend asks if a movie is worth watching

tips: Calling a person 나빠 means they are mean or unfair. It is common in teasing between friends and couples, but said seriously it is a real accusation.
Koreans often avoid a direct 나빠 for things and use 안 좋아 or 별로 instead. For example, bad weather is usually 날씨가 안 좋아 (nalssiga an joa).
The ㅃ in 나빠 is a tense "pp" sound: "na-ppa." 나쁘지 않아 (nappeuji ana) means "not bad."

faq.q: How do you say "not bad" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 나쁘지 않아 (nappeuji ana) casually or 나쁘지 않아요 (nappeuji anayo) politely. 괜찮네 (gwaenchanne, "it's decent") is also common.

faq.q: What does 나쁜 남자 mean?
faq.a: It literally means "bad man" and is used for the cold, rebellious "bad boy" type, a common character in romance stories.

intro: "Aunt" in Korean is 이모 (imo) when you mean your mom's sister, and 고모 (gomo) when you mean your dad's sister. Korean has no single word for "aunt": the word changes depending on which side of the family she is on and whether she is a blood relative or married in.

ways.note: Your mother's sister. The warmest and most commonly heard aunt word. Kids also call their mom's close female friends 이모.
Your father's sister.
The wife of your mother's brother (your 외삼촌).
The wife of your father's younger brother, also called 숙모 (sungmo). The wife of your father's older brother is 큰어머니 (keun-eomeoni).
A more respectful 이모. Also a common, friendly way to call an older woman working at a restaurant or helping in a home.

examples.context: Texting your mom's sister
Talking about your dad's sister
Thanking family for a gift

tips: Before you pick a word, ask two questions: is she on your mom's side or your dad's side, and is she related by blood or by marriage? Mom's sister is 이모, dad's sister is 고모, mom's brother's wife is 외숙모, and dad's brothers' wives are 큰어머니 or 작은어머니.
이모 is also used outside the family. Children call their mom's friends 이모, and many people call a friendly older woman at a restaurant 이모 or 이모님. It sounds warm and familiar, not rude.
The husbands of aunts have their own words too: 이모부 (imobu) for your 이모's husband and 고모부 (gomobu) for your 고모's husband.

faq.q: What is the difference between 이모 and 고모?
faq.a: 이모 is your mother's sister and 고모 is your father's sister. Koreans always use the specific word, so it helps to know which side of the family she is on.

faq.q: Why do people call restaurant workers 이모?
faq.a: It is a friendly, familiar way to address an older woman, a bit like calling her "auntie." 이모님 is a slightly more polite version.

intro: "Uncle" in Korean is 삼촌 (samchon), the everyday word for your parent's brother. Like aunts, uncles have more specific names depending on which side of the family they are on and their age, such as 외삼촌 (oesamchon) for your mom's brother.

ways.note: The general, familiar word for uncle. Traditionally it is used for your father's younger brother before he marries, but kids use it for almost any uncle.
Your mother's brother. 외 (oe) marks the mother's side of the family.
Your father's older brother. Literally "big father."
Your father's younger brother once he is married. Literally "small father."
The husband of your mother's sister (이모).
The husband of your father's sister (고모).

examples.context: Asking when your uncle will visit
Talking about your mom's brother
Holiday plans
examples.en: We're going to my uncle's house.

tips: 삼촌 is the word you will hear most in dramas and daily life, especially from children. Adults talking precisely about family will say 외삼촌, 큰아버지 or 작은아버지 instead.
Do not confuse 삼촌 with 아저씨 (ajeossi). 아저씨 is for a middle-aged man who is not family, like a shopkeeper or a stranger. Young people sometimes call a friendly older man 삼촌 to sound closer and warmer.

삼촌 comes from 촌수 (chonsu), the Korean system of counting family distance. Your parent's sibling is three "chon" away from you, so 삼촌 literally means "three chon." That is also why a cousin is 사촌, "four chon."

faq.q: What is the difference between 삼촌 and 외삼촌?
faq.a: 외삼촌 is specifically your mother's brother. 삼촌 is the general word and traditionally means your father's younger brother, though many people use it loosely for both.

faq.q: Is 아저씨 the same as uncle?
faq.a: No. 아저씨 is for an adult man you are not related to, like "mister." For a real uncle, use 삼촌 or one of the specific family words.

intro: "Son" in Korean is 아들 (adeul). When talking about someone else's son politely, Koreans use the honorific 아드님 (adeunim), and parents often say 우리 아들 (uri adeul), "my son," with a lot of affection.

ways.note: The basic word for son. Use it for your own son or when talking about sons in general.
The honorific form, for someone else's son. Use it when asking a parent about their child politely.
"My son." Parents also call their son this directly, like "my boy." Koreans say 우리 (our) instead of 내 (my) for family.
The eldest son. Traditionally carries extra family responsibility.
An only son.

examples.context: A proud parent
Asking another parent politely
Introducing your family

tips: Never call someone else's son 아들 when talking to their parent in a polite setting. Use 아드님. Using the plain word can sound like you are not showing respect to the family.
Korean parents often call their son 아들 directly, as a name. A text like 아들 밥 먹었어? (Son, did you eat?) is very typical from a Korean mom.
Pronounce 아들 as two clear syllables, a-deul. The ㄹ at the end is a light "l" sound.

faq.q: How do you say "my son" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 우리 아들 (uri adeul). It is the natural way, and it sounds loving. 내 아들 (nae adeul) is grammatical but sounds more dramatic or possessive.

faq.q: What is 아드님?
faq.a: It is the honorific word for son. Use it when talking about another person's son to show respect.

intro: "Daughter" in Korean is 딸 (ttal). For someone else's daughter, the polite honorific is 따님 (ttanim), and parents lovingly say 우리 딸 (uri ttal), "my daughter."

ways.note: The basic word for daughter.
The honorific form, for someone else's daughter. Note the spelling change: 딸 loses its ㄹ.
"My daughter." Parents also call their daughter this directly as a sweet nickname.
The eldest daughter.
The youngest daughter. 막내 means the youngest in a family or group.
An only daughter, an only child who is a girl.

examples.context: A parent's goodnight text
Complimenting someone's child
Talking about your family

tips: 딸 starts with a tense ㄸ sound. Say it sharply, with no puff of air: closer to "ddal" than "tal." Romanized as ttal.
When you talk to a parent about their child, use 따님 for a daughter and 아드님 for a son. Saying plain 딸 about someone else's child in a polite conversation can sound too casual.
Korean dads with daughters are sometimes called 딸바보 (ttalbabo), "daughter fool," meaning a dad who absolutely adores his daughter. It is a compliment.

faq.q: How do you say "my daughter" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 우리 딸 (uri ttal). Koreans use 우리 (our) for family members, and it sounds warm and natural.

faq.q: What does 딸바보 mean?
faq.a: It means a dad who dotes on his daughter, literally a "daughter fool." People use it fondly.

intro: "Husband" in Korean is 남편 (nampyeon). That is the word for talking about a husband, but wives rarely call their husband 남편 to his face; instead they say 여보 (yeobo) or 자기야 (jagiya), both like "honey."

ways.note: The standard word for husband, used when talking about him: 제 남편 (my husband).
What married couples call each other, like "honey" or "dear." Used by both husbands and wives.
"Babe" or "honey." Popular with younger couples, married or dating.
Literally "groom." Many wives use it casually to mean their husband, especially when newly married. Pronounced sil-lang.
A polite way to say someone else's husband. 분 adds respect.

examples.context: Talking about your husband
examples.en: My husband is a good cook.

examples.context: Calling your husband
Asking about someone's husband

tips: Many young Korean wives call their husband 오빠 (oppa), the word for an older brother, because they started using it while dating. You will hear this a lot in dramas.
